full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Delwar Hossain, J:- This Rule upon an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure was issued on 1.12.2001 calling upon the opposite party No. 1 at the risk of the petitioner to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 20.6.2001 of the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chandpur in Title Appeal No. 32 of 1998 affirming those dated 26.2.1998 of the Assistant Judge, Shaharasti, Chandpur in Title Suit No. 17 of 1997 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration of title by adverse possession in the suit land as described in the schedule to the plaint. 

3. The plaintiff's case, in short, was that the suit land measuring 0.25 acres out of 1.35 acres of plot No. 609 Khatian No. 56 appertaining to mouza Sengaon within police station Shaharasti, Chandpur originally belonged to Chandra Kumar Sutradhar who died leaving one daughter-Ditiya Sundari. The defendant No. 1 claiming reversionary heir of his maternal grandfather proposed to sell the suit land to the plaintiff. On 22 Agrohayan, 1380 B.S. corresponding to 6.12.1973 a meeting was held in presence of Joydep Chandra Sutradhar, Profulla Chandra Sutradhar and Arun Chandra Sutradhar in the house of the plaintiff where the consideration money for the suit land was fixed at Tk. 6,000/-. Out of the said consideration money plaintiff paid an amount of Tk. 5,000/- to the defendant No. 1 as earnest money on 10.12.1973 on execution of an agreement. Defendant No. 1 accordingly delivered possession of the suit land to the plaintiff on the same date and since then he had possessed the suit land. The plaintiff on several occasions requested the defendant No. 1 to execute and register the sale deed pursuant to the agreement for sale dated 10.12.1973 on acceptance of the balance consideration money of Tk. 1,000/, Without executing and registering the sale deed for the suit land in favour of the plaintiff, the defendant No. 1 with his lathials on 6.10.75 made an attempt to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land forcibly but failed due to resistance put by the plaintiff. The plaintiff had been possessing the suit land for more than 12 years and thus he acquired right, title and interest in the suit land by adverse possession. As plaintiff's title in the suit land clouded he instituted the suit on 30.6.1997. 

4. The opposite party No. 3 as defendant No. 3 contested the suit by filing a written statement and denying the material averments made in the plaint contended that the suit land belonged to Chandra Kumar Sutradhar who died issueless and leaving wife Suvadhra Sundari Sutradhar and S.A. Khatian was correctly prepared in her name and she sold the suit land along with other lands by a sale deed dated 24.6.1974 to the defendant No. 1 for legal necessity of performing religious ceremonie for salvation of soul of her late husband. She delivered possession of the land sold to the defendant No. 3 whereon he constructed house and planted trees and had been residing therein. During Survey operation the draft Khatian was prepared in his name. The defendant No.1 left for India where he had been residing. He thus prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

5. Upon the pleadings of the respective parties trial Court framed the following issues: 

1. Whether the suit was maintainable in its present form and manner?
2. Whether the suit was barred by limitation? 
3. Whether the suit was bad for defect of party? 
4. Whether the plaintiff acquired right, title and interest in the suit land by adverse possession? 
5. Whether the plaintiff was entitled to decree of declaration of title in the suit land as prayed for? 

6. Plaintiff to substantiate his case examined 3 P.Ws while the defendant No.3 D.Ws. Both the parties adduced documentary evidence which were duly marked exhibits. 

7. Trial Court upon hearing the parties and perusing the evidence on record by its judgment and decree dated 26.2.1998 (decree drawn on 1.3.1998) dismissed the suit. Against which the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No.32 of 1998 before the District Judge, Chandpur which ultimately was heard and disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge, second Court, Chandpur and upon hearing the parties and perusing the evidence by his judgment and decree dated 20.6.2001 (decree drawn on 27.6.2001) dismissed the appeal affirming those of passed by the trial Court. 

8. The plaintiff being dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree passed by the Appellate Court affirming those of passed by the trial Court moved this Court with this civil revision application and obtained the Rule. 

9. Mr. S.N. Goswami, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner assailing the judgments and decrease, passed by the - Courts below submits that plaintiff acquired right, title and interest in the suit land by adverse possession as he had been possessing the suit land since 10.12.1973 pursuant to agreement for sale of the suit land. He submits that plaintiff could prove his possession in the suit land by adducing sufficient evidence. He next submits that the plaintiff was threatened to dispossess from the suit land on 6.12.1975 by the defendant No. 1. He instituted the suit on 30.6.1997 and thus he acquired valid title by adverse possession in the suit land since he has possessed since 10.12.1973, that is, more than 12 years. He also submits that the cause of action for institution of the suit has to be gathered from the averments made in the plaint as a whole. He thus submits that both the Courts below misreading and on non-consideration of evidence on record dismissed the suit and those should be set aside making the Rule absolute. In support of his submissions the learned Advocate referred to the decisions in the case of Mr Laik Ali Vs. Standard Vacuum Oil Company (ESSO) and another, reported in 16 DLR (SC) 287, Md. Ashraf Ali and another Vs. Fatigue Chandra Saha and others, reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 315, Amir Hossain Khairati being dead his heirs Vs. 'Abdul Aziz Bepari and others, reported in 47 DLR (AD) 106 and Shahani Bibi being dead her heirs Mohammad Azim and others Vs. Nur Islam being dead his heirs Doly Islam and others, reported in 7 BLT 164. 

10. Mr. A.B. Roy Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 3, Shubal Chandra Sutradhar supporting the judgments and decrees submits that the plaintiff claimed that he entered into possession of the suit land on 10.12.1973 pursuant to the alleged agreement for sale of the suit land. He submits that the alleged threat of dispossession was made on 6.10.1987 and the suit was ' filed on 30.6.1997, that is, less than 10 years. So, he submits that the claim of the plaintiffs acquiring title in the suit land by adverse possession falls through. He next submits that the plaintiff did not disclose in the plaint as to when the cause of action for institution of the suit arose and for non-discloser of the cause of action the suit must fail. He further submits that the concurrent of finding of facts arrived at the by the Courts below should not be disturbed by this Court in its revisions jurisdiction. He finally submits that the appellate Court below did not commit error of law in dismissing the appeal affirming those of passed by the trial Court resulting in an error occasioning failure of justice and hence the Rule should be discharged. 

11. I have heard the learned Advocates at length and perused the civil revision application along with the judgments and decrees passed by the courts below and the evidence from the lower Court's records.  

12. In this Rule this Court is called upon to resolve whether the plaintiff could prove by cogent evidence that he acquired title in the suit land by adverse possession. 
13. The plaintiff to prove his case examined 3 PWs including himself as PW 1. In his evidence he stated “নালিশী ভূমি বায়না থেকে আজ পয্যন্ত আমি ভোগ দখল করে আসছি। PW 2 in his evidence sated নালিশী জায়গা বাদী ভোগ দখল করে। PW 3 in his evidence stated, “বায়না হয় ৬.১২.১৯৭৩ তারিখে দখল দেয় ঐ বায়নার দিনেই। দখল দেবার সময় আমি ছিলাম। The defendant’s witness DW 3 in his evidence supporting the possession of the plaintiff stated “বাদীর জায়গাতেই বাদীর বসত ঘর আছে। বাদী এই জায়গার মালিক কিভাবে হয়-বলতে পারব না।” 

14. From the evidence of P.Ws I to 3 and D.W 3 it appears that plaintiff had/has been possessing the suit land from the date of agreement for sale dated 10.12.1973. Prior to that on 6.12.1973 a talk was held for sale of the suit land and the agreement for sale was executed on 10.12.1973, exhibit-1. So, the plaintiff could prove his possession in the suit land from the date of agreement for sale on 10.12.1973. 

In the case reported in 16 DLR (SC) 287 their Lordships held as under: 

"When there is an invalid transfer in favour of a person and he holds possession of the property transferred as transferee, his possession is in his own right and adverse to the transferor. If he continues in possession of immovable property for more than twelve years he will acquire an indefeasible title." 

In the case in hand the plaintiffs claim of adverse possession against the real owner, the defendant No. 1 who did not contest the suit denying the plaintiff's claim, on the basis of an agreement for sale dated 10.12.1973, exhibit-I and since then he had/has been possessing the suit land for more than statutory period of twelve years adversely. 

In the case reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 315 their Lordships of the Appellate Division held as under: 

In this case plaintiff’s claim is against Jotis Chandra Mukharjee the real owner on the basis of Baina patra and they possessed the land on their right for more than the statutory period adversely against him and have perfected their title by such possession against him. 

15. In the case in hand also the plaintiff had/has been possessing the suit land on the basis of the bainapatra dated 10.12.1973, exhibit-1, executed by its real owner, the defendant No. 1, Nirmal Chandra Satradhar adversely for more than statutory period of 12 years since 10.12.1973 and thus perfected his title against the defendant No. 1 by such possession. 

Further it appears that both the Courts below concurrently found that the defendant No. 3 could not establish his title in the suit land. Of course the plaintiff will not get any benefit for the defect of the defendant No.3. 

16. So far as to cause of action it is a settled proposition of law that cause of action has to be ascertained on consideration of the plaint case as well as the materials on record. In the case reported in 47 DLR (AD) 106 their lordships of the Appellate Division has held as under: 
"Cause of action may be defined as every fact which it would be necessary for the plaintiff to prove, if traversed, in order to support his right for the judgment of the Court. In the case reported in 7 BLT 164 their Lordships of the High Court Division while dealing with the cause of action held as under: 

"Cause of action cannot be construed in an isolated way and the whole averments made in the plaint are to be seen and taken together to see whether any cause of action has been disclosed or not. It is the plaint as a whole is to be construed and not the terminology or for that matter, a few stray references. 

On a careful reading of the plaint as a Whole it appears that the plaintiff has disclosed the  cause of action for institution of the present suit for declaration of his title in the suit land by adverse possession. 

17. It is a settled proposition of law that a concurrent finding of fact should not be disturbed by the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction. In the case of Md. Nurul Islam and others Vs. Sree Nipendra Pathak and others, reported in 6 BLT (AD) 163 their lordships of the Appellate Division held as under: 

"It is no doubt true that findings of fact, whether concurrent or not are not ordinarily disturbed by the High Court Division in revision. But where there is a misreading of evidence or non-consideration of material evidence affecting the merit of the case the High Court Division can review the evidence and correct the error in exercise of its revisional powers." 

18. As I have already found that both the Courts below misreading and on non- consideration of the material evidence held that the plaintiff failed to prove his possession in the suit land which are contrary to evidence and dismissed the suit illegally which cannot be sustained in law.  

19. For the discussion made above I am of the view that the plaintiff could well prove his title by adverse possession in the suit land and thus the suit is liable to be decreed. 

20. In the result, the Rule is made absolute but without any Order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the Court of appeal below affirming those of passed by, the trial Court is hereby set aside and the suit is decreed declaring plaintiff's title in the suit land. 

21. Send down the lower Courts records.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Mamnoon Rahman, J:- In an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the illegal demand and extraction of Tk.60,00,00,000.00 (Sixty Crore) only from the petitioners and holding over such amount in an account maintained with Bangladesh Bank shall not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect and as to 'why the respondents shall not be directed to return/refund the said Tk.60,00,00,000.00 (Sixty Crore) only with all interest accrued thereon in favour of the petitioners and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The petitioners namely I to 7 are the companies incorporated under the law of the land and the petitioners No.8 to 10 are the Managing Director/Director of the petitioner Nos. l to 7 Companies purportedly functionless as office bearer pursuant to the Company Act of 2004. The petitioner Companies formed a group and running business with reputation and claimed to be one of the largest contributors in the revenue earning of the country. Apart from that they are also the employer of huge number of employees whose livelihood is absolutely depending upon the petitioner companies. During the period as stated in paragraph 6 of the writ petition the petitioner company's representative was called in the office of certain law enforcing agency and thereafter they were threatened of Serious consequences and asked to pay in cash to the Government an amount fixed by the authority forthwith. Following the instruction the petitioners refused to pay in any other form but in the official form by way of "Pay Order" in favour of the Government and accordingly the petitioners made payments as per paragraph 7 by Pay Orders addressed to the Government of Bangladesh. The said Pay Orders were duly encashed in favour of the Government by the Bangladesh Bank and the Bank also issued certificate to that effect. The respondents also vide Annexure-C wrote a letter to the National Board of Revenue to adjust the same in account of the VAT, Tax, duties etc. Vide Annexure-D a certain officer of respondent No.6 directed the Governor of Bangladesh Bank and Chairman of National Board of Revenue to adjust the money in question as payment against VAT, Income Tax etc. with a quotation, "Out of Court of Settlement". After the national election and after restoration of the democracy and election of the democratic Government the petitioners approached the Government for several occasions to refund the said money as because the same was obtained by under pressure and not against any head of account admitted under the Income Tax Ordinance 1984, VAT Act 1991 or any other revenue law for the time being in force Due to procedural difficulty and other aspects the Government failed to take any positive decision as because the present Governing is not responsible, in any manner, for such payment. Thereafter finding no other alternative remedy the petitioners served justice demand notice on 21.3.2010 and since there is no reply the petitioners moved before this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

3. The respondent No.6 and 3 contested the Rule by Filing affidavit in opposition. The case of the respondent No.6 is that the statements made in the writ petition are matter of fact and as such the same was not denied by the respondent No.6 However, the respondent No.6 asserted its case in the affidavit in opposition as follows; 

"That the respondent No.6 does not have any relation to the relief sought by the petitioner. The petitioners have in fact alleged in the Writ Petition that a certain amount of money has been extorted from the petitioner company and has been deposited in the exchequer of the Government of Bangladesh without sanction of law. Bill as a Governmental authority the respondent No.6 does not have any involvement in the whole matter for the reasons stated hereinafter. But if any officer of the office of the respondent No.6 has been found involved then the said officer is personally liable in his individual capacity for such action. For such involvement of any officials in extorting money from any citizen of the country, the respondent No.6 us governmental authority is taken performed and discharged in compliance of the law of the land through a well-defined procedure as stated hereinafter, more so the office of respondent No.6 is accountable to the Government of the Republic for all its actions." 

The respondent No.6 further stated as follows; 

"The respondent No.6 in reply to the allegations brought in the above mentioned paragraphs states that it is working under the Ministry of Defense of the Government of Bangladesh. It performs its duties under a prescribed and authorized charter of duties. The respondent No.6 is accountable to the Government of the Republic for all its actions. The respondent No.6 discharges its duty with utmost sincerity and honesty and as per the directive of the Government. Various sensitive and important responsibilities are reposed to the respondent No.6 by the Government which the respondent No.6 discharged as per the charter of duties and law of the land The allegation of the petitioners regarding involvement of the respondent No.6 in extorting money from the petitioner and compelling the petitioner to deposit the same in the name of the Government is not based upon material fact. However the officers of respondent No. 6 whose name have been mentioned in the Writ Petition, if collected any such pay orders as mentioned, is a clear )1 violation of lawful authority. If did so it malt be termed .that he has done it at his own capacity not at the official capacity. The respondent No.6 deprecate such usurpation of power. (Underlined by us) 

That in respect of the allegation arrest apprehension or detention, it is stated that the office of the respondent No.6 acts under the existing law of the land. The office of the respondent No.6 never violated the law of the land Moreover, as per the contents of Para-6 of the writ petition, if any officer violates the charter of duties and commits such act should be recognized as the individual act not the official act. Therefore the allegation brought against respondent No. 6 is not based upon material fact. 

That the officer of respondent No. 6 always delegates various duties to its responsible officers by way of issuing office order. The official record shows the respondent No.6 never issued any official order to the officials named in Paragraph 8 of the Writ Petition to collect any money or pay order from the petitioner for or oil behalf of the Government of the Republic. And this is not the duty, of the office of the respondent No.6 to collect any money or pay order for or on behalf of the Government. In the process of discharging duties, this office always honour and comply the law of the land. Therefore, the allegation against the respondent No.6 is not correct and hence denied. 

That as has been stated above, the official record shows the office of the respondent No.6 never issued any instruction by any written office order empowering the said Lt. Col. Saiful Islam Joarder in respect of the matter stated in the Writ Petition. So, if the said officer accepts any pay order exploiting the name of the office of the respondent No.6, then the office of the respondent No.6 is not liable to such allegation. For such illegal acts the said officer is liable to be prosecuted in his individual capacity and not the office i.e. respondent No.6. 

That the office of the respondent No.6 is respectful to the law of the land and accountable to the Government as per the law of the land. The office of the respondent No.6 nor violated any law of the land before neither shall violate law of the land in future. The official record shows the respondent No.6 never made any correspondence with Bangladesh Bank and Secretary of Ministry of Finance in respect of any collection of pay order or depositing the money. There is no official documents produced by the petitioners regarding collection and deposition of money to the effect with Bangladesh Bank and Ministry of Finance by the respondent No.6. If the named official by his own capacity in the garb of his purported exercise of power in the name of respondent No.6 deposited the cheques with Bangladesh Bunk in that case the respondent No.6 has no connection whatsoever with the depositing of cheques by such delinquent officer. So the allegation brought against the respondent No.6 is not based on material fuel/evidence. 

That is most humbly submitted that the office of the respondent No.6 never approved or instructed for collection of any money or pay order by the officer named in the Writ Petition. However if the officer named in the writ petition is involved as mentioned, is personally liable for doing such type of misdeeds. Therefore, this office does not recognize such Act. If the officers named in the writ petition acted beyond and without official instruction of the respondent No.6, in that case their activities are liable to be prosecuted for maligning the name of this office i.e. Respondent No. 6. 

Therefore, it is submitted that the office of the respondent No.6 acts as per the defined and authorized charter of duties. But the alleged action of the officer as mentioned in the Writ Petition, in compelling by way of intimidating the petitioners to give pay orders to the said officer does not fall within the charter of duties, as such the action of officer may be judged according to the prevailing law." 
4. The case of the respondent No.3 as stated in the affidavit-in-opposition is as follows: 

'The petitioner willingly deposited the pay orders in Government Account. The petitioner has intentionally tried to mislead the Court about the suspense account because no suspense account was opened in Bangladesh Bank. That the office of the Coordination Committee on Crime Prevention Mission collected the said pay orders jar onward collection from different commercial bank's Brunches, and to deposit the proceeds in the concerned Govt. Account. Respondent No. 3 deposited the money to Govt. Account No. 0900 (Finance Division within Govt. Account No.011 which is known as consolidated fund) as per instruction of Ministry of Finance. 

That statement made in paragraph 15 is denied. Respondent No. 3 deposited the said amount of money to Govt. Account No. 0900 (Finance Division within Govt. Account No. 001 which is known as consolidated fund) as per instruction of the Ministry of Finance. 

That the statement made in paragraph nos. 16 &18 of the Writ petition are incorrect misconceived and misleading and hence, denied. The Petitioner willingly issued pay orders form is Banks and handed over to the Joint Forces for depositing the proceeds in the Government Account. Respondent No.3 didn't impose or demand or collect any amount from the petitioners. The collection through the help of joint forces and holding over such amount in the suspense account is not true at all. 

That in response to statements made in Paragraph No. 16-18 it is submitted that according to section 16(1) an (13) of Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972. Respondent No.3 is eligible and obliged to receive or accept any amount of money from any Bank or any local authorities with or without interest and according to section 16(13) of Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972, Respondent No. 3 is entitled to draw, accept, make and issue any promissory note on its Own account or on account of the Government. The reference to Article 83 of the Constitution and Chapter II of Part V of the Constitution is absolutely irrelevant as Respondent No.3 had only accepted the pay orders from different commercial banks and kept the money in Govt. Account No.0900 (Finance Division within Govt. Account No.0001 which is known as consolidated fund). 

That the statements made in paragraph 19 of the Writ Petition are not correct No suspense account was created by the Respondent No.3, the question of freezing such amount and declare it to have been made without lawful authority is totally incorrect misconceived and motivated and hence, denied. 
That regarding statements made in paragraph 20-22 of the Writ Petition, necessary response is already made in Para 8 and 11 above. 

That it is submitted that Bangladesh Bank did not receive any money illegally. Bangladesh Bank can receive any deposit or collect the proceeds of the DD/pay orders issued in favour of the Government, but Bangladesh Bank cannot make payment form that account without authentication of the competent authority." 

5. It appears that the Rule was issued on April 13, 2010 and the same was made ready for hearing on August 2, 2010. The matter was fixed for hearing on August 5, 2010 and thereafter appearing in the daily cause list. The matter was heard on August 5, 2010 and fixed August 10, 2010 for judgment. On that date the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the state pray for adjournment. Accordingly the same was adjo6rned till August 24, 2010. 

6. Mr. Mahmudul Islam. the learned Senior Advocate appearing along with Mr. M.A. Hannan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners placed the Writ Petition, certain provisions of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh including the preamble, Part-II, Part-III as well as provision relates to money bill etc. The learned Advocate also referred Article 83, 84 as well as 85 of the Constitution and submits that the Constitution itself prescribed a manner of recovery of tax and other duties in accordance with law. By referring Article 83 of the Constitution he submits that no money bill or any bill which involved expenditure for public money or tax shall be levied or collected except by/or under the authority of Act of the Parliament. Apart from that by referring Article 84 of the Constitution he submits that the law prescribed for two accounts namely "Consolidate Account" and "Public Fund Account" and Article 84 of the Constitution clearly distinguished the nature and character of both the accounts. He submits that the State Bank namely the Bangladesh Bank is only authorized to receive such fund in the aforesaid two accounts as per Article 84 of the Constitution and such payment is receivable subject to strict compliance of Article 82 and 83' of the Constitution. The learned Advocate also referred the provisions as laid down in Income Tax Ordinance 1984, Valued Added Tax 1991, Customs Act 1969 and all other laws relates to revenue r collection. By referring the same the learned Advocate submits all the law provides procedures for adjudication, assessment demand and subsequently deposit of the fund. Apart from that no single money can be deposited without any particular date and Code Number as per the Bangladesh Bank rules and guideline. By referring certain provisions of Finance Act he submits that it is the Parliament who delegated the power to the National Board of Revenue to enhance or review the rate by issuing Supplementary Regulatory Order (SRO) and only in that case the same is permissible and the National Board of Revenue with prior approval of the government and pursuant to the relevant provision of the relevant law can pass such order of enhancement/ reduction of any tax, duty or other charges. Also certain provisions of law allowed the authority namely the Government even to, exempt of payment of taxes, duty but the same is also subject to law and only applicable after publication in the official gazette. Thereafter, the learned Advocate referred Part-II of the Constitution and placed the Articles contained therein. By referring, the provisions laid down in Article 8 of the Constitution he submits that the same relates to fundamental state policy and the policies as stated in Part-II are the policies for guidance of the state and that violation of any State policy is not subjected by judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution. He submits that, however, Article 44 of the Constitution as embodied in Chapter III clearly stipulated that if any person or persons right as guaranteed in Part-III is being affected in that case the same is amenable under the writ jurisdiction and this Court can see the legality or propriety of any action, in violation in law. Mr. Islam, referred the Writ petition and submits that without any imposition, assessment, adjudication in any law for the time being enforce the petitioners were forced to deposited the money in question which is not only illegal but clear violation Article 82, 83 and 84 read with Part-III of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. He submits that any tax, duty, etc. is to be deposited in a particular manner and as per Rules of Business, the amount is to be deposited either to the consolidated fund or to the public fund. As per the aforesaid the provision of law no money cannot entered or cannot be spent from the said funds, except the express approval of the Parliament as per the provision of the Constitution. By referring the golden Rule regarding the tax, duty and other charges, he submits that the state being highest authority and the revenue collector itself cannot take any single money without any law or any subordinate legislation approved by the parent law itself. In the case in hand, it appears that certain agencies who are not at all authorised by the Constitution or law in any manner to collect revenue by directing the petitioners to deposit certain amount and to be adjusted with certain tax or liabilities. The revenue law of the country as per Mr. Islam, specified the fields wherein tax, duty can be adjusted in advance and the same also is to be done in accordance with certain laws and subject to adjudication. Even if somebody evaded tax and duty there is a clear provision not only to recover the same but to impose penalty even to impose more hash punishment like section 202 of the Customs Act etc. The learned Advocate lastly referred Part IV, Chapter 2A of the Constitution and referred our attention to the Article 58(D) wherein the function of the Caretaker Government, which is very much evident. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the petitioners are entitled to get back the money with full interest as the money is being taken ultimately from financial institutions for which the petitioner are counting huge interest including some petitioners are public listed company having numerous share-holders. 

7. Mr. M. Amirul Islam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No.3 submits that that the instant Writ Petition is not maintainable and this Court exercising the power conferred under Article 102 of the Constitution of the Republic cannot direct the Government to refund the money in question. He submits that the petitioners deposited the money in the public fund voluntarily as a part of out of Court of settlement relates to certain duty, tax and other charges regarding some regular transactions as well as other claims and such deposition creates a legal character and in such circumstances onus is upon the petitioners to show that whether the same was lawful or not and such type of investigation can only be done by producing sufficient evidence and as such the High Court Division exercising the power conferred under Article 102 of the Constitution cannot dispose of such matter in a summary proceeding. 

8. Mr. Monjur Md. Shahnewaz, the learned Advocate appearing, on behalf of the respondent No.6 placed the affidavit in opposition (as quoted above) and opposes the Rule and denied the involved of respondent No.6 in the action as alleged herein. He submits that the function, Jurisdiction and working 'conditions of the respondent No.6 is very much defined being disciplinary force which has no involvement in public affair. He further submits that the sole function of the respondent No.6 is concerned within the activities of the different forces and of the national security and as such the action as alleged by the petitioners against the respondent No.6 is neither acceptable nor practical as because the respondent No.6 has no business in public affairs in any manner. He further submits that the impugned action is being done by personal capacity of any officer concerned but the respondent No.6 in no way responsible for 'any such action. 

9. We have perused the writ petition, affidavits in opposition, annexure, provision of laws and heard the learned Advocates for the contesting parties. 

10. On perusal of the same it appears that during the last period of Care Taker Government a certain agency by creating pressure directed the petitioners to deposit the fund as stated paragraph-6 as "Out of Court Settlement" and accordingly the petitioners deposited the same amount to the Bangladesh Bank vide Pay Orders drawn in the name of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. It appears that after election of the democratic Government, the petitioners applied for release of the same but since the present Government is not responsible, in any manner, for taking such fund the Government in a fix regarding the faith of the said money resulting which the petitioners served demand of justice notice and thereafter moved before this Court. 
11. On perusal of the affidavit in opposition placed by the respondent No.6 it appears that the respondent No.6 also denied the involvement of the Directorate in such activities and clearly stipulated the function and the power of the said Directorate. Apart from that the respondent No.6 categorically stated that the respondent No.6 as an organization is duty bound to follow the law and the rules involved in any manner as an institution and the Directorate cannot take the responsibility of any action of an individual person. 

12. In the year 1972, the New Nation "Bangladesh" adopted the Constitution namely the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh with the preamble: 

"We, the people of Bangladesh, having proclaimed our independence on the 26th day of March, 1971 and though a historic war for national independence established the independent, sovereign People's Republic of Bangladesh." 

Article 7 of the Constitution categorically stated as follows; 

7(1). All powers in the Republic belong to the people, and their exercise on behalf of the people shall he effected only under, and by the authority of this Constitution. 

(2) This Constitution is, as the solemn expression of the will of the people the supreme law of the Republic, and if any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void. 

So it appears that the all power of the republic is vested with the people and the same is to be exercised on behalf of the people, for the people and for the betterment of the people. Apart from that it has been declared that the Constitution is the supreme law of the Republic and any act/action done inconsistent with the Constitution is liable to be declared void. So as per Article 7 of the Constitution no further declaration is requires to declare any action inconsistent with the constitution itself. Part V, Chapter of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh deals with the provision of law making process and financial activities, Article 80 of the Constitution stipulates how a bill is to be placed before the Parliament for approval by the legislatures namely the representatives who acted on behalf of the people and who are the source of power as per preamble an Article 7 of the Constitution. 

13. The Rule of law is a basic feature of the Constitution of Bangladesh. It can be seen from the preamble that fundamental human rights and freedom, equality and justice, political, economic and social have been mentioned after rule of law as it' these concepts are not included in Rule of law'. From this one may argue that 'rule of law' as contemplated in the Constitution concerns the certainty and publicity of law and its uniform enforceability and has not reference to the quality of the law; the Constitution deals with substantive justice separately from 'rule of law'. This argument is merely academic. As there is difference of opinion as to the actual meaning of 'rule of law', the framers of the Constitution, after mentioning 'rule of law' in the preamble, took care to mention the other concepts touching on the qualitative aspects of 'law', thereby showing their adherence to the concept of rule of law as propounded by the latter viewers. If the relevant paragraph of the preamble is read as a whole in its proper context, there remains no doubt that the framers of the Constitution intended to achieve 'rule of law' as advocated by the latter viewers. To attain this fundamental aim of the State, the Constitution has made substantive provisions for the establishment of a polity where every functionary of the State must justify his action with reference to law. 'Law' does not mean anything that Parliament may pass. Articles-7 and 31 have taken care qualitative aspects of law. Article 27 forbids discrimination in law or in State actions, while Article 31 imports the concept of due process, both substantive and procedural, and thus forbids arbitrary or unreasonable law or State action. The Constitution further guarantees in Part Ill certain rights to ensure respect for the supreme value of human dignity. 

14. Article 81 of the Constitution is being inserted which deals with the money bill with a view that no taxation can be made upon the people without the sanction of the sovereign power. Article 81(2) as well as Article 91 of the Constitution deals with the elaborate provisions regarding financial bills, imposition of tax and other relevant law(s) Article 83 of the Constitution stated as follows; 

"83. No tax shall be levied or collected except by or under die authority of an Act of Parliament."

 Article 84 of the Constitution stated as follows; 

84(1). All revenues received by the Government, all loans raised by the Government, and all moneys received by it in repayment of any loan shall form part of one fund to be known as the Consolidated Fund. 

(2) All other public moneys received by or on behalf of the Government shall be credited to the Public Account of the Republic." So it appears that no taxation in any manner except or under Act of Parliament is allowed and Article 84 of the Constitution categorically stated the manner of deposition of such money. So from the plain reading of these Articles it is apparent that it is the Parliament which can impose tax or spent money either from the public fund or from the consolidated fund. The Parliament being the product of the Constitution is empowered under Article 80 to make law which includes all the revenue collection, tax administration and the taxation law. However, there is a provision for delegated legislation wherein the concerned authority exercising the specific section mentioned in the parent law time to time make rules, regulation, by laws etc. But as per the interpretation of statute the same is to be construed very strictly and by making a subordinate legislation the authority even cannot go beyond the very spirit of the parent law in any manner. The power of the legislature to delegate the function of framing laws to an outside authority is accepted in all countries having common law system. Having regard to judicial pronouncements, the framers of our Constitution specifically recognized the power of Parliament to delegate the legislative function to any outside authority and included all subordinate legislations in the definition of 'law'. However, the inherent limitation in delegating the legislative function is that the legislature cannot abdicate the essential legislative function. 

15. In numerous decisions this Court as well as of our Apex Court declared illegal many subordinate legislation on the ground that exercising, the power conferred under the parent law the authority exceeds its limit and thus affected the very spirit of the original law. 

So it is apparent that after enactment of the Constitution our Parliament exercising the power conferred under Article 80 enacted sufficient laws for the purpose of collection of revenue and every year the Parliament amended such laws by finance bill vide the Finance Act wherein the rate of tax, duty etc. may be increased or decreased or imposition, of new tax or amendment or insertion of the procedure to be followed. 

16. From the relevant provision of the Constitution it is apparent a person cannot, be subjected to pay a single penny without any approved sanction of the Parliament. The control of public finance is an important function of Parliament. It includes imposition of taxes, granting of money to the administration for expenses on public service and authorisation of' loans. Through it, Parliament exercises control over the executive. The executive in Bangladesh can neither levy tax nor spend money all by itself without any authorisation of Parliament. Only Parliament can impose a tax and grant funds to the executive to defray public expenditures. Government's policies and their implementation are invariable brought into focus whenever Parliament discusses financial matters. The government cannot make any expenditure without the sanction of Parliament. The mechanism of parliamentary control over appropriation is the Consolidated Fund out of which all governmental expenditure is met. Originally the British Parliament voted taxes to the King who was free to collect it and spend for purposes he liked and often the money was spent for purposes other than the purposes for which he asked it. Parliament then started to levy taxes and appropriate it for specific purposes as a result of which no money would be left for general purposes when it can to passing Budget. To avoid this situation, a single fund was created into which all revenues were deposited and from which all expenditure was met according to the. Budget passed by Parliament. In Bangladesh the Consolidated Fund is formed with all revenue receipts, all loans raised by the government and all moneys received by the government in repayment of its loans. No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund without an Appropriation Act passed by Parliament. Besides the Consolidated Fund, there is the Public Account in which are credited all moneys other than those which are to be put in the Consolidated Fund. Payment of money into and its withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund or the Public Account is to be regulated by an Act of Parliament and if no such Act has been passed, by the Rules made by the President. But no Appropriation Act is needed to withdraw money from the Public Account. 

Also Article 83 of the Constitution provides that no tax shall be levied or collected except by or under the authority of an Act of Parliament. The article provides a protection against arbitrary or illegal exactions which can be enforced through proper court proceedings. If a tax-payer is made to pay an unconstitutional tax, he can recover the amount paid by filing civil suit or writ petition if the tax is sought to be levied without following the mandatory provisions of the law. The word 'Tax' has been defined in Article 152(1) which runs as follows: 

"Taxation' includes the imposition of any tax rate, duty or impost, whether general, local or special, and 'tax' shall be construed accordingly. 

Thus the word 'tax' has been used in a comprehensive sense to includes all money raised by taxation and includes those known as 'rates' of other charges levied by local authorities under statutory powers. A tax cannot be levied or collected merely by an executive fiat or action without them being a law to support the same. In the Indian jurisdiction there is a conflict of judicial opinion as to whether levy or collection of tax by usage in ruled out. But there is no scope of any such conflict of opinion in Bangladesh as art.83 contains the expression by or under the authority of an Act of Parliament. Under art.83 not only the levy but also the collection of tax must be sanctioned by or under the authority of an Act of Parliament. The expression 'Levy' includes creation of liability realisation of tax. Not only a tax must be validly levied, its collection must also be in accordance with the Act of Parliament. Thus, when an Act of Parliament provides that a tax shall be collected in such manner as may be prescribed by rules, the tax cannot be collected until the rules are made. This article gives protection against arbitrary collection of tax. When an assessment is made in an arbitrary fashion, there is no collection of tax in accordance with an Act of Parliament. Apart from that the power of the Parliament in enacting legislations or ratification of certain action(s) is also subject to judicial review by the apex Country. If the Parliament enacts any law(s) inconsistent or ultra vires to the provision of the Constitution, the supreme law of the land, such enactment can also be interfered by the apex Court exercising the power conferred under Article 102 of the Constitution of the Republic. The decision passed by our apex Court in the case of 'Anwar Hossain Chy V. Bangladesh reported in 1889 BLD (Spl) I and the decision passed by the High Court Division (Affirmed upto the Appellate Division) in the case of Bangladesh Italian Marble Works Limited V. Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 2006 (Special Issue) BLT (HCD)1 lends support to the above contention. 

17. In the present case in hand it appears that the aforesaid payment was made by the petitioners not on the basis of any demand under the law of the land nor by any act of the Parliament nor by the any direction given by the Parliament. It has been alleged that an agency namely Respondent No.6 directed to deposit the same though there is no sufficient material to show that the said direction was made by the agency itself to deposit the same money. But we cannot ignore Annexure-D of the Writ Petition, which has been quoted as follows; 

SECRET 
Directorate General of 
Forces Intelligence 
Dhaka Cantonment 
1000/CT(1)/01								16 June, 2008

S. Alam Group,
1. S. Alam Group, Corporate Office, S. Alam Bhaban, 2119 Asadgoqj, Chittagong paid a total amount of Taka, 60,00,00,000.00 (Sixty Crore only), in favour of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh as rant of "out of Court Settlement: Details of payment made in the process is attached as annex-A. 

2. As the amount has already been deposited to the National Exchequer of Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh, we ) would now request you to kindly adjust the amount with following companies and related individuals of S. Alam Group) as Duty on Bond, Income Tax, VAT etc. under National Board or Revenue:  

a. S. Alam Steels Ltd. 
b. S. Alan Cold Rolled Steels Ltd. 
c. S. Alam Cement Ltd 
d. S. Alum Vegetable Oil Ltd, 
e. S. Alam Super Edible Oil Ltd. 
f Alhaz Md. Saiful Alam. 

3. Please acknowledge. 
MD. MOAZZEM HOSSAIN
Lieutenant Colonel
For Director General.

Distribution 
External: 
Action: 
Dr. Saleh Uddin Ahmed 
Governor, Bangladesh Bank 
Motijheel C/A, Dhaka 
Mr. Mohammad Abdul Majid 
Chairman 
National Board of Revenue Dhaka 
I of 2 
SECRET 

18. On perusal of the same it appears that the letter was addressed to the petitioners with a copy to Dr. Md. Salahuddin Ahmed, Governor of Bangladesh Bank and Mr. Md. Abdul Majid, Chairman, National Board of Revenue, Government of Bangladesh. It is admitted in the said letter that the petitioners paid certain amount in favour of the People's Republic of Bangladesh as out of Court of Settlement. In second paragraph the, Bangladesh Bank and the National Beard of Revenue has been advised to adjust the same with the income tax, VAT etc. It is apparent that Bangladesh Bank is a statutory body as per the Banking Companies Act 1991 as well as the Bangladesh Bank order 1972. The power and function of Bangladesh Bank is very much stated thereon and the said bank is as independent body controlling the financial institutions as well as the monitory policy of the state and secondly the Chairman National Board of Revenue is also the Secretary internal Resource Division of the Ministry of Finance and the highest authority in terms of collection of revenue on behalf of the state. As per the Constitution both the authority are to act in accordance with the Constitution and related laws and no other authority but only the superior authority can direct the authorities namely the National Board of Revenue or Bangladesh Bank to undertake a particular act/action. But from the said letter it appears with utter surprise that an agency is directing the aforesaid authorities to adjust money in question though there is no specific claim regarding any tax, duties, charges etc. in any manner. It has been stated earlier that if there is any adjudication order or if there is any short payment the petitioners are under legal obligation to pay the Same but the same is to be done in accordance with law and following the provision laid down in the relevant laws of the land.

19. There are some constitutional assumptions which need be expressed and kept in view while interpreting and applying the statutes in specific cases. The first is that the general powers of the government arc constitutionally committed to the three principal branches of the  government and though Parliament has not the exclusive power of making laws, it is the principal source of legislation and the power of Parliament in making laws takes precedence over the law making power of the executive and judicial branch of the government and it has to enact laws within the limits prescribed by the Constitution. The Court is required, as far as is possible, to construe a provision of a statute in accord with the constitutional provisions. Thus, if a provision of law is capable of two interpretations one of which will render it constitutionally valid and the other not, the court will have to adopt the former. A principle of statutory interpretation derives from the wider policy of the law, which in turn is based on what is called public policy. The interpreting court is required to presume, unless the contrary intention appears, that the legislator intended to conform to this. The constituent elements of legal policy include parliamentary enactments, past judgments, ideas of natural law and the writings of Jurists. 

20. Parliament confers powers on public functionaries to be used reasonably to achieve the purpose of the statute and not to abuse such powers. Accordingly, a statute conferring powers should be so construed as to prevent any attempt to abuse of those powers, and the court must be ready to inquire into the bona fides of a purported exercise of a statutory power. Even when Parliament grants discretionary powers in absolute terms, the modem tendency is to construe statutes so as to negative any grant of absolutely untrammeled and untrammeled exercise of it. 

21. It is a well-established principle that taxing statutes are to be strictly construed. A fiscal statute imposing a burden on the subject is to be strictly construed and no tax can be imposed on a person without using unambiguous and clear words by which tax is imposed. When there is doubt and interpretation which is favourable to the subject should be preferred. When a particular provision is suspectable of two or more interpretations, the one most favourable to the citizen must be accepted. The subject is not to be taxed without clear words creating liability and every Act of Parliament must be read according to the natural Construction of its words. A provision intended for the benefit of the tax payer is to be construed barely in favour of the tax payer. In a taxing statute one has to look merely at what is clearly said and there is no room for intendment. There is no equity about a tax and there is no presumption as to tax. Nothing is to be read in, nothing is to be implied and one can only look fairly at the language used. By Strict construction of taxing statue it is meant that the subject is not to be taxed unless the words of the taxing statute unambiguously impose the tax on him. In the words of Bhagwati J of the Indian Supreme Court, "In construing fiscal statutes and in determining the liability of a subject to tax one must have regard to the strict letter of the law. If the revenue satisfies the court that the case falls strictly within the provisions of the law, the subject can be taxed. If, on the other hand, the case is not covered within the four comers of the provisions of the taxing statute, no tax can be imposed by an inference or by analogy or by trying to probe into the intentions of the legislature and by considering what was the substance of the matter. 

22. The petitioners in the case in hand praying for payment of interests. It has been stated earlier that as per Article 81 and 83 of the Constitution no payment can be made or no money can be receipt/spent without the special sanction of the Parliament. If this Court passed any order directing the authority to pay interest in that case the same is to be made either only from the public fund or from the Consolidated Fund which is not permissible in the eye of law. For the wrong of some individual person(s) the Government namely the public fund cannot be subjected to any loss or injury. There is no scope to allow any interest or excess money either from the consolidated fund or from the public fund as because the state is not responsible for such type of deposition of money as because the same is not in accordance with law. The petitioners, in no circumstances, can claim any such interest or additional amount as because the same is not permitted by the Parliament. The Parliament is to pass a law regarding deposition of tax or payment only for welfare of the people and for that purpose Parliament requires a financed bill to be placed every year and to be passed/approved the expenditure and income. Apart from that for necessity the Parliament is also empowered to consider supplementary budget, if any. Even, if the Government spent money beyond the scope of the budget that also requires ratification by the Parliament by way of supplementary budget etc. In such circumstances, since the money is being extruded from the petitioners not by the state it is not reasonable to pay any interest or the additional charges in any manner. 

23. Before part, we are expressing our deep concern about such type of activities read  with Article 58D or the Constitution of the Republic which categorically stated the limitations of the particular Government. As per the said Article it is being understood that the only function of such type of Government is to run the day to day affairs of the state and to hold a free and fair national election. The Constitution puts specific bars in taking any policy decision by such government, in any manner. The impugned actions as alleged in our view is a colorable exercise of the power by certain authority and have been done without following any provision of law or norms, in any manner. The impugned action is neither backed by any law, rules nor any lawful authority of the state, in any manner. On further perusal of the affidavit in opposition filed by the respondent No.6 we have sufficient reasons to believe that the whole affairs of the matter as stated in the Writ Petition has been done unlawfully and without any lawful jurisdiction or without any formal or written order or instruction from the respondent No. 6, by few individuals serving, in that organization at the relevant period and as such necessary legal and departmental steps should be taken against such person(s) as per the provision of the relevant law(s) applicable in the case in hand. 

24. Considering the facts and circumstances, provision of law as well as the discussions made hereinabove, we find merit in this Rule. The Rule is made absolute without-any order as to cost. The impugned action is declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal affect. The respondents are directed to refund the money as stated in paragraph-7 of the writ petition (as evident in Annexure "A" series) only to the petitioners within 90(ninety) days from the date of receipt of this judgment. 

End.

case_source: From the Judgment and Order dated 16-11-1976 passed by the High Court in Civil Revision Case No. 850 of 1975
full_judgment:
K. Hossain, C. J. Lave was granted to consider three questions which are as follows:-

1. Whether the Courts below on the evidence on record were well founded in law in holding, that the tenant did not deposit the rent in compliance with the provisions of Rent Control Ordinance, 1963.

2. There are some decisions of the Dacca High Court on the earlier Rent Control Act, the language of which is substantially the same as that of the present Ordinance, wherein it has been held that the point of default that is to be decided by the Court, is whether the tenant has paid rents allowable under the Act to the full extent at the time of the decree or order for ejectment is made and not an earlier date, Reference is to be made to the cases of Ananda Sundari, 12 DLR 720, and A.K. Fazlul Huq 19 DLR 901. The learned Single Judge obviously proceeded upon a different interpretation of Section 18(1) of, the Ordinance, to determine the point of default, and in this view of the matter an authoritative pronouncement of this differing interpretations, has become essential by this Court.

3. Whether the trial Court below, upon the finding that the trade license of the tenant was in the name of 'Universal Repairing Works and the assertion of the landlord that the tenant was carrying on the repair work of worn out materials in the suit premises, drew a correct inference in treating the tenancy a commercial one and not one of manufacture.

2. Facts involved in the three questions are that against the tenant appellant, plain-tiff-respondent brought a S.C.C. Suit for ejectment before the 3rd Subordinate Judge, Dacca on the footing that the appellant was a monthly tenant-at-will at Tk. 40/- per mensem. The tenant was to pay the rent within the 3rd day of the following month, according to Bengali Calendar. The tenant paid rent upto Bhadra, 1380 B.S. and thereafter he defaulted in payment of rent from Aswin, 1380 B.S. The landlord accordingly served a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, terminating the tenancy. The defense was the denial of the case of default and the plea of insufficiency of the notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was set up. He claimed that the tenancy was for a manufacturing purpose, and so fifteen days' notice was insufficient in law. He also claimed that he deposited rents with the Rent Controller after the landlord had refused to accept the rent for the months of Kartik and Aswin, 1380 B.S. tendered to him.

3. The trial Court found that the tenant used to pay rent sometimes for two or three months together, and in the instant case, he failed to tender rent within time, and that he deposited the rent for Aswin and Kartik 1380 B.S. with the Rent Controller not within the time prescribed by law. The trial Court from the trade license of the tenant, and from the evidence of plaintiff's witnesses, and disbelieving the defense witnesses, held that the business of the tenant was for repair work of worn out materials, and so he was running a repairing business which is com-metrical, and not a manufacturing one. On revision the learned Single Judge of the High Court considered the question of default, and concurred with the finding of the trial Court but did not consider the other question of the sufficiency of notice to quit or the nature of the tenancy and dismissed the revisional case.

4. Of the questions set out above, we think ground Nos. 1 and 2 are interdependent and they may be considered together. The consideration involves the question of interpretation of some of the Sections of East Pakistan Premises' Rent Control Ordinance1963 as amended and extended from time to time. The relevant sections that require to be considered are Sections 18(1), 18(5) and Section 19(1) of the Ordinance, the relevant parts of which are as follows : "18(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, or the Contract Act, 1872 no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made as long as the tenant pays rent to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance and performs the conditions of the tenancy;

(5) No tenant shall be entitled to the benefit of this section in respect of any premises unless he pays the rent due by him in respect of such premises to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance within the time fixed id the con-tract within his landlord or, in the absence of such contract, by the fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable, or in the cases provided for in section 19, unless the tenant has deposited such rent or any subsequent rent in respect of such premises as provided in that section together with in the case mentioned in clause(b) of sub section (1) of that section, the cost of transmission referred to in that clause within the time specified in that section.

Explanation-A landlord shall not for the purposes o this sub-section be deemed to have refused to accept any rent unless the rent is remitted within the period referred to above in this sub-section by postal money order to the address of the landlord and the rent so remitted is returned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered either on account of the landlord having refused to accept pad meat thereof or for any other cause.

19 (1) When a landlord refuses to accept any rent referred to in section 18 remitted by postal money order by a tenant in respect of any premises the tenant may

(a) deposit such rent within a fort-night of the date on which the rent so remitted is returned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered, and

(b) unless the landlord signifies by notice in writing to the tenant his willingness to accept any subsequent rent which becomes due in respect of such premises, also deposit such subsequent rent within a fortnight of the date on which such rent becomes due, from expiry of the time within which rent is required to be paid under sub-section (5) of scrim 18 together with the cost of transmission by postal money order of the money deposited to the landlord."

5. It is to be observed that East Pakistan Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 has made substantial encroachment into the tenancy law of the country, its purpose is to protect the tenant from ejectment from the tenanted premises and has given the tenant 	certain benefits, notwithstanding the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act or the Contract Act. The general law governing relationship of landlord and tenant relating to 	premises are to be kept in view, while interpreting the sections of the Ordinance. Under 	the Transfer of Property Act which is the general law governing the relationship of 	landlord and tenant for this kind of tenancy, the landlord has the right to terminate the tenancy by giving a notice quit on the tenant in the manner prescribed under section 106 of the Act. This right has been substantially curtailed by the Ordinance. The Ordinance, however, has not totally done away with the operation of the provisions of Transfer of 	Property Act but has made serious encroachment on the rights of the parties in a tenancy 	agreement' the right of landlord being curtailed.

6. We now turn to the three provisions set out earlier of the Ordinance to see the combined effect of them in case of ejectment of such a tenant. These three provisions mainly relate to default in payment of rent by the tenant. As said earlier the Ordinance seeks to give protection to the tenant from ejectment to some extent and one of such is that, if the tenant pays rent to the full extent permissible under the Ordinance, amongst others, he is protected from ejectment. We are, therefore, to see how far the Ordinance 	has given the protection to the tenant and how far the landlord's right to eject on this score has been curtailed.

7. Section 18 (1) says that notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act 1882 or the Contract Act, 1872 no order or decree f r recovery of possession of any premises shall be made so long as the tenant pays rent to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance and performs the conditions of the tenancy. It is limited by five provisos but they do not concern us for the present and so they need not be gone into. The provisions of section 18(5) have been set out above.

8. To turn to section 19 which deals with the deposit of rent, we find that the relevant provision is that when a landlord refuses to accept rent referred to in section 18 remitted by postal money order by the tenant, he may deposit such rent within a fortnight of the date on which the rent due so remitted is returned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered, unless the landlord signifies by notice in writing to the tenant of his willingness to accept any subsequent rent which has become due in respect of such premises. There are other conditions as to the deposit of rent but they do not call our attention in the context of the present case and we refrain from dilating on them.

9. In the case of default in the payment of rent, the combined effect of the three provisions set out above clearly shows that a tenant is protected, notwithstanding the pro-visions of Transfer of Property Act or the Contract Act from ejectment as long as he pays rent to the full extent allowed by the Ordinance and he performs the conditions of the tenancy. The expression 'as long as tenant pays rent' in our opinion, no doubt, indicates that the point of default on the part of the tenant will be not only the date of filing of the suit but will continue till decree is passed. It does not, however, mean that if the tenant subsequent to the filing of the suit has deposited the rent with Rent Controller, the default incurred earlier is cured. On the contrary the tenant's liability for default even after the filing of the suit continues under the law till the passing of the decree. On this point, however, we find that a view has been taken by a Single Judge of the Dacca High Court contrary to the language of the section in the case of A.K. Fazlul Haq vs. Nibaran Chandra Saha (1967) 19 DLR 901. The learned Single Judge of the Dacca High Court has taken the view on the language of East Bengal Premises Rent Control Act (XVI of 1953) the language of which is substantially the same as that of the present Ordinance, that if the tenant deposits rent any time before the passing of decree, he shall not be deemed to be in arrears. The learned Judge has purported to base his decision on the authority of two earlier decisions in the cases of Mullah Mahbub Ali vs. Jonah All (1956) 8 DLR 418 and Annanda Sundari Karmakar vs. Dr. Mazammel Huq. (1960) 12 DLR 720. In the case of Mullah Mahbub All it has been held that the material time to consider whether there has been default in payment of rent is the date on which the decree or suit comes to be passed by the Court. We find on the analogous provision of the earlier enactment in both the decisions, it has been so interpreted in a language which is perfectly in accord with the facts of each case but is equivocal as a general construction of the section. The moot question in Ananda Sundari's case was whether a preliminary determination of default by the Rent Controller precluded the Civil Court in a suit for ejectment from going into that question, and in that context the observation was made that the expression 'as long as' in section 17(1) of the Act of 1953 indicates that the point of time at which it has to be decided whether the tenant has paid the rents allowable under the Act to the full extent or not is the point of time at which the order or decree for eviction is to be made. We have said earlier that this observation divorced from the context of fact is equivocal. There is nothing in the language of that decision from which a further inference could be drawn that deposit of rent subsequent to the date of default will cure thee fault. In fact this decision is in accord with the interpretation we have given. In this view of the matter the decision of the learned Single Judge in A. K Fazlul Huq's case cannot be approved.

10. Apart from the three decisions set out above, there are several other decisions of the Dacca High Court and that of High Court Division on the question of default. The view consistently taken therein is that if default had occurred in terms of the Ordinance the default, and the tenant's protection given under the Ordinance on the basis of due payment of rent disappears. The decisions may be referred to for our present consideration.

In East Bengal Paper Traders vs. Md. Waziullah, (1969) 21 DLR 572, it has been held that once a tenant is a defaulter he is always a defaulter. A tenant not having paid rent to the landlord in terms of section 18 (5) or not having deposited it with the Rent Controller according to the provisions of section 19, is not entitled to protection from eviction.

In Sk. Md. Emdaduddin vs. Jasimuddin (197 25 DLR 404, the view has been taken that the benefit of sub-section (5) of section 18 of Bangladesh Premises Rent Control Ordinance (XX of 1963) can be claimed only where tenant pays rent due to the full extent in due time, the defaulter ca not seek protection. In Zainul Abedin Vs. Nazira Banu, (1974) 26 DLR 221 the view taken is that the failure to deposit the, amount of rent on the alleged ground that the necessary permission of the House Rent Controller has not been accorded for such deposit will not protect the tenant from being a defaulter within the meaning of sub-section (5) of section 18 of the Ordinance. In Must Haytunnessa vs. Abdur Rahman, (974) 26 DLR 342 the view taken is that the payment of rent must comply with the contract made or the terms of section 18(5) to get protection against eviction 	In Dr. Md. Arfan Ali Vs Md. Baziur Rahman Chowdhury, (1976) 28 DLR 443, it has been held that to get the benefit of Section 18(5) of the Ordinance, the tenant must clear his rent dues in terms of the cataract or within fifteen days of the next following month and once the Court finds that the tenant is a defaulter, the prayer for ejectment cannot be refused on the plea that he is not a habitual defaulter.

11. The Supreme Court in the case of Abul Layes vs. Mst. Anwara Khatun, (1977) 29 DLR (SC) 13 has held that onus is on the tenant to prove the circumstance which entitled him to deposit rent with the Rent Controller and when the conditions in section 19 are not satisfied, the tenant is not entitled to deposit rent in Court and such a deposit is not a valid tender and the tenant must take care that he will not become a defaulter.

The views expressed in the different decisions in diverse language, in our opinion, require restatement so far as the ejectment on the ground of default in payment of rent is concerned. To revert back to the relevant provision of the statute set out earlier we find that the protection of the tenant against ejectment is on the fulfillment of certain conditions. He should pay rent to the full extent allowable by the Ordinance and if he does so, he is protected from ejectment on the ground of default in the payment of rent of further sets out the terms of payment ( f rent. It is to be paid within the time fixed by the contract, and in the absence of any such contract, within fifteenth day of the month next following for which the rent is payable or he can deposit rent in terms of Section 19. The explanation of sub-section (5) of section 18 is very clear which says that a landlord shall not be deemed to have refused to accept any rent unless the rent is remitted within the period referred to in that sub-section by postal order and there has been compliance with other details given therein.

<u>12. The provision for deposit of rent is in section 19 wherein provisions have been made for deposit of rent to meet diverse contingencies. We are concerned with the deposit following tender by the tenant and refusal by the landlord to accept rent. This provision is contained in section 19(1) of the Ordinance. It clarifies the earlier provision regarding the tender of rent by the tenant. The section says that when the landlord has refused to accept rent in terms of section 18 remitted by the tenant by postal money order the tenant may deposit the rent with the Rent Controller within a fortnight of the receipt of the undelivered rent sent through the postal authorities. To sum up, the tenant must pay rent in terms of the contract, and in the absence of the contract within fifteenth day next following month on which the rent falls due, and if the landlord refuses to accept the rent tendered by the tenant, the tenant must remit the rent within the aforesaid fifteenth day of the following month by money order. If the rent remitted by money order is refused, the tenant can deposit the rent with the Rent Controller within a fortnight from the date of the receipt of the undelivered rent sent through the postal authority, and when these conditions as prescribed in the Ordinance are fulfilled by the tenant, he gets the protection, otherwise the protection from ejectment on ground of default in the payment of rent granted by the Ordinance is clearly taken away by the express language of sub-section (5) of section 18.</u>

13. It is true that enquiry about compliance of the provisions of the statute may call for consideration of facts at each point. There may be a case of waiver or acquiescence or such supervening facts and circumstances as to make the compliance with the enactment beyond the control of the tenant. However, it will depend on the facts of a particular case to see whether there has been default in the payment of rent in terms of the statute but once the fact is established in terms of the Ordinance, legal consequence flowing there from cannot be averted. The decisions set out above on this question are to be considered in the manner we have just construed.

<u>14. To turn to the facts, it is the concur-rent finding of the Courts below that the ten-ant failed to prove that he did tender rent for the months of Kartik and Aswin, 1380 B.S. as alleged by him, and the remittance and the deposit were made beyond the time prescribed by the law. The default in the payment of rent has taken place in terms of the Ordinance. The tenant appellant before us by the clear language of sub-section (5) of section 18, is disentitled to the protection from ejectment on the ground of default in the payment of rent. The Ordinance makes no distinction between default for one month or default for more than one month or a habitual defaulter. If the default has taken place the protection from ejectment is with-drawn and that has occurred in the particular case.</u>

15. Mr. T. H. Khan, learned Counsel however has tried to argue that evidence on record is there to show that the appellant did tender the rent in time and it was refused by the landlord. This is a question of facts and no leave has been granted on this question and as such it cannot be reopened at this stage.

<u>16. We now turn to the third question, and it will not take us long in view of the fact that the tenant never made out a case that the tenancy was created for any manufacturing purpose. All that was pleaded was that the tenant was running a repairing shop and he made some Kerosene Stove and steel body van carrier and as the tenancy was for the purpose of manufacture fifteen days notice was insufficient. But the clear finding of the trial Court is that the tenant appellant was running a repairing business and the trade license was in the name of Universal Repairing Works and it was not a manufacturing factory. It has further been found that the tenant's business at the premises was for repairing work of worn out materials. On this finding of fact, we do not find that the trial Court came to any wrong conclusion as to the character of defendant's tenancy that it was for commercial and not for manufacturing purpose. It is now well sett-led that manufacture means the change in the character of goods or materials used, so that new goods or materials come into existence. Even where the dominant work is to repair and in the process some minor or inconsequential manufacture of a thing is done, the business does not become a manufacturing one. In this regard, we cite with approval, a decision of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Allen bury Engineers (Private) Ltd. vs. Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia, AIR1973 (SC) 425. In conclusion, we find no merit in this appeal, which is dismissed with costs.</u>

End.
