case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 5.4.1976 passed by the High Court Division in F.M.A, 96 of 1974).
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J —This appeal by special leave arises out of the Judgment dated 5th April, 1976 of the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 96 of 1974, Facts in short relevant for disposal of the appeal are like this. Respondent nos. 1 and 2 filed an application under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1960 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act," in the Court of the Additional Subordinate Judge, Noakhali being miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 1970, stating Inter ails that the respondent. Nos. 3 and 4 by a registered kabala dated 28th August, 1969 transferred .34 acres of land of plot No. 1594; .07 acres of land of plot No. 1596 ; 3.9 acres of land of plot No. 1601; 2.98 acres of land of plot No. 1602 and .08 acres of land of plot No. 1605, all appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 294 of Monza Tamta P S. Ramganj, District Noakhali for a sum of Tk. 15,000/ in favour of the appellants who are strangers, Respondents 1 and 2 claiming to have land contiguous to plot Nos. 1602 end 1605 prayed for pre-emption in respect of 2.98 acres of lend out of plot No. 1602 and, .08 acres of land out of plot No. 1605 out of the kabala land comprising 3,R6 acres of land. The respondents deposited proportionate value of the said land calculating the same at Tk. 895/00 with usual compensation.

2 The application was opposed by the appellants by filing a written objection, contending, inter alia, that the application for partial pre-emption of the kabala lend by making partial deposit and In the absence of all necessary parties is not maintainable.

3. The learned Subordinate Judge held that the application for partial preemption by the tenants having land contiguous to two plots transferred was maintainable and the deposit made by the pre-emptors was accepted as correct. The learned Subordinate Judge also held that the necessary parties were impleaded in the application for preemption. Accordingly, the prayer for preemption was allowed. On appeal by the transferee pre-emptors a Division Bench of the High Court Division took the view that prayer for partial pre-emption was made under misapprehension of law, although the pre-emptors are entitled to pre-empt other lands to which they have no contiguous land. On this finding the learned Judges dismissed the appeal and (Wooed the pre-emptors to pay up the balance of consideration money with usual compensation within four weeks from the date of arrival of records of the case. This appeal is directed against that Judgment.

4. Leave was granted to consider whether in view of the finding that the application for partial pre-emption with partial deposit is not maintainable and the law requires the deposit of entire consideration of the kabala under preemption is to be made along with the application for preemption or within four months, the order of the learned Judges of the High Court Division allowing the pre-emptors to preempt in full on depositing the balance amount of the consideration within the specified time is In accordance with law.

5. For proper appreciation of the question relevant sub-sections of section 96, that is, sub-section (1), (2) and (5) are quoted below:-

"96 (1) If a portion or share of a holding of a radiant is transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding may within four months of the service of the notice given under section 89 or, if no notice has been served under section 89, within four months of the date of the knowledge of the transfer, apply to the Court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves; and if a holding or a portion or share of holding is transferred, the tenant or tenants holding land consign us to the land transferred may, within four months of the date of the knowledge of such transfer, apply to the Court for the holding portion on share to be transferred to himself or themselves :

(2) In an application made under lobe section (1) by a co-sharer truant or co-sharer tenants, all other co-sharer tenants or the holding and the transferee shall be made parties; and in such an applicant  dun made by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, all the co-sharer tenants of the holding and all the tenants holding lards contiguous to the land transferred and the transferee shall be made parties.

(5)(a) If (1) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by inheritance and (ii) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by purchase and (ill) a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred apply under this section and comply with the provisions therein contained, the applicant or applicants shall have the prior right to purchase under this section In the order in which they have been mentioned above.

(b) If more than one tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred apply under this section, the Court shall determine the order of priority as among such tenants having regard to-

(i) the total quantity of land in possession of each of the tenants applying

(ii) Whether the contiguous land of the tenant is homestead land or any other class of land :

(iii) extent of contiguity;

(iv) to what extent it is necessary for applicant to have possession of the contiguous land, and

(v) the right of easement, If any, of the applicants".

<u>6. From a Plain reading of sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act, it appears that it consists of two parts the first part giving right of pre-emption to one or more co-sharer tenants : and the record part giving right of pre-emption to a tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the lead transferred. Subsection (2) also consists of two parts. The first part deals with an application for preemption by achier tenant or tenants. The second part deals with an application for preemption by a tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred. In the former case all other co-sharer tenants of the holding and the transferees are to be impleaded and in the latter case all the co-sharer tenants and all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred and the transferee are to be made parties Glues (a) of sub-section-(5) shows that the law recognizes three classes of preemption :</u>

<u>(i) a cod sharer tenant whose Interest has accrued by inheritance;</u>

<u>(ii) a co-shavers tenant whose interest has accrued by purchases; and</u>

<u>(iii) a tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred.</u>

<u>The statute gives priority to the co-sharer-tenant whose interest has accrued by inheritance. The first class excludes both second and third class, and the second class excludes the third class. Clause (a) provides necessary guidance for determining the order of priority among the tenants claiming pre-emption on the ground of having lands contiguous to the lands transferred. If more than one tenant holding lands contiguous to the land transferred apply under sub-section (1), the court shall determine the order of priority as among such tenants having regard to the total quantity of land in possession of each to the tenants applying; whether the contiguous land of the tenants is homestead land or any other class of land; extent of contiguity; to what extent it is necessary for the applicant t) have possession of the contiguous land; and right of easement, if any, of the applicants. Guidance as provided in clause (b) of sub-section (5) sufficiently Indicates that a tenant claiming pre-emption on the ground of having land contiguous to the land trans., (erred for which the tenant cannot satisfy the requirements of clause (b). From the expression "tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred" mentioned in the second part there Is hardly any scope for doubt that in the latter case test is as to whether the pre-emptor is a "tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred" gets support from the different provisions of section 96 itself. Subsection (2) of section 96 provides that in an application made under sub-section (1) by one or more co-sharer tenants all other co-sharer tenants of the holding shall be made parties, but in the last of an application made by a tenant or tenants "holding land contiguous to the land transferred" all the co-sharer tenants of the holding and all the tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred shall be made parties. This sub-section in plain language provides that when an application for pre-emption under sub-section (1) is made by one or more co-sharer tenants, all other co-sharer tenants of the holding shall be made parties but when the application is filed by a tenant claiming to be the owner of contiguous land to the land transferred, all co sharer tenants plus all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land sought to be pre-empted are to be made parties.</u>

<u>7. Section 96 of the Act gives right of pre-emption to co-sharer tenant of holding and to tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred. In the latter case also it is true that the expression a "holding or a portion or a share of a holding" has been mentioned but unlike in the former case the right of pre-emption has been given to "the tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred". In such a case instead of mentioning "one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding" "tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land" has been mentioned. If lands consisting of several plots are transferred by a kabala, the tenant or tenants hold, lug land contiguous to the land of particular plot or plots are entitled to pre-empt only the land or lands to which they have contiguous lands. In such a case the pre-emptor or pre-emptors are required to implead all the co-sharer tenants of the holding and all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred and the transferee.</u>

8. Mr. M.H. Khondker, learned Counsel appearing for the appellants, submits that the learned Judges of the High Court division failed to notice that clause (a) of sub section (3) of section 96 of the Act, requires that application for pre-emption must be accompanied by a deposit of the entire consideration money of the property transferred or stated in the notice served under section 89, together with compensation @ 10 pc thereon, and She deposit being a condition precedent to the filing of the application, it cannot be entertained and its non-fulfillment renders the application liable to be dismissed; and that in the absence of any power to extend the time stipulated in the Act, the order is wholly illegal and without jurisdiction and cannot be sustained. The learned Counsel further submits that the pre-emptors were entitled to preempt the entire kabala land, but they having abandoned a portion of their claim in contravention of subsection (1) of section 96 of the Act. The direction given by the learned Judges of the High Court Division for depositing the balance of the consideration money with a view to converting the application to one for pre-emption of the entire kabala land is bad in law. With reference to subsection (1) of section 96 of the Act the learned Counsel submits that there is no scope for partial preemption, when a holding or a portion or a share oh holding is transferred. According to the learned Counsel even in the case of tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred may, within four months from the date of knowledge of such transfer, apply to the court for the holding or portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves; only restriction being no co-sharer tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred shall have the right to purchase under this section unless he is a person to whom transfer to the holding or the portion or share thereof, as the case may be, can be made under sections 88 and 90 of the Act. This, as the learned Counsel submits, is necessary to avoid sub-division of holding.

9. The learned Counsel in aid to his argument for applying the rule of partial pre-emption to the case refers to the or serrations made In the case of Makhanlal Nag V. Reajuddin Sepal (1961) 13 D.L.R. 323. The observation is as follows:

"It is well settled that if out of five plots originally claimed by the petitioners by way of pre-emption, the petitioner was allowed to press only with respect to three, although he was otherwise entitled to claim preemption with regard to all the five plots, the petitioner's case should be hit by the bar of rule of partial preemption and as such the entire claim should fail."

10. The learned Counsel then refers to another decision of the Dacca High Court in the ease of Syed Abdul Karim Vs. Haren  dra Chandra Dhupi (1962) 14 D.L.R. 847, in this case a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court made some observations to the effect that in a pre-emption case under section 96 of the Act by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, is entitled to preempt entire land transferred even if he Is not holding the land contiguous to all the lands transferred by the kabala.

11. The learned Counsel also refers to several other decisions of the Dacca High Court and of the Calcutta High Court, namely, in the cases of Salimuddin Mondal Vs. Mahitosh Biswas (1962) 14 D.L.R. 79s; Brojendra Chandra Saha vs. Debendra Chandra Saha (1965) 17 DLR 618; Mosammat Asimon Nessa vs. Md. Akbar Ali Sheikh. (1967) 19 DLR 659; Ruhul Amin Mestory Vs. Fazar Banu, (1969) 21 D.L.R. 647; Serdjuddin Ahmed Vs. Sadar Ali (1970) 22 DLR 64; Tamijuddin Ahmed Vs. Guljau Bibi (1974 26 DLR 93; Motilal Sikder Vs. Binodin Das (1976) 28 DLR (AD) 5; Behari Lal Roy Vs Pullin Behari Paul, 38 CWN 654; Surabala Basu Vs Rukmini Kanta Barman Roy 42 CWN 288 and Monoran Chatterjee Vs. Pavari M han, 43 CWN 220.

12. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan, learned Counsel for the Respondents finds it difficult to sup, port the view taken by the learned Judges of the High Court Division to the effect that the pre-emptors are entitled to claim preemption of the entire land transferred, although they may not have land contiguous to all the five plots. Learned Counsel submits that the learned Judges did not take correct view of the matter, although the application for preemption for part of the land transferred under the Kabala, on the ground of pre-emptors having land contiguous to only three plots, In conformity with subsection (1) of section 96 of the Act. The learned Counsel frankly concedes that a tenant claiming preemption on the ground of having land contiguous to the land transferred, is entitled to claim pre-emption of the land to which he hat contiguous land. He cannot claim provisions of the land, bough transferred under the same Kabala, but to which he has no contiguous land. The learned Counsel relies more on the construction of the different provision of section 96 than on any decision. He, however, refers to a decision of a Single Judge of the Dacca High Court is the case of Srimati Monkushi Das Vs. Abdus Sobhan Mia and others, (1977) 29 DLR 195. In this case the learned Judge repelled the contention that a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred may pre-empts all the lands transferred by the Kabala although he may not have contiguous land to all the lands.

13. A little more discussion about the history of introduction of the right of pre-emption as available to a Muslim under the Mohammedan Law, in the Land Laws in Bengal, will further clarify the present discussion on the question of applicability of the rule of partial pre-emption to a case by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred. By the Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1938 (Bengal Act VI of 1938), right of pre-emption was given to co-sharer tenants of holding. According to the amended section 26-F of the Bengal Tenancy Act one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding, a portion or share of which is transferred, could apply for pre-emption within the specified time. Section 26F after amendment created a right of pre-emption which is somewhat akin to a co-sharer's right of preemption under the Mohammadan Law, but tin right so created was not limited to the Muslim tenants only. It belonged only to the co-sharer tenants of an occupancy relate holding. Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides the right of pre-emption to a cashier tenant of the holding corresponding to the provisions of section 26.F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and also give the right of preemption to a tenant or tenants on the ground of holding laud contiguous to the land transferred.

14. The right of preemption given to the latter category can be exercised only on the ground of contiguity of land to the land transferred. The rule of partial preemption barring the right is only applicable to a case where preemption is claimed in the exercise of the right of a cohere tenant of the holding. This bar, however, cannot be applied to a case where a tenant claims pre-emption on the ground of contiguity of his land to the one transferred as in that case he is preempting the whole of the claim he is entitled to.

15. On perusal of the decision in the case of Makhanlal Reajuddin Sepal (1961) 13 D.L.R. 323 cited by Mr. Khandker it appears that the question of application of the Rule of partial preemption barring the right was considered in a case under section 96 of the Act wherein the pre-emptor has claimed pre-emption in respect of five plots out of eight plots conveyed under the sale deed.

16. In this case further question for consideration was whether it is necessary to Imp; lead all the tenants having land contiguous to those five plots even if he failed to establish his claim of having land contiguous to all the five plots. The learned Judge refrained from giving his decision on this question but the learned Judge observed that "It is well settled that if out of five plots originally claimed by the petitioners by way of pre-emption, the petitioner was allowed to press only with respect to three, although by was otherwise entitled to claim preemption with regard to all the five, the petitioners case should be hit by the bar of rule of partial preemption and, as such, the entire claim should fail". The learned Judge, however, further observed that if it appears that excepting three plots the petitioner had no land contiguous to any other plots, then certainly he cannot be hit by She rule of partial pre-emption. With these observations the case was remanded to the trial court. The above noted decision, in our opinion, cannot be cited as an authority for the proposition that a tenant claiming preemption only on the ground of contiguity of land is entitled to pre-emption of all the lands transferred by a kabala although he has no contiguous land to all the demised lands. This decision, rather, supports the case of the pre-emption respondents.

17. The decision in the can of Salimuddin Mondal (1962) 14 DLR 796 again cited by Mr. Khandker has no application to the facts of the case. IS has been held by a Single Judge of the Dacca High Court that an applicant for preemption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act cannot claim the liberty while exercising his right of preemption, to make a choice of his own and to make an arbitrary selection of one properly out of several properties although he is in a position to ask for pre-emption as a co-sharer tenant with respect of all of them.

18. In the case of Syed Abdul Karim V. Harendra Chandra Dhupi (1962) 14 DLR 847 as Mr. Khandker cited, question for consideration was as to whether the pre-emptors seeking pre-emption in respect of land in some plots out of several plots transferred by a kabala were required to implead all the tenants having contiguous land to all the plots. In this case transferred lands consisted of ten plots and the pre-emptors claimed preemption of all the plots under section 96 of the Act, both as co-sharer tenants and as tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred. In course of trial pre-emptor abandoned their claim of preemption in respect of three plots as they were not in a position to prove that they were holders of lands contiguous to those plots. Therefore, they had to confine their claim to the rest of the lands of the kabala. Their claim that they were co-sharers in the holding was also not accepted by the Court. Ultimately preemption was allowed in respect of the remaining plots on the ground that they are holders of the lands contiguous to those plots. On appeal by the preempted only question pressed before the appellate court was that some of the tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred not having been impleaded within the time the original applications was bad for defect of parties and in spite of subsequent addition of those persons as parties, the application was barred by limitation. The learned Judge being of the view that all the necessary parties not having been impleaded in the application when it was filed, the application was not properly constituted. Accordingly the order of the trial court allowing preemption was set aside. Against this order the pre-emptors filed an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. While considering this question Division Bench of the Dacca High Court made the following observation:

"It is no doubt true that preemption must be for the whole of the land transferred and there cannot be any partial preemption. But so far as the holder of the land contiguous to the land transferred is concerned, the section nowhere says that he must be contiguous to all the lands or plots of land transferred, .particularly, in view of the constitution of holding in this part of the country which generally does not form a compact block but consists of different parcels of land scattered over a field or fields in one or more villages. The Legislature could not have intended that contiguous holder on whom right of preemption has been given should have contiguity in respect of all the lands sold. It is clear from the fact that it has been made incumbent that all the contiguous holders of land should be impleaded as parties to the preemption proceeding so that every contiguous holder may get their legitimate share in the preemption. But suppose the other contiguous holders are not claiming any preemption within the time allowed as in the present case then does it necessarily follow that the claim of pre-emption of the whole of the land transferred, by a holder of land contiguous to only a portion of the land transferred should fail or should it fail in respect of the other lands transferred In that case, would it not be a partial pre-emption which is contrary to law and principle of preemption. On the other hand, if it is held that land contiguous to the land transferred means contiguity to the whole of the land transferred, then one who has contiguous land to one side or one of several plots of land transferred means contiguity to the whole of the land transferred, then one who has contiguous to one side or one of several plots of land transferred shall have no right of pre-emption. This would be against the provision of section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and tenancy Act, 1950. From the construction of the whole section this cannot be inferred, until and unless we read something which is not in the section."

The case was remanded to the trial court for determination of the question raised therein and disposal of the case. The question we are considering in this appeal was not under consideration in the said case. This also cannot be cited in support of the contention of the appellants that the application for preemption is hit by the bar of rule of partial preemption.

19. On perusal of the other decisions cited by Mr. M.H Khandker namely, 17 D1 R 618, 10 DLR 659, 21 DLR 647, 22 DLR 61, 26 DIR .e3, 28 DLR (A.D.) 5, 38 CWN 288 and 38 CWN 654, and 43 CWN 200 it appears that none of the decisions has got any relevancy to the question under consideration. In all those cases the question of applicability of the rule of bar of partial preemption was considered either in a case of preemption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act or in a case under the first part of section 96 of the Act.

<u>20. The decision in the case of Sreemoti Monkhuhi Das Vs. Abdus Subhan Mean and others (1977) 29 DLR 195 cited by Mr. Ahmed Subhan in support of the proposition that the application for pre-emption of two plots transferred by a registered kabala is maintainable on the ground of having contiguity of land, appears to be relevant for our present consideration. In this case the pre-emptor filed an application for preemption under section 96 of the Act for preempting two plots out of three plots by the kabala on the ground that he has no land contiguous to the other plot. Preemption was allowed by the learned Munsif who held that in the facts of that case claim for pre-emption was not hit by the rule of partial preemption. On appeal the order of preemption was affirmed. In revision at the instance of the preemption under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the question was as to whether in an application for preemption by a tenant or tenants holding land "contiguous to the land transferred", the pre-emptor has been given the option to confine his claim to any part of the land transferred by the kabala. The learned single judge of the High Court after examining the language of different sub sections of section 96 of the Act did not accept the contention of the petitioner that a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred may preempt all or none. The learned Judge, with reference to the language of subsections (1)(2) and (5) b) of section 96 of the Act has correctly taken the view that the pre-emptor having been found to be a tenant holding land contiguous to only two plots out of three plots transferred, was entitled to preempt only the land to which he holds land contiguous thereto.</u>

<u>21. In the instant case we have noticed that the facts are simple. The pre-emptors having land contiguous to only two of the five plots transferred claimed preemption, and the case comes under the second part of sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act. It has been already noticed that in case of preemption coming under the first part, the pre-emptor is required to establish his locus stands by showing that he is a co-sharer tenant of the holding. In such a case rule of partial pre-emption has been applied. In a case of preemption coming under the second part of sub-section (1) of section 96 of the act the tenant is not required to meet the same test. A tenant's right of preemption falling under the second part, the pre-emptor is required to establish that he has land contiguous to the land transferred. The expression holding land contiguous to the land transferred cannot be stretched to support the view that even in such a case the pre-emptor is required to include in the application for pre-emption also the lands to which he does not hold contiguous land and implead all the tenants holding contiguous lands to non-contiguous lands. This view cannot be reconciled with the different provisions of section 96 of the Act, as noticed above.</u>

<u>22. A little more elucidation on the topic with reference to the different sub-sections of section 96 will help in bringing home the point under present discussion. In section 96 the word 'Land' has been suitably used both in singular and plural. In sub-section (2) the word 'land' has been used both in singular and plural. In an application for pre-emption by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, all the co-sharer tenants of the holding and all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the hand transferred are required to be impleaded. From the use of the word 'land' in singular as indicated above, it can be safely inferred that a pre-emptor coming under the second part of sub-section (1) of section 96 cannot maintain his application for pre-emption for the land transferred to which he has no contiguity. According to sub-section (5)(b) in such an application only those tenants holding lands contiguous to the lands sought to be pre-empted are to be impleaded; and tenants holding lands contiguous to other lands transferred under the kabala but not subject of pre-emption, are not required to be impleaded. Sub-section (5) (b) removes any doubt that there might be. "Extent of contiguity" of land is the only test for determining the order of priority as among tenants claiming preemption on the ground of holding land, contiguous to the land transferred. If land transferred consists of one plot, all the tenants having land contiguous to the land under preemption are to be impleaded. Their right is to be determined in the manner as provided in sub-section (5) (b). In a case where land transferred consists of more than one plot a tenant or tenants having land contiguous to the plot or plots may apply for pre-emption, but in such a case, a tenant having land contiguous only to one of the plots, cannot claim pre-emption of other lands. Otherwise this will amount to allowing right of pre-emption to a tenant not having land contiguous to the land transferred. In an application by a tenant claiming preemption on the ground of contiguity of land, may apply to the Court for the holding or portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves. On comparison of the two parts of sub-sections (1) it becomes clear that in the case coming under the first part the pre-emptor is required to ask for preemption of entire portion or share of the holding transferred. But in the case coming under the second part, the pre-emptor is required to claim pre-emption for the holding or portion or share. Instead of mentioning said portion or share the expression "the holding or portion or share has been mentioned. If the land under preemption forms an entire holding, the pre-emptor is to apply for preemption of the holding the land under preemption forms a portion of the holding the pre-emptor is to apply for the portion only. Similarly if the pre-emptor is required to apply for the share only. Determination of the claim of the pre-emptor in such a case would be only on the basis of the contiguity of land and not on the basis of 'holding' or portion or share thereof.</u>

<u>23. Before concluding the discussion regarding compliance of the requirement of sub-section (2) of section 96, we consider it necessary to make it clear that the view taken by us with regard to compliance of subsection (2) of section 96 is in accordance with the view taken by this court in the case of Matilal Sikd Jr V. Binodini Das, (1976) 28 DLR (Appellate Division) 5. It is the requirement of the statute that all the co-sharer tenants of the holding and all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred and the transferee shall be made parties, but a case of preemption under section 96 may not be defeated on the analogy of non-joinder of all co-sharers in a suit for partition. The reason is obvious, because, in a suit for partition non-joinder of a co-sharer may prove fatal to the suit, but the position in a preemption case is different. Right of preemption accrues on a transfer of a portion or share of a holding of a radiant or when a holding is transferred which gives rise to an application for preemption either under the first part or second part of sub-section (1) of section 96. This right is not absolute but subject to the right of other coherers and holders of land contiguous to the land transferred as the case may be. Requirement of the statute of impleading those in whose favour right of pre-emption accrued, is for the sole purpose of enabling the court to adjudicate the claim of all the parties having right to pre-empt according to the provision under sub-section (5) of section 9( in one proceeding and avoiding multiplicity of proceedings. So, for the sake of full am complete adjudication of the rights and gran ting relief there should not be absence of an, necessary party.</u>

<u>24. In the case of Motilal Sikdar Vs. Binodini Das it has been observed that the question whether a person is a necessary party under sub-section (2) is a question of fact and the object of this provision is to provide the co-sharer tenants and the holding of contiguous lands with the opportunity of availing themselves of the provision of the said sub-section, but the benefits conferred under the sub section are meant for certain individuals and they can be waived. Any objection as to omission of a necessary party must be taken at the earliest possible opportunity and such objection if not so taken, may be deemed to have been waived.</u>

<u>25. In the reported case objection on the ground of omission, of necessary party in the pre-emption case was taken for the first time in the High Court in revision, and the High Court accepting the contention of the preempted that the proceeding was not properly constituted, dismissed the application for pre-emption. In disapproving the action of the High Court, and in the context of the facts and circumstances of the case it was observed as follows: "Since the benefit conferred under the said provision is meant for certain individuals they can very well be waived. In that view of the matter the positive injunction contained in the said sub-section as to making of parties in spite of its being couched in mandatory language, should be read as directory.</u>

26. The above noted observation is intended for the guidance of the Court in adjudicating the rights of the parties in a pre-emption proceeding under section 96 to see that so long there are parties before the court wherein the rights under the proceeding could be fully adjudicated the action shall not fail for defect of parties, but this cannot be read to minimise the responsibility of the pre-emptor or pre-emptors to comply with the requirement of impleading the necessary parties as provided under Subsection (2) of section 96.

<u>27. In our opinion in the instant case the application for pre-emption for 3.06 acres of' land consisting of two plots out of five plots measuring 3.86 acres of land, is in conformity with sub section (1) of section 96 of the Act. From the judgment of the High Court it appears that the learned Judge without noticing the difference, between the two parts or subsection (J) of Section 96 held:</u>

<u>"The pre-emptor must preempt the entire land of the holding or portion there of which has been transferred" That this view was taken without carefully noticing the difference in the language of different sub-sections of section 96 is evident from the subsequent observation made in the judgment. Therefore the view taken by the High Court cannot be sustained.</u>

<u>28. Further question for consideration is as to whether the direction given by the High Court Division for depositing the balance consideration money out of time is warranted by the law? Subsection (3) of section 96 of the Act requires that an application for preemption must be accompanied by deposit of the entire consideration money of the property transferred as stated in the notice under section 89 together with compensation @10% thereof. The statutory deposit being a condition precedent to the application being entertained, its noncompliance renders the application liable to be dismissed. The direction for depositing the balance consideration money out of time is also illegal and without jurisdiction.</u>

29. In the result, the appeal is allowed; the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division are set aside and those of the learned Subordinate Judge are restored. In the facts and circumstance of the case we allow half of the costs to the appellant.

End.

full_judgment:
Ms. Zinat Ara, J: In this writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution the petitioner challenged the legality of Order No.15 dated 30.11.2003 passed by the Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Khulna in Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2003 allowing an application under order XXVI Rule 11. of the Code of Civil Procedure and appointing a Chartered Accountant Firm to examine the accord of respondent No.2 on commission. 

2. The facts relevant for disposal of the rule are asunder: 
The petitioner Janata Bank (shorty, the Bank), having its head office at Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka and a Corporate Branch at Khulna; on an application of respondent No.3 on behalf of respondent No.2 opened Letter of Credit No. K.L.N/ L.C./CASH/24/1999 for import of 15000 metrictons of wheat. The imported wheat having been shipped, the shipping documents were negotiated by the foreign supplier and the negotiating bank sent the shipping documents to the Bank. As per terms of the said Letter of Credit, the negotiating bank lodged a claim for payment against the negotiated bill with City Bank N.A. the corresponding bank of the Janata Bank and obtained payment of US$ 20,64,871.50 being the value of the import bill from the Bank. The Bank after adjusting the Letter of Credit margin deposited by respondent Nos.2 and 3 (defendant Nos. l and 2) against the said import bill lodged PAD No.36 of 1999 in the name of respondent No.2 (defendant No.1). The Bank requested the above respondents to retire the said shipping documents on payment of the balance import bill but the above respondents did not come forwarded for payment of the same in spite of several reminders. The Bank came to know that respondent No.3 (defendant No.2) in connivance with the authority and the persons concerned managed to take delivery of the said imported goods without retiring the original shipping documents from the Bank and in this way the outstanding in the PAD Account No.36 of 1999 remained unadjusted. Respondent No.3 promised through letters to repay the said loan and on 25.10.2000 respondent Nos.3-9 (defendant Nos.2-8) documents executed personal guarantee and undertaking to pay the dues of the loan account of respondent No.2 and also deposited the original title deeds of some immovable property. There fore the above respondents are liable to pay the outstanding dues M the said PAD Account No.36 of 1999. The mortgaged property is liable to be sold for the realization of the outstanding dues of TIE. 2,31,80.431.30 as on 30.4.2003. The respondents were served with final noticed dated 17,102001 and legal notice dated 6.12.2001 through the learned Advocate of the Bank. The defendant respondents did not adjust the said amount. 

3. Under the above facts and circumstances the Bank as plaintiff instituted Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2003 before the Artha Rin Adalat, Khulna (shortly, the Adalat) for realization of the said amount of Tk. I 2,31,80,431.30 against defendant Nos.l-8 (respondent Nos.2-9). The defendants appeared and filed separate written statements to contest the suit. Defendant Nos. l and 2 also filed an additional written statement and the suit was fixed peremptory hearing on 20.102003. On that day, defendant Nos. I and 2 filed an application under Order XXVI Rule II of the Code of Civil Procedure (shorty the Code), for appointing a Chartered Accountant Firm to examine on commission and report about the statement of accounts of defendant No. 1 relating to suit Letter of Credit No. K.L.N/ L.C/CASH/24/1999 as well as 19 other letters of credit and PAD numbers which are not relating to the subject matter of the suit. The Bank opposed the said application by filing a written objection stating that except one letter of credit the other letters of credit are not related to the subject matter of the suit and the application for appointment of a Chartered Accountants Farm to examine all the letters of credit on commission is in order to delay the realization of outstanding dues in PAD Account No.36 of 1999. The Adalat without considering that the other letters of credit arc not related to the subject matter of the allowed the prayer illegally. The impugned order is contrary to the provision of Order XXVI Rule 12(2) of the Code. The impugned order is also contrary to the provision of  Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 since counter claim has been allowed by the impugned order.

4. In the backdrop of aforesaid facts and circumstances this writ petition has been filed and rule was obtained. 

5. Mr. S. N. Goswami, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No.3 opposes the rule. However, he did not file any affidavit in opposition controverting the statements made in the writ petition.

 6. Mr. Shameem Khaled Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the suit was filed by the Bank relating to PAD Account No.36 of 1999 arising out of a particular letter of credit dated 18.7.99 as mentioned in the plaint and there is no allegation about any over charge or claim relating to the said PAD Account No.36 of 1999. He further submits that the Adalat illegally allowed the Commissioner relating to 19 other letters of credit against the claim of the Bank which are not the subject matter of the suit. He next submits that the impugned order is contrary to the provisions of Order XXVI Rule 12(2) of the Code. He further submits that the impugned order is also contrary to the provision of section 18(2) of the Artha Rin. Adalat Ain, 2003, inasmuch as. by the impugned order the Adalat virtually allowed inclusion of a counter claim of the defendants and thus, the impugned order passed by the Adalat is beyond jurisdiction, illegal and is liable to be struck down. 

7. Mr. Goswami, the learned Advocate for the respondents contends that the impugned order as an appealable order and hence the present writ petition is not maintainable. He further contends that the impugned order was passed by the Adalat under the claim has been allowed by the impugned provision of Order XXVI Rule 11 of the order. Code in accordance with law and so. there is no scope to interfere within. Mr. Goswami. to fortify his contention refers to the decision in the case of Md. Mokaddas Ali and others Vs. Artha Rin Adalat (Subordinate Judge), Dinajpur and others, reported in 15 BLT (AD)237. 

8. In reply as to the question on maintainability, Mr. Shammem Khaled Ahmed has taken us through the provisions of Section 44(2) and 18(2) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (hereinafter stated as the AM), Order XXVI Rule 12(2) of the Code and then submits that the impugned order was passed on 30.11.2003 after the Ain came into force and according to section 44(2) of the AM, there is no scope to challenge any interlocutory order passed by the Adalat to the higher Court in appellate or revisional forum and, as such, the petitioner has no other alternative or efficacious remedy except under Article 102 of the Constitution. He next submits that in the case reported in I5 BLT (AD) 237, the impugned order dated 12.10.1999 was passed on an application under Order XXI Rule 89 of the Code before the Ain came into force. He further submits that in the instant case impugned order was passed under Order XXVI Rule 1 I of the Code after the Ain came into force and so, the said decision is not applicable in this case. He also submits that an order passed under Order XXVI Rule I I is not an appealable order under Order XLIII Rule I of the Code and therefore, the present writ petition is well maintainable. 

9. As per submissions made by the learned Advocate of the contending parties, the
moot questions to be decided in this Rule are as under : 
(i) whether the writ petition is maintainable 
(ii) whether the impugned order is legal and in accordance with law. 
Perused the writ petition and the materials on record. 

10. It is an admitted proposition that the petitioner instituted Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2003 before the Adalat for realization of Tk.12,31,18,431.30 as stood on 30.4.2003. Admittedly, respondent No.3 (defendant No.2) and other defendant had been contesting thee suit by filing written statements. Further that defendants Nos.' and 2 also filed an additional written statement and the suit was fixed for peremptory hearing. There is also no dispute that defendant Nos. l and 2 (respondent Nos.2 and 3) filed an application under Order XXVI Rule II of the Code for examination of 20 letters of credit in relation to the account of defendant No.I on commission by appointing a Chartered Accountant. Admittedly, out of the 20 letters of credit only the letter of credit dated 18.7.99 is the subject matter of the suit. The Adalat allowed that application by the impugned order with the following observation: 
“উভয় পক্ষের বিজ্ঞ কৌশুলীগনের বক্তব্য পর্যালোচনায় ও নথি দৃষ্ট হিসাব নিকাশের ক্ষেত্রে পক্ষগনের মধ্যে বিরোধ বা দ্বন্ড বিদ্যমান তাহা বলিবার অপেক্ষা রাথে না। একজন সি/এ কর্তৃক হিসাব নিকাশ অন্তে রির্পোট দাখিল হইলে সেই ক্ষেত্রে অত্র মোকদ্দমার নিষ্পত্তির ক্ষেত্রে জটিলতা নিরসন পূর্বক মোকদ্দমা নিষ্পতি্তর দ্রুততর হইবে। বলা নিস্প্রযোজন তাহা ছাড়া উক্ত রুপ হিসাব নিকাশ হইলে সেই ক্ষেত্রে কোন পক্ষের আদৌ কোন ক্ষতির সম্ভাবনা আছে তাহা পরিলক্ষেত হয় না। তদুপরি অনরুপ রিপোর্ট সাক্ষ্য আইনের বিধান মোতাবেক কোন কনক্লুসিভ প্রুফ বিধায় বিবাদীপক্ষের সি/এ নিয়োগের প্রার্থনায় আনীত দরখাস্ত মজ্ঞুর করিতে কোন বাধা দেখি না।”

11. Now let as first examine the question raised on maintainability. Accordingly to Mr. Goswami the present writ petition is not maintainable inasmuch as the impugned order is an appealable order. 

12. The impugned order was admittedly passed on 30.11.2003 after Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 came into play. 

13. In order to decide the question of maintainability, it is necessary to examine section 44(2) of the Ain which runs as under: 
“৪৪। অন্তর্বতীকালীন আদেশ।–
(১)------------------------।
(২) উপ-ধারা (৩) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে এই আইনের অধীন কোন আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত কোন অর্ন্তবতীকালীন আদেশকে উচ্চতর কোন আদালতে আপীল বা রিভিশন আকারে বির্তকিত করা যাইবে না ।----।”

So, it is clear that an interlocutory order passed by the Adalat can neither be challenged in the appellate form nor in the revisional forum. 

The decision reported in 15 BLT (AD) 237, as referred to by Mr. Goswami, is relating to an order dated 12.10.99 passed by the Artha Rin Adalat when Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 had been in force and before the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 came into operation. 
In Artha Rin Adalat Ain. 1990 there was no provision like section 44 of the Ain and provision of the Code was mostly applicable. Moreover, an order passed under Section XXVI Rule I I is not an appellable order under Order XLIII Rule I of the Code also. Therefore, the decision as referred to by Mr. Goswami has no manner of application in the present case. We are unable to accept the contention of Mr. Goswami, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.3. 

Thus, we are of the view that since specific provision has been made in Section 44(2) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 providing that an interlocutory order passed by the Adalat can not he challenged in appellate or revision forum and, there having been no other alternative remedy available to challenge the impugned interlocutory order, the present writ petition is maintainable. 
Accordingly we answer question No.(i) in the positive. 

14. Now let us turn to consider the next question i.e. the legality of the impugned order. 

15. In the application tiled by defendant Nos. l and 2 (vide annexure —C to the writ petition) it has been stated as follows: 
“এই বিবাদী ব্যাংকের ২৪টি এল সি খুলিয়া ৮০ কোটি টাকার বিভিন্ন প্রকার মালামাল আমদানী করেন। বাদী ব্যাংকের উক্ত এল সির জন্য এই বিবাদীর নিকট হইতে চলতি হিসাব সি ডি হইতে আইনানুগ হার অপেক্ষা অধিক বেআইনী ভাবে বিভিন্ন প্রকার চার্জ কর্তন করিয়াছেন ও সুদ ধার্য্য করিয়াছেন। যাহার পরিমান ৪ কোটি টাকার  উর্দ্ধে হইবে। ইহা ছাড়া এই বিবাদী জাবাবে বাদীর হিসাব অসামজ্ঞস্যপূর্ণ ও তঞ্চকতা করিয়াছেন তাহা দাবী করিয়াছেন। সে কারণ এই বিবাদীর নামীয় সি ও হিসাব ও তপশিল বর্ণিত এল সি গুলির ও পি এ ডির লেজার পরীক্ষা করিবার জন্য কমিশনার(চাটার্ড এ্যাকাউন্ট নিয়োগ) দেওয়া আবশ্যক। নতুবা এই বিবাদীপক্ষ ক্ষতিগ্রস্থ হইবে। তপশিল বর্ণিত এল সির সমুদয় হিসাব চাটার্ড এ্যাকাউনোটর দ্বারা নিরীক্ষা করিলে দেখা যাইবে বাদীর কোন টাকা পাওনা নাই।
 
16. Admittedly, the suit was for realization of TK.12,31,18,341.30 and it appears from the Paragraph 4(a) of the writ petition that the plaintiff field the suit for realization of loan relating to letter of credit dated 18.7.99 and the said letter of credit has been stated as the last item of the schedule of the application tiled under order XXVI Rule 11 of the Code by defendant Nos.l and 2 (vide annexure-C). There is no dispute that the other letters of credit Nos.29, 34, 57, 64 of 1994; 55, 72, 73, 78, 84 of 1995; 2. 18, 21, 23, 34 of 1996, 52 of 1992. 7, 14  33 18 of 1998 are not related to the subject matter of suit. The said letters of credit are of the years 1992, 1996 and 1998. The suit is relating to letter of credit dated 18.7.99. 

17. From the application (Annexure-C) it appears that the defendants did not claim before the Adalat that they ever raised any objection to the Bank about adjustment of account in relation to the aforesaid letters of credit (not the subject matter of the suit) by way of filing any application. Be that as it may, since the letters of credit , as stated above are admittedly not related to the subject matter of the suit, there is no scope to examine the account of respondent-defendant No.1 relating to the aforesaid letters of credit. Defendant Nos. l and 2 had no legal scope to counter claim. In this case, it appears that the defendants tiled an additional written statement (vide annexure-B to the writ petition) stating counter claim. Submission of written statement including set off or counter claim in a suit filed by the financial institution is prohibited under 1 section 18(2) of the Ain. So, by allowing application containing counter claim, the Adalat virtually 'allowed inclusion of counter claim in a suit filed by a financial institution. So, the impugned order clearly violated the provision of section 18(2) of the Ain, which reads as follows: 
“(২) কোন ঋণগ্রহীতা কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের বিরুদ্ধ এই আইনের অধীনে আদলতে সংশ্লিষ্ট ঋণ হইতে উদ্ভত কোন বিষয়ে কোন প্রতিকার দাবী করিয়া মামলা দায়ের করিতে পারিবে না িএবং ঋণ গ্রহীতা বিবাদী বাদী আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক দায়েকৃত মামলার লিখিত জবাব দাখিল করিয়া উক্ত লিখিত জবাবে প্রতিপক্ষগন (Set-off) বা পাল্টা দাবী (Counter claim) অন্তর্ভক্ত করিতে পারিবে না ।“(Bold and underlined emphasis given) 

18. Thus, it is found that the Adalat acted beyond its jurisdiction by allowing examination on commission of the 19 letters of credit, which are nor related to the subject matter of the suit. However, the claim of the defendants with respect to letter of credit dated 18,799 may only be examined on commission by the appointed Chartered Accountant Firm to ascertain whether the claim relating to letter of credit dated 18.7.1999 is proper. 

19. In view of the above, we find that the impugned order allowing examination of the account of defendant No.1 relating to letter of Credit dated 18.7.1999 is in accordance with law but the impugned order allowing examination of the account of defendant No.1 relating to the other letters of credit is not lawful and beyond jurisdiction. 
We answer question No. (ii) accordingly. 

20. In the result, the Rule is made absolute in part. The impugned order allowing examination of letters of credit Nos. 29, 34, 57, 64 of 1994; 55, 72, 73, 78, 84 of 1995; 2, 18, 21, 23, 34 of 1996, 52 of 1992, 7, 14, 33, 38 of 1998 on commission by Chartered Accountant Firm hereby declared to be without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

21. The order of stay stands vacated. 

22. Artha Rin Adalat, Khulna is directed to dispose of the suit expeditiously. 

23. No order as to cost. 
End.

full_judgment:
This appeal has been preferred by the purchaser pre-emptee-appellant against the judgment and order dated 08.01.2013, passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Narasingdi, in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No.06 of 2010 allowing the prayer for pre-emption under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act made by the pre-emptors-respondents.

The respondents pre-emptors instituted the case for pre-emption under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in respect of 322 decimals of land out of 47 decimals appertains to R.S. Plot Nos.1083 and 1084 under R.S. Khatian No.500 corresponding to S.A. Khatian No.717 of Mouza Virindi, under Police Station and District-Narsingdi. The pre-emptor’s claim in brief that the case land alongwith other lands belonged to Sultan Uddin Khan having jote right, C.S. Khatian No.649 in respect of that land was prepared in his name. While Sultan Uddin Khan had been enjoying and possessing the same became father of Siraj Ullah Khan, Kabur Ullah Khan, Jamir Ullah Khan, Atik Ullah Khan, Sabur Ullah Khan and Ketub Ullah Khan. Out of them Sabur Ullah Khan and Ketub Ullah Khan died in their childhood. The said Sultan Uddin Khan transferred 322 decimals of land of C.S. Plot No.600 to his wife Mojahara @ Majehara as gift by executing a deed, and as such the S.A. Khatian No.717 in respect of the said land was prepared jointly in the names of said Mojahara Khatun @ Majehara Khatun and with other co-sharers. Out of the entire land of C.S. Plot No.600 R.S. Khatian No.1083 was prepared in respect of 7 decimals R.S. Khatian in repsectg of said two plot were prepared correctly in the name of said Mojehara Khatun alone. Out of that land Mojehara Khatun transferred decimals of land by executing a deed of gift dated 26.11.1973 to her grand sons the pre-emptee No.3 Asam Ullah Khan, Pre-emptee No.4 Aziz Ullah Khan and their brother Nasir Uddin Khan by her deceased son Kabur Ullah Khan and she remain in possession and enjoyment of the rest measuring 142 decimals. While she had been	enjoying and possessing said 142 decimals of land died leaving behind 2 sons Siraj Ullah Khan and Jamir Ullah Khan with other grand children. After her death, by amicable partition Siraj Ullah Khan alone got aforesaid 142 decimals in his share and he had been residing thereon by constructing residential huts. Siraj Ullah Khan while had been enjoying and possessing  said  142 decimals  of  land  died  leaving behind the pre-emptor No.1 Rabeya Akter Khanom as his wife and other pre-emptors as his children. The pre-emptors have been residing in southern part of land appertains to R.S. Plot No.1084. The land of the disputed plot recorded in ejmali in R.S.

Khatian No.500. The aforesaid Jamir Ullah Khan died leaving behind the pre-emptee Nos.5-9 Janu, Runu, Jhinu, Lipa and Atik Ullah, that Atik Ullah died leaving behind the pre-emptee Nos.10-13 named Soyab, Shahid, Dipa and Khuki. The pre-emptee Nos.3 and 4 named Asam Ullah Khan and Aziz Ullah Khan and their brother Nasir Ullah transferred the case land to one Golam Kibria by registered kabala dated 10.01.1978. They made such transfer secretly, but subsequently it was disclosed. Since that transferred land is adjacent to their residence and for their convenience of movement it was necessary, but for financial disability they could not purchase the same after discloser of such transfer and for their convenience they made it purchased by the pre-emptee No.2 Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan by Kabala dated 16.10.1978. Now they (pre-emptors) attained the ability to purchase the same, but the pre-emptee No.2 Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan without any notice to them transferred the pre-empted land to the pre-emptee No.1 Amena Siddika. Such transaction was made collusively and secretly without any notice to them, otherwise they ought to have purchased the same. The said land was transferred at a consideration of Tk.6,00,000/-(six lacs) and as co-sharer by inheritance they prayed for pre-emption after depositing Tk.6,00,000/- (six lacs) alongwith the other cost as required by the law. The pre-emptee purchaser is a stranger in the pre-empted holding and she is not owner of any land contiguous to the pre-empted land. In the southern side of the pre-empted land residence of them (pre-emptors) is situated and it is necessary for them. The said transfer was made by executing a registered kabala dated 11.11.2009 and after knowing about such transfer they obtained the certified copy of the deed of such transfer on 06.01.2010 and instituted the case within the period of limitation. That the pre-empted land was illegally mutated in the name of pre-emptee No.2 Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan vide Mutation Case No.1448 of 2006-07 by order dated 26.08.2007 without any notice to them. About such mutation proceeding they were not at all informed and as such that mutation was illegal and collusive and obtained beyond the scope of law provides in Section 117(C) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and that is not binding upon them.

The purchaser pre-emptee No.1 named Amena Siddika opposed the prayer for pre-emption by filing written objection denying the material averments and stating that the pre-emptors have got no cause of action to file the case, the prayer for preemption is not maintainable under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, barred by waiver, estoppel and acquisition, as well as by limitation, suffers from defect of parties. It is further stated that admittedly Majehara Khatun was owner of the land appertains to R.S. Plot Nos.1083 and 1084 alongwith other lands, the R.S. Khatian No.500 was prepared in her name, and while she had been enjoying and possessing the pre-empted land transferred the same by executing a deed of Heba-bil-ewaz dated 26.11.1973 to Aman Ullah Khan, Azizur Rahman Khan and Nasir Uddin Khan and handed over its possession. While they had been enjoying and possessing the same by executing a kabala dated 10.11.1978 transferred the case land to Golam Kibria within the knowledge of the pre-emptors, while the said Golam Kibria had been enjoying and possessing the his purchased land sold the same by executing a kabala dated 16.10.1978 within the knowledge of the pre-emptors to Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan and handed over possession. The pre-emptors or none of their predecessors, did not raise any objection against such transfer nor they filed any pre-emption case. After such purchase Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan within the knowledge of the pre-emptors mutated her purchase land in her name and by opening a separate Khatian by order dated 26.08.2007 passed in Mutation Case No.1448 of 2006-07 had been paying rents to the Government. The said mutation was made within the knowledge of the pre-emptors. For want of money said Rawshan Ara Khan proposed to sale the pre-empted land to the pre-emptors and other co-sharers, but since the pre-empted land is not necessary the pre-emptors and their co-sharers denied to purchase and said that in case of purchase by somebody else they would have no objection. Thereafter the said Alhaj Rawsahn Ara Khan requested the pre-emptor Nos.2-4 for making arrangement of the sale of the pre-empted land. On her request the pre-emptee No.1 agreed to purchase the same with assurance that in case of purchase by her they would have no objection and they will never pray for any pre-emption. Thereafter in presence of the pre-emptors and at their mediation sitting in the house of the pre-emptors and in presence of the pre-emptee Nos.1 and 2 the value of the land was fixed at Tk.6,00,000/-(six lacs), the said amount paid by the purchaser was counted by the pre-emptee No.2 himself, and after such counting he handed over that amount to the vendor pre-emptor No.2 Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan on 10.11.2009. On the next day i.e. on 11.11.2009 the kabala was executed and registered. The pre-emptor Nos.2-3 were supposed to sign that kabala as witnesses, but cunningly they avoided and by making false claim made the prayer for pre-emption. In presence of the pre-emptors the vendor pre-emptee handed over possession of the pre-empted land to the purchaser pre-emptee on 12.11.2009 and since then she has been enjoying and possessing the same by growing crops therein. Previously the same land was transferred for more then one occasion and in respect of the same a separate khatian was open in the name of the vendor the pre-emptee. That the pre-emption proceeding is not maintainable and liable to be rejected.

After hearing the parties the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Narshindi by the impugned judgment and order dated 08.01.2013 allowed the prayer for pre-emption finding with others that pre-emptors are co-sharers by inheritance in the pre-empted holding and they made the prayer for pre-emption within time and are entitle to get pre-emption as per the provision of law.

Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order the purchaser pre-emptee Amena Siddiqa preferred this appeal.

Mr. Md. Zakir Hossain, alongiwth Mr. A.K.M. Bodruddoza, Advocates appear for the purchaser pre-emptee/appellant and on the other side Mr. Moqbul Ahmed, alongwith Mr. Jafor Alim Khan, and Mr. Ranjan Chakrabarti, Advocates appeared for the pre-emptors-respondents.

Mr. Md. Zakir Hossain, learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submits that admittedly the pre-emptors or their predecessors were co-sharers in the pre-empted holding, but now they are no more co-sharers for admitted separation of joma by the mutation proceeding mentioned above. Moreover, admittedly at first the pre-empted land was transferred to Golam Kibria by a kabala dated 10.01.1978. At the time of such transfer the pre-emptors or their predecessors did not raise any objection nor made any prayer for pre-emption. Thereafter while the said Golam Kibria had been enjoying and possessing the pre-empted land sold the same by executing a kabala dated 16.10.1978 to Alhaj Rawshan. In the occasion of that sale the pre-emptors or none of their predecessors did not raise any objection nor made any prayer for pre-emption. Admittedly said Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan had been enjoying and possessing the pre-empted land for long time up to 2009 till its transfer by the pre-emptd kabala dated 11.11.2009 and it is also admitted that the sold land had been mutated in the name of said Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan on 26.08.2007. After such separation of joma or opening of a new Khatian and payment of rent vide that separate khatian the pre-emptors can not claime them as co-sharers in the pre-empted holding. Moreover, for not raising any claim of pre-emption since long time about 35 years the present claim of the pre-emptors is barred by waiver, estoppel, and acquiescence. In last 35 years the pre-emptors did not claim for pre-mption for the case that they were unable to make payment of the value, but now they became able and sought for pre-emption. Such claim can not be entertained as per the provision of law provides in Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or under any other law of the land in respect of pre-emption. In support of his such contention Mr. Zakir Hossain cited the decisions in the cases of, Iqbal Hossain Talukder Vs. Md. Joynal Abedin Talukder and others reported in 55 DLR 604, Shah Alam (Md.) Vs. Md. Shahidur Rahman and others reported in 55 DLR 214, and also an unreported judgment of the Appellate Division of this Court dated 20.07.2010 passed in Civil Appeal No.300 of 2003.

In reply of his such argument Mr. Maqbul Ahmed, appearing for the respondents pre-emptors submits that admittedly in January, 1978, pre-emptor’s co-sharer transferred the pre-empted land to Golam Kibria and it is also admitted that Golam Kibria sold the same to Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan. The said second transfer was not for the interest of Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan but for convenience of the pre-emptors. As per the pre-emptors their residence is situated in a land adjacent to the pre-empted land and for their movement from and to their residence the pre-empted land is necessary for them. But the transfer by their co-sharer to Golam Kibria in January 1978 was made secretly without their knowledge and without any notice to them. They had the right to sought for pre-emption, but for their inability to make payment of the value they did not sue for pre-emption, rather for their convenience they made it purchased by their relation Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan for their use. Though said Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan purchased but she as relation allowed them to use the pre-empted land. Subsequently after 35 years without their knowledge she transferred the pre-empted land to the appellant. Such transfer was made secretly and collusively without any notice to them, otherwise they ought to have purchase the same since by this time they attain the ability to purchase the pre-empted land which is necessary for them. For their movement from and to their residence it is required by them. Hence, they sought for pre-emption by depositing the required money. Though the pre-empted land had been mutated in the name of Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan by the above numbered Mutation Case No.1448 of 2006-07 but that case was not legal one for want of service of notices upon them as per Section 117(C) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The said mutation proceeding is illegal and not binding upon them. For such illegality separation of joma as made in the instant case will not be effective and they will be treated as co-sharers in the disputed holding. He further submits that for not raising any objection or for not making any prayer for pre-emption at the time of transfer in January 1978 by their co-sharers to Golam Kibria and in October 1978 by Golam Kibria to Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan their right of pre-emption can not be barred by estoppel, waiver and acquiescence or by limitation since they are till co-sharers in the pre-empted holding. They did not sought for pre-emption or raised objection to sale or not made attempt to purchase the pre-empted land for their inability to make payment of the value, but now they became able to make payment and after 35 years they legally made the prayer for pre-emption on the new cause of action arose in 2009. That cause of action is separate one and they are legally entitled to sue for pre-emption on the new cause of action as they made in the instant case. He further submits that allowing prayer for pre-emption is discretion of the Court and as such the Court below considering necessity and requirement of the preemptors allowed their prayer finding that they are till co-sharers in the pre-empted holding and their claim of pre-emption is not barred by limitation, nor by the principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. In support of his such contention Mr. Md. Maqbul Ahmed cited the decisions in the cases of, Most. Kohinoor Begum Vs. Abdul Khaleque reported in 11 BLT (AD) 172, Fajar Uddin Vs. Moijuddin and others reported in 44 DLR (AD) 62, Haji Aktaruzzaman Vs. Jagannath Paul and another reported in 17 DLR 384, Abdur Rouf and others Vs. Ahmuda Khatoon reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 269, Chandra Kumar Maladash Vs. Abdul Mutaleb and others reported in 19 BLD (SC) 36, Begum Asia Rahman Vs. Abdul Bashir Bhuiyan reported in 26 DLR (SC) 58, Jodoy Chandra Mali Vs. Abdul Khaleque and others reported in 27 DLR (AD) 114, Asir Uddin Sheikh Vs. Siraj Uddin Talukder and others reported in 30 DLR 75.

I have heard the learned Advocates, gone through the record, and the decisions cited by the learned Advocates of both the sides. On perusal of materials on record it appears that Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan had been enjoying and possessing the pre-empted land since October 1978 after purchasing the same from Golam Kibria who purchased the same land from admitted co-sharer of the pre-emptors in January 1978. As per the pre-emptors at the time of transfer by their co-sharer to Golam Kibria they were unable to make payment of value of the case land though it was claimed that such transfer was made collusively. For their inability they did not sought for any pre-emption, but for their convenience on their request their relation Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan purchased the same from Golam Kibria in October 1978 after possessing the same for 9 months by him. As per the pre-emptors the said Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan is their relation. The pre-empted land is adjacent to their residence and for their movement to and from their residence the same is necessary. For them their relation Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan on their request and at their instance purchased the same. Now their said relation Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan without offering the pre-empted land to them secretly and collusively sold the same to the purchaser pre-emptee without any notice to them though by this time they attain the ability to purchase the said land even at the cost of 6,00,000/-(six lac) though they failed to make payment of 8,000/-(eight thousand) in 1978 by which Golam Kibria purchased the same. The question remains whether the said plea or story of purchase by their relation Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan for their convenience on their request and at their instance is believable. At the same time the pre-emptors also claiming that they are till co-sharer by inheritance in the disputed holding or in same joma even after separation of the same. As per them by the admitted mutation proceeding the joma was separated but the said mutation proceeding is illegal because it suffers from the defect of non service of notices upon them or upon all co-sharers as it required under Section 117(C) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The said mutation or separation of joma is not binding upon them as being illegal, as such till they are co-sharers by inheritance as their predecessors in the disputed holding. But apparently the said separation of joma or order of mutation is till in existence. It has not been set aside or cancelled by any higher authority. Even the pre-emptors did not take any step to get it cancelled. As such, it is difficult to hold that the joma has not been separated rather it is apparent that the joma has been separated before two years of purchase by the pre-emptee. The another question raised by the pre-emptee that the pre-emption proceeding is barred by estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. On perusal of the decisions cited by the learned Advocates of both the sides I find such question was discussed in the decisions reported in 11 BLT and 44 DLR as cited above. In those decisions their lordships of the Appellate Division expressed the view that such claim is barred by estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. I do not find any reason to differ with such view, rather I am inclined and bound to follow the same. As per those decisions the decisions about the question of acquiescence and waiver, differs and varied on different circumstances. In deciding such question the circumstances should be considered by the Court. The other decisions cited above do not appears to me as so relevant because the pertinent question in this case is nothing but the question of waiver, estoppel, as well as separation of joma. In the circumstances mentioned above, it appears that before 35 years the co-sharers of the pre-emptors transferred the pre-empted land to Golam Kibria in January 1978 without any objection from them and they did not sue for pre-emption. In October 1978 the said Golam Kibria transferred the same to Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan who had been enjoying and possessing the same for last 35 years. As per the pre-emptors the said Alhaj Rawshan Ara Khan is their relation and for their convenience they made it purchased by her. But now they are alleging that their said relation transferred the same to the appellant without any information to them. So, their claim of relationship with Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan or purchase of the pre-empted land by her for their convenience is not believeable at all. Rather it appears to me that they tried to claim the right of pre-emption as of their luxury which is not permitted by the law. I hold the view that the right of pre-emption is a special right permitted by the laws, like The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, The Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, or The Mohammedan Law. But none of those laws allow any such luxury to make such prayer for pre-emption after 35 years on the plea that at the first occasion of transfer they were unable to purchase and now they became able. In the instant case the cause of action for pre-emption arose in 1978 and since 1978 up to 2009 the preemptors did not pray for pre-emption. But in 2009, after the third transfer by Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan to the appellant they sought for pre-emption on the plea that till they are co-sharers in the pre-empted holding since the separation of joma made in favour of Alhaj Rowshan Ara Khan in 2007 is illegal for want of service of notices as mentioned above. I have already observed above that the separation of joma is till in force and after such separation the pre-emptors have no reason to claim themselves as co-sharers in the pre-empted holding. Hence, they have no right to sought for pre-emption.

Accordingly, this appeal is hereby allowed. The impugned judgment and order dated 08.01.2013 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Narasingdi, in Miscellaneous Case No.06 of 2010, is hereby set aside.

However, there is no order as to cost.

Send down the lower Court’s records immediately.

End.

Minal Kanti Biswas, Advocate-For the Petitioner. 
Gobinda Chandra Tagore, Advocate-For the Opposite Party

Swapon Kumar Gain ------ Petitioner
Vs.
