full_judgment:
By these Rules the opposite party was called upon to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 12-6-2000 passed by the District Judge, Dhaka in Family Appeal No. 22 of 1993 reversing these dated 10-5-1993 passed by the Assistant Judge, 4th Court and Family Court, Dhaka in Family Suit No, 11 of 1987 should not be set aside or such other of further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. These two rules arose out of judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka reversing those of the Family Court Judge and 4th Court of the Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Family Suit. Family suit was dismissed and an appeal preferred by the plaintiff was allowed and the suit was decreed. Against the said decree the plaintiff preferred Civil Revision No. 1058 of 2001 while the defendant preferred Civil Revision No. 4785 of 2000 and both the revisions were heard together and are being disposed of this common judgment.

3. The opposite party as plaintiff instituted Family Suit No. 11 of 1987 in the 4th Court of the Assistant Judge, Dhaka against the present petitioner praying for a decree for restitution of conjugal rights and for realisation of maintenance cost alleging, inter alia, that the plaintiff and defendant were involved in love affairs and they ultimately, got married on 3-8-1986 and thereafter swore an affidavit before a notary public confirming the marriage held at Dhakeswari Mandir on observance of religious ceremony. It is also alleged that the marriage was consummated and the plaintiff and the defendant, who used to live separately in Hall and hostel, used to pass nights at different residential hotels in Dhaka for sexual intercourse. It is also asserted that the plaintiff and defendant became acquainted with each other for long before their marriage and the defendant was student while the plaintiff was a service holder as a Nurse of Dhaka Medical College Hospital and she used to assist the defendant financially for prosecuting his studies and that the plaintiff in all paid about Taka 45,000 for the purpose of treatment of her father-in- law excluding financial support to the defendant while the defendant was a student. The plaintiff then alleged that the defendant created pressure upon the plaintiff to bring Taka 2 lac from her father but as she refused to get the said amount, the defendant assaulted the plaintiff and ultimately denied their marital ties. The plaintiff thus instituted the suit for her restitution of conjugal rights and for realisation of maintenance cost at the rate of Taka 2000 per month.

4. The defendant did not contest the suit and accordingly, the suit was decreed ex parte on 6-1-1990. The defendant got the said ex parte decree set aside by filing an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. After the restoration of the suit the defendant did not appear to contest the suit and this time the trial Court dismissed the suit on the sole ground that the plaintiff could not produce any paper in support of the marriage.

5. The plaintiff then preferred Family Appeal No. 22 of 1993 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka. The appeal was transferred to the Court of Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Bishesh Adalat, Dhaka under a Memo of Ministry of Law and Parliamentary Affairs but subsequently in view of an unreported decision of the High Court Division taking the view that Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Bishesh Adalat has no jurisdiction to bear Family Appeals, the appeal before Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Bishesh Adalat, Dacca was re-transferred to the learned District Judge for disposal. The learned District Judge allowed additional evidence to be produced by the plaintiff and also took deposition of few witnesses on behalf of the plaintiff and then by a judgment and decree dated 12-6-2000 held that the plaintiff has proved her case of marriage with the defendant and accordingly, allowed the appeal and decreed the suit declaring that the material tie between the plaintiff and defendant subsists and the defendant was directed to pay maintenance of the plaintiff at the rate of Taka 800 per month.

Being aggrieved thereby the defendant obtained a Rule in Civil Revision No. 4785 of 2000 and the plaintiff obtained a Rule in Civil Revision No. 1058 of 2001.

<u>6. Mr Minal Kanti Biswas, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in Civil Revision No. 4785 of 2000 has placed both the judgments and all other evidence on record before me and submits that, the memo of appeal was not signed by the plaintiff-appellant before the lower appellate Court and therefore, there was no appeal preferred before the learned District Judge against the judgment and decree of the trial Court by which the suit was dismissed. Mr Biswas then submits that the lower appellate Court committed an error of law in allowing additional evidence to be produced before the appellate Court overlooking that Family Court Ordinance does not provide for application of Civil Procedure Code excepting only sections 10 and 11, Mr Biswas then submits that, the plaintiff could not prove the two essential elements of Hindu marriage, namely, invocation before the sacred fire and saptapdai. In the absence of any proof of fulfilment of invocation before the sacred fire and saptapadi, a Hindu marriage is not complete and thus the plaintiff is not entitled to any relief in the suit. In support of his submission. Mr Biswas has relied on few decisions which includs a case between Amullya Chandra Modak. petitioner vs State reported in 35 DLR 160. The learned Advocate has further relied on a decision in the case of Nelly Zaman vs Giasuddin Khan reported in 34 DLR 221 to support his contention that a suit for restitution of conjugal right at the instance of the wife is not sustainable. The learned Advocate has also relied in the case of Sharmin Hossain alias Rupa vs Mizanur Rahman reported in 2 BLC 509 in support of his submission that a suit for restitution of conjugal right is void.</u>

<u>7. Mr Gobinda Chandra Tagore, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party, on the other hand, supports the decision of the lower appellate Court and submits that the defendant did not appear in the suit to contest the suit and did not file any written statement and thereby admitted the assertions made by the plaintiff in the plaint and thus on the admission of the defendant the suit could be decreed. The learned Advocate has further submitted that, the Court of the District Judge is the principal civil Court of the District and an appeal lies from a judgment, decree or Order of a Family Court to the District Judge who is not a persona designata and the provision of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure for additional evidence is applicable. The learned Advocate has also relied on a decision in the case of Moinuddin (Md) vs Amina Khan Majlish reported in 42 DLR 483 in support of his submission that under section 17 (1) of the Family Court Ordinance an appeal shall lie from a judgment, decree or order of Family Court to "the Court of the District Judge" The latter being a civil Court, provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure applies in the appeal preferred before the learned District Judge who is not a persona designata but a civil Court. The learned Advocate has also relied on a decision in the case of Md Sirajul Islam vs Helana Begum and others reported in 3 BLT 40. The learned Advocate has further relied on a decision in the case of Hasibur Rahman (Md) vs Shakila Begum and others reported in 53 DLR 152 in support of his submission that the District Judge referred to in section 17(1) of the Family Court Ordinance is the Judge of the principal Civil Court of the District and never a persona designata and the Code of Civil Procedure is very much applicable to family appellate proceeding before the learned District Judge. The learned Advocate further relied on a decision in the case of Utpal Kanti Das vs Monju Rani Das reported in 50 DLR (AD) 47 to support his submission that, once the celebration of a marriage in fact is established there shall be a presumption of there being a marriage in law and observance of the essential ceremonies.</u>

<u>8. I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for both the parties and perused the impugned judgment and all other evidence on record. It is not disputed that the suit was decreed ex parte and the defendant challenged the ex parte decree by filing a case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and got the ex parte decree set aside and the suit was restored but did not appear to contest the suit by filing any written statement. The plaint shows that the plaintiff clearly made an assertion that marriage under the Hindu law in terms of Vedic ceremonies was observed in Dhakeswari Mandir by a Purohit this clear assertion of the plaintiff, as made in the plaint, has not been denied or challenged by the defendant by filing any written statement. The plaintiff, however, made an assertion that there was exchange of garlands before the deity Kalimatha but such statement alone would not disqualify the marriage held in  Dhakeswari Mandir by a "Purohit" upon observance of all formalities as required under the Hindu Law. The lower appellate Court being the final Court of fact has, on consideration of the evidence on record, come to a finding of fact that a marriage took place between the plaintiff and the defendant. This finding of fact with regard to marriage carried a valid presumption that a marriage in law under the Hindu system was solemnised upon observance of all the legal formalities including saptapadi and invocation before the sacred fire. I have myself perused the plaint and the evidence of 'Purohit' who solemnised the marriage and stated in his evidence that there was saptapadi at the time of marriage also. The defendant has not taken any step to dislodge the evidence touching observance of essential ceremonies of marriage under the Hindu Law. When a marriage, in fact, is proved our Appellate Division in 50 DLR (AD) 47 held "As marriages in fact has been proved in this case, marriage in law must be presumed. In the absence of any evidence to the contrary, it is, therefore, amply proved that the plaintiff and the defendant were married according to the Hindu Shastra" Admittedly, the defendant did not raise the plea of invalidity of the marriage because of non-performance of any essential ceremony. In view of the aforesaid decision of the Appellate Division, we are permitted to presume a valid marriage in law from the finding of fact of the appellate Court that a marriage, in fact, took place between the plaintiff and the defendant. I have already noticed that the defendant did not deny or challenge the factum of marriage between the plaintiff and the defendant. I am therefore, inclined to take the view, in agreement with the learned District Judge, that a legal and valid marriage took place between the plaintiff and the defendant upon observance of all legal formalities according to Hindu Shastra.</u>

<u>9. I am now called upon to consider whether additional evidence is permissible before the appellate Court against a judgment, decree or order passed by the Family Court. An appeal lies to the learned District Judge against a judgment, decree and order of Family Court under section 17(1) of the Family Court Ordinance, 1985. The Court of the District Judge has not been defined in the Family Court Ordinance, 1985. I am therefore, in respectful agreement with the view expressed by a single Bench in the case reported in 53 DLR 152 holding "District Judge" means the "Judge of the Principal Civil Court" of the District. The "District Judge" as the 'Family Appellate Judge' cannot be ascribed to be 'Persona Designata' 'District Judge' being the "Principal Judge of the Civil Court" of the District, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure is very much applicable to family appellate proceeding before Judge or the transferee Judges like Additional District Judge and Subordinate Judge. "The same view was expressed by a Division Bench in the case reported in 42 DLR 483 holding the view that "Thus there is no scope for thinking that the District Judge referred to in the said Ordinance is a persona designata or a Family Court; On the other hand, it appears that the appellate Court under the said Ordinance also includes any Court of Additional District Judge or Subordinate Judge under the administrative control of the District Judge. These are all Civil Courts and the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable to proceeding before these Courts", The decision reported in 38 DLR (AD) 172 relates to the provision of Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983 and their Lordships of the Appellate Division took the view that the District Judge mentioned in the said Ordinance is not a persona designata but is a Principal Civil Court of the District and is subject to both the appellate and revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division, From the aforesaid decisions it is concluded that a Family Appellate Court is a Court permitted to receive additional evidence under Order XLI, 1 rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned District Judge has taken additional evidence in respect of both documentary and oral evidence and, on consideration of those documents, came to the conclusion that a marriage took place between the plaintiff and the defendant. This finding of fact of the final Court of fact being based on assessment and consideration of evidence, I do not find any ground to disagree with such finding of fact. The learned Advocate for the petitioner could not point out any misreading of evidence or non-consideration of evidence or misconstruction of evidence to permit this revisional Court to disturb the finding of fact recorded by the final Court of fact. The submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the memorandum of appeal before the learned District Judge filed by the plaintiff- appellant was not signed by the plaintiff-appellant is totally incorrect and misconceived, I have myself perused the memorandum of appeal preferred before the learned District Judge, Dhaka and I find that on all the pages of the memorandum of appeal the plaintiff-appellant had put her signature. The memorandum of appeal before the appellate Court contains 4 pages and in all the 4 pages I find the signature of the plaintiff-appellant. The submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that two essential ceremonies, such as, saptapadi and invocation before sacred fire of a valid marriage under the Hindu law have not been proved by the plaintiff is again without any basis. The evidence on record, clearly indicate that a marriage took place between the plaintiff and the defendant in Dhakeswari Mandir conducted by a "Purohit" and the said "Purohit" in his evidence stated that he conducted the marriage upon compliance of all the formalities of Hindu Shastra. The evidence of the "Purohit" was corroborated by 4 other witnesses who were present during marriage in Dhakeswari Mandir. The decision reported in 35 DLR 160 as referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner though arises out of a Criminal Proceeding is of no help to the learned Advocate as a valid presumption is permitted to be drawn from the fact that marriage between the plaintiff and the defendant took place in Dhakeswari Mandir. The presumption is that all the legal formalities under the Hindu law were complied with and though such presumption is rebuttable but the defendant has not rebutted the presumption. I have already held that the plaintiff has proved a valid marriage under the Hindu law between the plaintiff and the defendant. The decision reported in, 2 BLC 509 as referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner relates to a marriage under the Muslim law and has no manner of application in respect of marriage under the Hindu law. The decision reported in 34 DLR 221 as referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner also relates to Muslim marriage and can not be applied in connection with Hindu marriage. In view of my above consideration, I do not find any substance in any of the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner' in Civil Revision No. 4785 of 2000.</u>

10. Mr Gobinda Chanpa Tagore, in support of Civil Revision No. 1058 of 2001 has invited my attention to the prayer made in the plaint where the plaintiff prayed for monthly maintenance at the rate of Taka 2000 per month. The lower appellate Court has allowed maintenance cost at the rate of Taka 800 per month, The marriage took place on 3-8-1986 and the defendant disowned the wife and the marriage on 1-1-1987. The family suit was instituted on 11-3-1987. The learned District Judge did not assign any reason for directing the defendant to pay Taka 800 per month to the plaintiff by his judgment and decree dated 12-6-2000. For an adult lady Taka 800 was not sufficient for maintenance even in June, 2000. The learned District Judge did not consider the existing price level and the requirement of an individual to lead a simple life, and with comfort and Taka 800 was not sufficient.

11. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case I am of the opinion the plaintiff should get at least Taka 2000 as she claimed in the suit as monthly maintenance from the defendant but this amount the plaintiff will get now with any retrospective effect but from the month of June, 2005. The plaintiff shall get Taka 800 per month from the date of the Judgment of the learned District Judge from 26-6-2000 and the defendant is directed to send Taka 2000 every month from June, 2005 at the address of the plaintiff which is mentioned in the revisional application of the defendant being Civil Revision No. 4785 of 2000 in default whereof the plaintiff shall be at liberty to attach the salary upto the amount of Taka 2000 from the salary of the defendant or to realise the amount in accordance with law.

12. In the result Civil Revision No. 4785 of 2000 is discharged without any order as to costs. Civil Revision No. 1058 of 2001 is also discharged with the modification that the defendant shall pay an amount of Taka 2000 per month from the month of June, 2005 by way of money order within 10th of every English calendar month to the address of the plaintiff, as mentioned in the cause title of Civil Revision No. 4785 of 2000. The plaintiff is further directed to notify the defendant, if any change in her address takes place by a registered post with acknowledgement due so that the defendant may remit the monthly maintenance for every month. In the facts of the case, I do not make any order as to costs.

13. The order of conditional stay as granted 10-1-2001 is hereby vacated.

The learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that, his client has duly paid the monthly amount of Taka 800 up to the months of March, 2005.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J:  Defendant No.1 presented the appeal against judgment and decree dated 28-9-99 passed by Subordinate Judge, Court No.1 at Chittagong in Other Suit No. 42 of 1998, which decreed the suit.

2. On 8-1-97 respondent No.1 as plaintiff instituted Other Suit No. 4 of 1997 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge at Sadar in Chittagong against the appellant and others for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and for further declaration that ex-parte judgment and decree dated 30-7-95 passed In Other Suit No. 151 of 1999 by Second Commercial Court and Subordinate Judge at Chittagong in respect of the suit property described in schedule-1(Kha) to the plaint was forged, collusive, illegal, false, void and not binding upon the plaintiff. The suit was then on transfer renumbered Other Suit No. 42 of 1998 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge at Chittagong.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that defendant No. 2, partnership firm obtained lease of entire suit property as described in the schedule to, the plaint for 99 years on 7-8-63 from the Public Works Department of the erstwhile East Pakistan Government. While said firm was thus in owner in possession a suit being Other Suit No. 228 of 1981 was filed in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge for partition of said property amongst the partners. The suit ended in compromise. Defendant Nos. 3 to 5 got schedule property partitioned amongst them by a deed of partition being No. 2008 dated 1-11-84. Defendant No.5 Anwara Begum got the property of schedule-1(Ka) and defendant No.3 and 4 schedule-1(Kha) property, Defendant Nos. 3 and 4. Taherul Anowar, and Nilufar Anowar got their names mutated in respect of schedule-1(Kha) property and possessed by raising boundary wall surrounding said property and payment of rents.

4. Then, said defendant Nos. 3 and 4 entered into an agreement to sell the property to the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 10,00,000 and on receipt of Taka 9,70,000 on 8-9-86 executed an agreement.

5. Then, on 25-7-90 said defendants gave a power of attorney to Shamsul Huq to execute and register necessary sale deed transferring said schedule-1(Kha) property to the plaintiff and accordingly, Shamsul Huq transferred the suit land by a registered deed being No. 196 dated 13-1-91. The plaintiff got his name mutated in respect of said schedule-(Kha) property and possessed on payment of rents under the mutated khatian,

6. In December, 1996 the plaintiff received a notice from Double Mooring Police Station and on inquiry came to know that defendant No.1 company obtained aforesaid ex-parte decree dated 30-7-95 in Other Suit No. 151 of 1992. The plaintiff had no knowledge about the suit nor did said defendant No.1 make him party in the suit.

7. The decree was therefore, collusive, fraudulent and obtained behind the back of the plaintiff. Hence, the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession.

8. Defendant No.1 Bengal Bricks Industries Limited contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the entire case of the plaintiff.

9. It was contended that the suit as framed was not maintainable. The plaintiff got no locus-standi under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act to seek the relief as prayed for in the suit. The purchase of schedule-1(Kha) land by the plaintiff was hit by the principles of lis pendens as provided under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act.

10. It was further contended that defendant No. 1 was a private limited company while defendant No. 2 was a partnership firm. Defendant No.3 and 4 were partners of the firm. Defendant No.3, as managing partner entered into a contract with defendant No.1 for sale of the entire property of the firm as described in schedule-1 at a consideration of Taka 18,00,000 and on 27-2-81, on receipt of Taka 5,00,000 executed an agreement, clearly stipulating to execute and register a sale deed within three months of the agreement after obtaining necessary income tax certificate permission, etc and on receipt of the balance of the consideration. Failing which, defendant No. 3 further stipulated to hand over possession of said property.

11. There were originally three partners namely, defendant No.5, defendant No.6 and one Akmal Mia, father of defendant No.7 of the firm. On 27-7-77 Akmal Mia and defendant NO.6 retired from the firm.

12. Defendant No.3 was taken in as partner. Then, in April 1981, defendant No. 5-retired from the firm and defendant No. 4 was taken in as partner. Defendant No.3 became managing partner. At the end of 1981 defendant No.3 again received Taka 1,00,000 and handed over possession of said property. Defendant No.1 surrounded schedule-I property with walls.

13. Even after several correspondences defendant Nos. 5, 6 and said Akmal (since deceased) instituted Other Suit No. 228 of 1981 in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge at Chittagong for declarations that they were the only partners of the firm that, they acquired the schedule-1 property; that defendant Nos. 3 and 4 acquired no interest in such property; that they were not partners of the firm and that they had no right or authority to transfer said property to defendant No.1.

14. Then they obtained an ad-interim injunction. Pursuant to summons, defendant Nos. 1 and 3 and 4 appeared and opposed the application for temporary injunction. The application for temporary injunction was rejected and ad interim injunction was vacated. Said defendant Nos. 5, 6 and Akmal then presented FMA No. 17 of 1983 before this Division and obtained an order of stay rejecting prayer for injunction in Civil Rule No. 137 (FM) of 1983. Then, .in April, 1983 defendant. No 3 again, approached defendant No. 1 for Taka 60,000 and defendant No.1 paid him Taka 60,000. But defendant No.3 along with defendant No.5, who was his mother, started conspiracy to deprive the defendant No.1 of said property. Said defendants then entered Into an agreement for partition amongst themselves.

15. It may be noted that defendant No. 3 opposed the claim of his mother in the suit property by filing a written objection. Defendant Nos. 6 and 7 ultimately disclaimed any right, title or interest in the suit property.

16. But defendant No. 3 did not obtain the permission from the Public Works Department and income tax clearance certificate and failed to execute and register the sale deed. In the situation, defendant No.1 was on 10-4-84 constrained to institute Other Suit No. 31 of 1984 in the same Third Court of Subordinate Judge against defendant Nos. 2 to 7 for specific performance of the contract dated 27-2-81. The suit was ultimately renumbered as Other Suit No. 151 of 1992. Defendant No. 3 appeared and filed a written statement admitting the contract dated 27-2-81, receipt of money thereupon and delivery of possession. He also said that due to the pressure of his mother and other relations he had to yield to them. When defendant No.5 found that they could not resist the decree she approached defendant No.1 for compromise. She paid Taka 7,00,000 to defendant No.1 and this defendant gave up his claim in schedule-1(Ka) which she got by way of compromise with her son defendant No.3.

17. After such giving up schedule-1 (Ka) property by compromise with defendant No. 5defendant No.1 got his plaint amended and sought for a sale deed in respect of schedule-1 (Kha) property only. Then defendant Nos. 1 obtained a decree dated 30-7-95 which directed defendant No. 2 to 4 to execute and register a sale deed in respect of schedule-1 (Kha) property.

18. The plaintiff obtained the agreement dated 8-9-86 and then a sale deed dated 13-1-91 from defendant Nos. 3 and 4 with full knowledge and during pendency of Other Suit No. 151 of 1992. Even defendant No.3 did not mention anything about his entering into any agreement with the plaintiff on 8-9-86 in his written statement filed on 4-9-88 in Other Suit No. 832 of 1984, which was then renumbered as Other Suit No. 151 of 1992. Whole transaction of the plaintiff was fraudulent to defraud this defendant. As the plaintiff himself collusively obtained a deed from defendant Nos. 3 and 4 during the pendency of the suit of this defendant, he was not entitled to say that the decree dated 30-7-95 was collusive. The plaintiff is bound by the decree.

19. On the pleadings following issues were framed:

(a) Was the suit barred by limitation?

(b) Was the suit barred by principles of lis pendens under section 52 of Transfer of Property Act?

(c) Was the suit barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act?

(d) Was the suit bad for defect of parties?

(e) Whether the plaintiff was entitled to the relief as prayed for? And

(f) What relief the plaintiff was entitled to?

20. Plaintiff examined seven witnesses, including himself to prove his case while the defendant No.1 examined one of its officers as DW 1. Plaintiff adduced number of documents, which were marked exhibit 1 to 16 while the papers and documents of defendant No. 1 were marked as exhibit 'Ka' to 'Neo-(1)'.

21. Plaintiff AI-haj Mohammad Ishaque Chowdhury as PW 1 deposed in support of his plaint case. He stated defendant Nos. 3 and 4 ultimately got suit schedule-1 (Kha) property on the basis of a compromise decree dated 8-11-84 passed in Other Suit No. 228 of 1982. They entered into a contract to sell the property to him at a consideration of Taka 10,00,000. The agreement was executed in 1986 when possession was delivered. Defendant Nos. 3 and 4 gave a power of attorney to PW 4 Md Shamsul Huq to execute and register necessary salt deed transferring the suit property. Then. in 1991 PW 4 Md Shamsul Huq executed and registered a sale deed. In 1996, he got a notice from Double Mooring Police Station. He went to the police station and came to learn that defendant No.1 company was claiming title over the suit property on the basis of a decree. Then, he came to know about the suit and decree. He claimed the decree passed in other/Suit No. 151 of 1992 was collusive. He went into possession of the suit property with the know ledge of the defendant No.1 but he was not made party in the suit. The ex-parte decree caused him harm.

22. In cross-examination, he said that he was 64 years old. He read up to class six. He had no business. He knew defendant No.3 Taherul Anwar since 1986. The agreement was direct without mediation of any broker.

23. But he could not remember the date of agreement. He told that it was done in the seventh month. That day he paid Taka 2.5 lac but he did not remember the date of payment. He could not remember the date of 1996 when possession was delivered. He could not say whether on the agreement he paid Taka 2.5 lac was written in the plaint. In 1991, power of attorney was given, original of which was not yet obtained. Defendant No.2 was a partnership firm, Original partners were Anwara Begum, Akmal Mia, Faroque Ahmed. Anwara Begum was the managing partner Faroque Ahmed and Akmal Mia retired in 1977. Then, Taherul Anwar was inducted as a partner. On 15-8-81, Anwara Begum retired and in her place Nelufar Begum was inducted. Taherul Anwar and Nelufar Begum, defendant Nos. 3 and 4, gave him the kabala. Anwara Begum would not depose in the case. Anwara Begum filed written statement. Then, he said Anwara Begum filed no written statement. On 20-11- 84 he had no relation with defendant Nos. 2 to 5. In other Suit No. 151 of 1992 Taherul Anwar submitted a written statement. He remained silent when he was suggested that defendant No. 3 executed an agreement on behalf of defendant No.2 firm and received Taka 6,60,000 from defendant No.1 company. He also kept mum when he was further suggested that defendant No. 5 admitted the agreement with this defendant in her written statement; He however, denied that in her written statement Anwara Begum mentioned his name. Taherul Anwar never mentioned about his agreement, he denied. Taherul Anwar left the country for America in 1989-90 for good. He denied that there was an agreement with defendant Nos. 1 and 2 at a consideration of Taka 18,00,000 on 27-2-81. He had no knowledge about delivery of possession and apportionment to the tenant. He had no knowledge whether Anwara Begum paid Taka 7,00,000 to the defendant No.1 for the property of schedule-1 (Ka).

24. PW 2 Saleh Ahmed deposed that he was a mason. He worked In the suit land, He supervised the work which progressed up to roof with foundation.

25. In cross-examination, he said that he had no papers about his works under Eshaque Chowdhury. There was no written contract nor worked out rate, He was paid monthly. He got the

job through the consultant. Work was stopped since 1994,

26. PW 3 Md Nurul Alam deposed that he was a deed writer, He wrote the deed being No. 1196, exhibit 15 for vendors Taherul Anwar and Nelufer Anwar represented by their attorney Shamsul Huq. in cross-examination, he stated that, he did not witness payment of Taka 9,70,000.

27. PW 4 Shamsul Huq deposed that he used to work under the father of Taherul Anwar. They gave him power of attorney dated 26-7-90. On their behalf he executed and registered the sale deed, The power of attorney was marked exhibit-3. He also witnessed a receipt written by Advocate Nandy. 28. In cross-examination, he stated that, he did no work, He had no profession. He remained silent to the suggestion that the property did not belong to Taherul Anwar and Nelufar Anawar. He denied that he created the power of attorney in collusion with Anwara Begum.

29. PW 5 Nargis Sultana deposed to be an Advocate, She held local investigation as an advocate Commissioner after service of notice upon both parties, She submitted her report, exhibit 16.

30. In cross-examination. she stated that at the time the work was going on, foundation was made ready.

31. PW 6 Md Babul deposed that, he did not know anything about the suit property and then said he knew the suit property. There was a three-storied building on the land. Chowdhury Sahab was doing. In cross-examination, he stated that there was no relation with the plaintiff. He had no knowledge whether Eshaque Chowdhury was the owner of the property.

32. PW 7 Dipu Shankar Nandi, an Advocate, deposed that on 4-10-88 he wrote a receipt executed by Taherul Anwar. Taherul Anwar put his signature before him, In cross-examination, he stated that he could not remember where he wrote the receipt but where he wrote there Taherul Anwar put his signature on the receipt. At the time Eshaque Chowdhury and others were present.

33. On behalf of defendant No.1, company Md Golab Uddin was examined as DW 1. He stated that there was an agreement entered into by the managing director of defendant No.1 and defendant No.2. At the time he worked as Assistant Director. Defendant No.2 was a partnership firm. Defendant Nos. 3 and 4 were partners of defendant No.2, firm. The agreement was filed in other Suit No. 151 of 1992. He also tendered a copy of the agreement into evidence. He identified the signatures of his managing director on the agreement. After comparison with the original agreement the copy was marked as exhibit 'Ka', Taherul Anwar signed the agreement. Price was settled at Taka 18,00,000, out of which Tk. 5,00,000 was first paid. He knew who received the money. It was stipulated to execute and register the kabala within three months. When he failed to procure certificates he was asked to give possession and then on 2-12-81 possession was delivered. That day he received further Taka 1,00,000. That was acknowledged on the back of exhibit 'Ka', The letters dated 2-12-81, 6-1-82 and 8-1-82 Informing the tenants were marked as exhibit 'Ga' series. Defendant No.5 issued notice through learned Advocate Aminul Islam. Anwara Begum claimed partnership in defendant No. 2 firm. The notice was issued on 13-11-81. Before the execution of the agreement exhibit 'Ka', latest position of the firm, copy of the kabala were submitted. Having seen and understood defendant No.3 had right to enter into agreement on behalf of the defendant No.2, they obtained the agreement. The original partners of said firm were Anwara Begum. Ahmed Hossain and Akmal Mia. In 1977, Ahmed Hosain and Akmal Mia retired. Taherul Anwar was inducted. Defendant Nos. 3 and 5 were partners of defendant No.2, firm. Defendant No.5 Anwara Begum retired in 1980. Defendant No.4 was Inducted. They were still partners. Defendant No.3 was the main partner. Defendant No.5 then instituted other Suit No. 228 of 1981. In the suit Taherul Anwar, Nelufar Anwar and Abdul Matin Chowdhury were made defendants.

34. He further said that after taking possession they constructed pucca wall surrounding the suit property. In other Suit No. 2.28 of 1981 Abdul Matin Chowdhury was made party as defendant No. 3 and subsequently by order dated 4-11-84, his name was struck off at the instance of defendant Nos. 3 to 5 before the compromise decree was passed. On 13-1-84 solenama was filed. Taherul Anwar was party to that. But defendant No.2 was not a party in other Suit No. 228 of 1981 he deposed on the basis of solenama on 8-11-84. The compromise decree was nothing but a collusive one passed in other Suit No. 228 of 1981 between mother and son.

35. In their other Suit No. 151 of 1992, Taherul Anwar and Nelufar Anwar were made parties. Anwara Begum was made party. When she did not appear in spite of summons on 20-3-86 notice was published in the daily papers which were submitted and marked as exhibit 'Uma(3)' and 'Uma(4)'. He also filed certified copy of the plaint, written statement of Taherul Anwar and application for amendment of the plaint, copies of order being Nos. 28, 92, 93, 97 and 98 of their suit,exhibit 'Jha' series. Anwara Begum and others signed the written statement. In the written statement. she admitted that Taherul Anwar admitted the agreement and receipt of Taka 6,60,000 and asked the tenant to attom. There was a compromise with defendant NO.5 in other Suit No. 151 of 1992 for which they relinquished their claim in schedule 1(Ka) property and received Taka 7,00,000 for defendant NO.5. He filed the copy of compromise application, deposition of Anwara Begum and order passed thereon. exhibit 'Jha' series. Then. the suit was decreed ex parte against the defendant Nos. 3 to 4 and dismissed against Anwara Begum. Taherul Anwar took step in the suit up to 1993.

36. In cross-examination, he said that in December 1996 the plaintiff forcibly entered into the suit property. As there was none of them present at the time so they could not resist. In the second week of December they came to know about the entry of the plaintiff.

37. Upon the aforesaid evidence oral and documentary, on record the trial Court decreed the suit as prayed for.

38. On behalf of the appellant the decree was challenged on number of grounds.

Firstly, Mr TH Khan, learned Senior Counsel, submitted that the claim of the plaintiff was barred by the principles of lis pendens under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act since he entered into an agreement and obtained a sale deed during the pendency of other Suit No. 31 of 1984/832 of 1984/151 of 1992.

39. He further submitted that when defendant Nos. 3 and 4 were parties in other Suit No. 151 of 1992 the plaintiff was not entitled to be added as a party in the suit and the suit therefore, would not be bad for defect of parties.

<u>40. In support Mr TH Khan cited Md Yaqoob Khan vs Sahib Khatoon and others (1998) 20 CLC 1576; Mukhtar Baig vs Sardar Baig 2000 SCMR 45; Jamila Khatum vs Md Lutfar Rahman alias Nefasur and others 3 BLC 306; Jamaluddin vs Rabeya Begum 32 DLR 63; Nesmohammad and others vs Mosammat Jamila Khatun and others 6 BLT (AD) 276; Golam Kader being dead his heirs Nurun Nahar Begum and others vs Abdul Khaleque Choukder and others, 43 DLR (AD) 107 and Haji Md Eshaque vs Rupali Bank 43 DLR 621.</u>

41. He submitted that learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in holding that after the compromise entered Into by defendant No.1 with defendant No. 5 in respect of schedule-1 (Ka) property. the original agreement had undergone novation since the contract was not substituted.

42. Lastly, he submitted that the compromise decree dated 8-11-84 and the sale deed dated 8-9-86 obtained by the plaintiff thereupon were all collusive to defeat the right of the defendant No. 1.

43. On the other hand, Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Senior Counsel, submitted that defendant No.1 must be held to have accepted the decree dated 8-11-84 when it relinquished schedule-1(Ka) property which defendant No.5 got on the basis of partition of said decree.

44. Secondly, he submitted that after relinquishment of schedule-(Ka) property, the agreement dated 27-2-81 as claimed by defendant No.1 had undergone novation and could not be

enforced in law.

45. Lastly, he submitted that without making  the plaintiff party in other Suit No. 151 of 1992, the ex-parte decree obtained therein was not binding upon the plaintiff.

46. We have perused the record and heard the learned Senior Counsels at length. The main question facing us is, whether the learned Subordinate Judge was justified in decreeing the suit in its entirety. Fate of the suit appears to depend more on law than on facts.

47. On 8-1-97 the plaintiff instituted the suit for a decree for declaration of his title and confirmation of possession in the suit property described in schedule 1 (Kha) to the plaint; and also for further declaration that the ex-parte Judgment and decree dated 30-7-95 passed in other Suit No. 151 of 1999 by Second Commercial Court and Subordinate Judge at Chittagong in respect of said property was forged, collusive, illegal, false, void and not binding upon the plaintiff.

48. It is not disputed that on 7-8-63 defendant No. 2 M/s Taher and Company, which was a partnership firm got, lease of 0.758 big has of land at Agrabad Commercial Area comprising of plot No. 18 together with one-storied building thereon schedule-I to the plaint from the Public Works Department of the government of erstwhile East Pakistan. Said firm continued to own and possess said property.

49. It is the case of the plaintiff that other Suit No. 228 of 1981 was instituted in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge at Chittagong for partition. Defendant Nos. 3 to 5 partitioned said property amongst themselves by a deed of partition being. No. 20008 dated 1-11-84. On the basis of such partition, said defendants obtained a compromise decree dated 8-11-84.

50. Defendant No. 5 got schedule 1 (Ka) property while defendant Nos. 3 and 4 schedule-1 (Kha) property which is the suit property.

51. His further case is that said defendant Nos. 3 and 4 thus being owners possessed the suit property by payment of rents after mutation of their names and making boundary walls surrounding the property. Then, they entered into a contract with him to sell the suit property at a consideration of Taka 10,00,000 and executed an agreement dated 8-9-86 and delivered possession. He since then possessed the suit property.

52. He paid them Taka 9,70,000. He obtained a sale deed dated 13-1-91 from PW 4 Md Shamsul Huq who was appointed attorney by defendant No. 3 and 4 to execute and register the deed. In 1996, he came to know about the decree of defendant No.1 passed in other Suit No. 151 of 1992 and such decree cast a cloud over his title and hence, he was constrained to institute the suit.

53. In order to succeed to have his title declared, the plaintiff is required first to prove his contract dated 8-9-86, payment of consideration and genuineness and validity of the transfer effected by sale deed dated 13-1-91 and then, his locus standi to relief of declaration in respect of Judgment and decree dated 30-7-95 passed in other Suit No. 151 of 1992.

54. The plaintiff did not produce his agreement dated 8-9-86. He claimed in his deposition that he paid defendant Nos. 3 and 4 Taka 9,70,000 on several occasions but they could not give him the sale deed. He could not find a single witness to prove payment of such huge payment. He adduced the sale deed dated 13-1-91 exhibit 15. PW 3 Md Nurul Alam scribe and PW 4 Md Shamsul Huq attorney proved said deed. But the power of attorney giving PW 4 Md Shamsul Huq authority to execute and register a sale deed was not at all proved by anyone who witnessed execution of said transaction.

55. In this regard, testimony of PW 4 Md Shamsul Huq demands deep consideration. He said in examination-in-chief that the vendee paid the consideration as mentioned in the power of attorney before its execution. But, in cross-examination, he said that the deed was written in English and he could not read English. He denied that the power of attorney was created for the suit.

56. On payment of consideration we have noticed that the plaintiff said that he paid Taka 9,70,000 in several installments before the deed of power of attorney and sale. While PW 3 Md Nurul Anwar said that on the date of sate deed money was paid. PW 4 Md Shamsul Huq said that in the power of attorney money was mentioned to have been paid. Neithen PW 3 and PW 4 witnessed payment of any money.

57. On the above evidence, it must be held that, the plaintiff failed to prove payment of any consideration and the authority of PW 4 Md Shamsul Huq to execute the sale deed dated 13-1-91. Evidence of the plaintiff and PW 4 Md Shamsul Huq clearly shows that they came from the same background and it is difficult to rely upon them.

58. Besides, we must deal with the most important question whether the sale deed was a valid transaction.

59. The plaintiff claimed in his plaint that defendant Nos. 3 to 5 instituted other Suit No. 228 of 1981 for partition and got a compromise decree on the basis of partition deed being No. 20008 dated 1-11-84 Exhibit 2. By the decree defendant No.5 got schedule 1 (Ka) while  defendant Nos. 3 and 4 got schedule-1 (Kha).

60. The plaint of other Suit No. 228 of 1981 Exhibit (Jha) however, shows that defendant Nos. 5 to 7 instituted the suit for declaration, that defendant Nos. 5,6 and Akmal Mia, father of defendant No.7 acquired the schedule 1 property from the Government by lease deed dated 7-8-63, that defendant No.3 Taherul Anwar was never a partner of defendant No.2 firm and defendant Nos. 2 to 3 acquired no title or interest in said property. Abdul Matin Chowdhury as managing director of defendant No.1 company was impleaded as defendant No.3 in that suit. On 30-9-84 defendant Nos. 5 to 7 and another, and defendant Nos. 3 and 4 made a joint application for compromise exhibit 14 (Gha). By order No. 35 dated 4-11-84 name of defendant No.3 was struck off by said plaintiffs.

61. In the application for compromise, it is however, stated that defendant Nos. 3 and 4 would continue as partners of defendant No.2 firm and defendant Nos. 5 to 7 would retire from the partnership with effect from 30-7-84. But defendant No.5 would get schedule-1(Ka) while defendant Nos. 3 and 4 schedule 1 (Kha). On the basis of such compromise petition the decree dated 8-11-84 was passed exhibit 10(Ka). It should not escape the attention that the intention in bringing the suit was to have a declaration that defendant Nos. 3 or 4 was never partner of defendant No. 2 firm nor they acquired any interest in schedule-1 property but ended in recognising them partners and giving them schedule 1(Kha). Collusion is so apparent and striking that it requires no other evidence. The plaintiff claimed to have purchased the schedule- 1 (Kha) property by a sale deed dated 13-1-91.

62. Admittedly, at the time other Suit Nos. 31/1984, 831/1984,151 of 1992 were pending against defendant Nos. 2 to 7 for specific performance of a contract dated 27-2-81, exhibit 'Ka'. Defendant Nos. 3 and 4. vendors of the plaintiff, were very much present in the suit.

63. Both defendant Nos. 3 and 5 appeared and filed separate written statements dated 4-9-88 and 19-7-88. exhibit Jha(2) and Jha (3). In his written statement defendant No.3 admitted the agreement dated 27-2-81 and receipt of Taka 6,60,000.00 from defendant No.1 as part performance of the contract.

64. But defendant No.5 took the view that as she was not a party so she was not bound by the agreement.

65. Then, defendant No.5 and defendant No.1 on 10-1-95 filed a compromise petition for dismissal of the suit against her only, exhibit-Jha(9). In the petition, she admitted the agreement dated 27-2-81, receipt of Taka 6,60,000 by defendant No. 3 and entire case of defendant No.1. She paid Taka 7,00,000 to defendant No.1 for schedule-1(Ka) property and in return defendant No.1 relinquished all his claims in respect of said property. It was also agreed that upon payment of Taka 6,60,000 to defendant No.3 and Taka 7,00,000 to defendant No. 5, the suit would proceed against the rest for a sale deed on payment of rest of the consideration of Taka 18,00,000 that is Taka 40,000 in respect of schedule 1(Kha). On the compromise petition both defendant No. 5 and Abdul Matin Chowdhury on behalf of defendant No.1 company deposed. By order dated 21-1-95 the suit was disposed of against defendant No. 5 and ordered to proceed against the rest, exhibit-Jha(5).

66. Then, in view of such order effecting compromise defendant No.1 got the plaint amended for a sale deed in respect of schedule-1 (Kha) property only on payment of Taka 4,40,000 only. Then defendant No.1 obtained an ex-parte decree dated 30-7-95, Exhibits 9 and 10.

67. The deed dated 13-1-91 obtained by the plaintiff is clearly hit by the doctrine of lispendens since the transfer took place when other Suit No. 151 of 1992 for specific performance of a contract dated 27-2-81 was still pending. By such purchase the plaintiff became transferee pendente lite. He purchased without leave of the Court.

68. The phrase 'lis pendens' which is Latin, means 'Utlite pendente nihil innovetur' that is,

during a litigation nothing should be introduced. The doctrine is now codified under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

69. Section 52 prohibits transfer of the property or otherwise dealing with such property by any party to a suit or proceeding during the pendency of the suit or proceeding which is not collusive so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto. Such prohibition is absolute only subject to leave of the Court.

<u>70. A proceeding before a Court of law is solemn and sacred. Intention of the law is very clear that no party in such proceeding would be allowed to intervene or interfere with the proceeding to affect the rights of other party. It is now well settled that a transferee pendente lite would therefore, be bound by the proceedings in the suit and the decree passed therein and shall take his transfer subject to the result of the suit.</u>

71. The parties in such pending suit are under no obligation to implead such transferee pendent lite nor is such transferee entitled to be impleaded as party to the suit. Cf: Nesmohammad and others vs Jamila Khatun and others 6 BLT (AD) 276 = 3 BLC 306; Golam Kader & others vs Abdul Khaleque Choukdar 43 DLR (AD) 107 and Muktar Baig vs Sardar Baig, 2000 SCMR 45.

72. In similar circumstances, in a recent case of Tek Chand vs Deep Chand, (2001) 4 SCC 488 the Supreme Court of India upheld a decree decreeing a suit for specific performance of contract on affirming the findings that the family arrangement by the vendor amongst his heirs after the agreement and the decree obtained thereupon by such heirs were collusive and transfer by such children on the basis of the decree to others was hit by the doctrine of lis pendens.

73. One Deep Chand instituted a suit against second respondent Kare for specific performance of an agreement dated 8-12-86. Kare admitted the agreement but took the plea that he did not intend to sell but mortgage. After the agreement the children of Kare got the suit property by way of a family arrangement. They also obtained a decree on 1-10-87 on the basis of the family arrangement. Then the children transferred the suit property to defendant Nos. 5 to 8. The children contested the suit on the basis of their decree of title. Said defendant Nos. 5 to 8 also contested the suit claiming title over the suit property by way of purchase from said children.

74. The trial Court dismissed the suit. First appellate Court set aside the decree of the trial Court and decreed the suit. It held the agreement dated 8- 12-86 true and genuine: that the family settlement as also the decree of title obtained by the children of Kare were collusive transactions and they had no right to transfer the suit property and that the alienation by said children in favour of defendant Nos. 5 to 8 appellants was hit by doctrine of lis pendens. Second appeal preferred therefrom by the transferee pendente lite was dismissed by the High Court at Chandrigarh.

75. Other Suit No. 151 of 1992 was pending since 1984. It would be too much for the plaintiff to claim that the suit was collusive to harm him unjustly when he purchased in 1991. The plaintiff, therefore, would not be entitled to maintain any suit challenging a decree passed in such suit and the instant suit of the plaintiff must be held to be not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act since he acquired no right to the suit property.

76. We find learned Subordinate Judge unnecessarily exercised to find that the agreement dated 27-2-81 suffered "novation". Section 62 of the Contract Act has defined novation as hereunder:

"If the parties to a contract agree to substitute a new contract for it, or to rescind or alter it, the original contract need not be performed".

Section 62 or the illustrations thereto clearly indicate that only after substitution of the original contract by a new contract or rescission and/or alteration the contract need not be performed. But here in the case before us defendant No. 1 just relinquished and waived a part of the contract which is clearly severable and independent from the other part, that is schedule 1 (Ka)".

77. Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act clearly entitles the plaintiff to seek enforcement of the contract in respect of schedule 1(Kha) property when he relinquished and waived his right to other part of the contract schedule-1 (Ka). After the defendant No. 1 relinquished all his claims to further performance and all his rights to compensation for loss or damages sustained by him for default of defendant No.3, such giving up would not constitute the contract dated 27-2-81 suffered novation.

78. For the above reasons impugned judgment and decree of the trial Court cannot be maintained in law. Appeal therefore, succeeds.

79. In the result, the appeal is allowed with cost. Impugned judgment and decree are hereby set aside. The suit is dismissed.

Send down the records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
D. C. Bhattacharya, J.— ঞn this appeal special leave was granted, by the Supreme Court of Pakistan to consider the question whether a share-holder of a private limited company has locus standi to apply under Order 21, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside an auction sale of immovable property belonging to the said Company.

2. Respondent No. 3, a private limited Company, was the owner of Rupkatha Cinema Hall situated at Pabna town : Respondent No. 2 having obtained a money decree against the said company got the said Cinema Hall put up for sale in execution of the said decree in the First Court of Subordinate Judge Pabna and Respondent No. 1, purchased the said property in auction for a sum of Rs. 3000/-, subject to two mortgages amounting to Rs. 1,00,000/-and odd, on the 29th June, 1960 Delivery of possession of the auction purchased property was taken by Respondent No. 1 in due course on the 18th September,1960.

3. On the 18th September, 1964 i.e., after more than 4 years from the sale, the petitioners, who are four in number, claiming themselves to be share-holders of the respondent company, filed an application under order 21, rule 90 of the Code for setting aside the said sale held in June, 1960 on the ground of fraud and material irregularity in publishing and conducting the sale. Respondent No. 1 contested the application of the petitioners denying all the material allegations as to fraud and irregularity in regard to the impugned auction sale and contended, inter alia, that the petitioners being mere share-holders of the company had no locus standi to apply for setting aside the sale under the provision of the Civil Procedure Code.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge by an elaborate judgment allowed the said application and set aside the auction sale holding that there was fraud and material irregularity in publishing and conducting the sale and that the petitioners being share-holders of the company had locus standi to apply for setting aside the sale of the property belonging to the said company. On an appeal against the said order, the learned District Judge of Pabna gave effect to the objection of Respondent No. 1 as to locus standi of the petitioners to apply for setting aside the sale and held, relying upon two decisions, one being of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Basanta Kumar Roy Vs. Chart Chandra PaI. 62 C.W.N 132; 1958 Cal. 543 and the other of Madras High Court in the case of Vaidyanatha Vs. Bank of India AIR. 1955 Mad. 486, that a share-holder of a limited company was not a person whose interests were affected by a sale of the company's property and as such had no locus standi to apply for setting aside such a sale under Order 21, rule 90 of the Code of civil Procedure.

5. The petitioners, the share-holders, having moved the Dacca High Court against the said order of the learned. District Judge dismissing their application for setting: aside the sale, a Division Bench of the said Court expressed its dissent from the general formulation of the law as made in the aforesaid two Indian decisions to the effect that the word, 'interests' as used in the rule meant an existing or present interest in the property sold by holding that such a view was too narrow an interpretation of the said expression, but nonetheless, affirmed the. order of the learned District Judge on the view that a share-holder had no interest in the company's property nor had he any say in the management of the affairs of the company and that the pecuniary injury which a share-holder might suffer on account of a sale of a company's property at a low price would be so remote and distant that it could not be said that he was one of the persons whose interests are affected by the sale, within the meaning of the law.

6. This appeal against aforesaid judgment of the High Court has been filed by the petitioners on obtaining special leave to consider the question as to their locus standi in a proceeding under Order 21, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

7. Mr. Syed Nasiruddin, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellants, has submitted that the learned judges of the High Court took a much restricted view of the kind of interest affected by the sale as has been contemplated in Order 21, rule 90 of the Code. It is true, learned Counsel has contended, that a private limited company is a justice Person different from the body of its share-holders and is, in law, the owner of all its properties, and a share-holder has no direct say in the management of the affairs of the company, 'but it is the share-holders who provide the share capital of the company, and have the ultimate control over its management and for whose benefit the company is constituted and in the ultimate analysis, it is they who are going to suffer for the loss of a very valuable property belonging to the company in consequence of disputed auction sale. Reliance has been placed by the learned Counsel on this point or certain observations of Chief Justice Munir of Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of the Commissioner of Income Tax Vs. E V. Miller (1959) 11 DLR (SC) 430—P.L.D. 1959 S.C 219. Learned Counsel has further submitted that the allegations being that respondent No. 1 after getting control of the Rup Katha Cinema Hall due to the negligence and connivance of the Managing Director, who had been living abroad, got the said Cinema Hall fraudulently sold in auction in collusion with respondent No. 2 and purchased the property himself, the learned Judges of the High Court ought to have Mid that in the special circumstances of the case the , share-holders could be said to have their interests affected by the said auction sale within the meaning of the Code, or that, in any event, exciting Court had inherent power to set aside the sale which had been fraudulently held as a result of a conspiracy. In support of this contention, learned Counsels has referred to a certain passage from the principle of Modern company Law by L.C.B. Gower (1957) at pages 319-323 dealing with the legal nature of shares and also cited a Single Bench decision of the Punjab High Court of the Indian jurisdiction in the case of Punjab Mercantile Bank Ltd. Vs. Sardar Kishan Singh, reported in AIR 1963 Punjab, 230.

8. Mr. M.H. Khondker, learned Counsel for the contesting respondent, has, on the other hand, submitted that a limited company being a legal personality quite distinct from its shareholders and the share-holders having no existing and present interest in the properties belonging to the company, such share-holders cannot be said to have their interests affected by the sale of the  properties of the company within the meaning of the relevant Rule, and has referred, in addition to the cases of Vaiydamttha Vs. Indian Bank Ltd. AIR 1955 Mad 486 and Basanta Kumar Ray Vs. Chant Chandra Pal 62 C.W.N. 132 which were considered by the High Court, to two cases of Indian jurisdiction, namely, Mrs. Bacha F. Gazdar Vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, AIR 1955 S.C. 74 and Shyamlal Vs. Jagannath AIR 1969 Cal. 424 and also an English decision; namely, Flitcrofts case (1882) 21. Ch. 519 (C. A.) in support of his contention.

9. For the proper appreciation of the question in its true perspective, it will be useful, we think, if we look at the several legislative changes in respect of the provision relating to setting aside, a sale by an application made to the executing Court when appear to have been made in keeping with the judicial interpretation of the said provision from time to time. The relevancy of such legislative changes to the interpretation of a certain statutory provision was emphasised by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Abdur Rahim and others Vs. Syed Abu Barker Ali and others, L.R. 55 I A. 96: 32 C.W.N. 482: AIR 192 P.C. 16. ILR Cal. 519 where Lord Sinha made the following observations in course of the judgment of the judicial Committee:

"It is a sound rule of interpretation to take the words of the statute as they stand and to interpret them ordinarily Without any reference to the previous state of the law on the subject or the English law upon which it may be founded; but when it is contended that the Legislature intended by any particular amendment to make substantial change in the pre-existing law, it is impossible to arrive at a conclusion without considering what the law was previously to the particular enactment and to See Whether the words used in the Statute can be taken to effect the change that is suggested as intended.

The original provision as to setting aside a sale, as contained in section 256 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 1859, was to the following effect:

“....at any time within 30 days from the date of the sale application may be made to the Court to set aside the sale on the grounds of material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale; but no sale shall be set aside on the ground of such irregularity unless the applicant shall prove to the satisfaction of the Court that he has suffered substantial injury by reason of such irregularity."

10. It will appear from the said provision that it did not specify the person who could file an application to set aside the sale, but the latter part of the said section, which was a kind of proviso to the substantive provision, indicated that proof of substantial injury suffered by the applicant because of the sale was a pre-condition for the exercise of the power of setting aside the sale by the Court. There was however, a conflict of judicial views in the Courts of India as to the interpretation, of the said provision of the Civil Procedure Code of 1859. The Calcutta High Court was of the opinion that it was only the judgment debtor who could apply to set aside a sale under the said provision while the Bombay High Court, on the other hand, held that such a right was not confined to the parties to the suit, but it was available to any person who had sustained injury by reason of the irregularity of the sale. It was perhaps because of this conflict of authorities that it was specified in section 311 of Act X of 1877, which replaced the Code of 1859, that the person competent to apply for setting aside the sale was "a decree-holder or any person whose immovable properly has been sold". The provision of section 311 of the Code of 1882 which was enacted on the repeal of Act X of 1877 was the same as its predecessor.

12. The expression, "any person whose immovable property has been sold" received liberal interpretation in the Courts of India and a Full Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Asmatunnessa Begum Vs. Ashruff Ali. (1888) I.L.R. 15 Cal. 438 expressed the view that the words were used intentionally to enable other persons than the judgment-debtor to apply if they were injured by the irregularity, Sir Corner Petheram, Chief Justice in delivering the judgment of the Bench expressed its view in this regard in the following words:

"The words are any person whose immovable properly has been sold under this Chapter may apply, but the sale is not to be set aside unless the applicant proves that he has sustained substantial injury. We think that this means that the substantial injury must be the direct result of the irregularity, and that this could only be the case where the property of the person applying had not only been put up for sale and knocked down, but had been said in the sense that the applicant's interest had been legally affected by such sale.

In spite of the Full Bench decision, there was a difference of opinion between two Judges of a subsequent Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Abdul Gani Vs. Dunne (1892) 20 Cal. 418 on the question whether a benamadar of a property had any locus standi to apply for setting aside a sale and the view of Ghosh, J on this question, which was supported by Petheram, C.J., to whom the case was referred on such differerce as the third Judge, was to the following effect:

"The remedy under section 311 of the Code is not confined to the decree-holder and judgment-debtor; and when any third party comes upon the ground that his interest in the properly has been affected by the sale, the Court cannot help determining whether he has any interest in the properly."

13. This expression, "a person whose immovable property has been sold" came up for consideration before another Full Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Paresh Nath Singh Vs. Naha Gopal Chatteradhya, (1901) I.L.R. 29 Cal. 1 : 5 C.W.N. 821, where the Chief Justice and three ether learned Judges of the Bench (Rampini, J dissenting) held that the said expression was of the wider and more general import than the owner of the property and that a mortgagee of a tenure or holding sold in execution of a decree for arrears of rent was "a person whose immovable property has been sold" within the meaning of section 310-A of the Code of 1882, which was similar to section 311 and applicable in case of a sale in execution of a decree for arrears of rent. Ameer Ali, J, one of the learned Judges of the Bench expressed the view on the question in the following manner :

"In my opinion, the words 'any person whose property has been sold' include every person who has an interest in the property in question whether qualified, partial or absolute".

14. We, therefore, find that in the Civil Procedure Code of 1908 which was enacted by repealing the Cede of 1882, the provision relating to the setting aside of a sale by the executing Court on an application made to it as contained in Order 21, rule 90 of the new Code, was redrafted and has been worded as follows :

“Where any immovable property been sold in execution of a decree, the decree-holder or any person entitled to share in a rateable distribution of assets or whose interests are affected by the sale may apply to the Court to set aside the sale on the ground of a material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting it:

Provided that no sale shall be set aside on the ground of irregularity or fraud unless upon the facts proved the court is satisfied that the applicant has sustained substantial injury by reasons of such irregularity or fraud."

<u>15. As we find, under this new provision, apart from the decree-holder, a class of judgment creditors who can claim a share in rateable distribution of the assets of the judgment-debtor, as provided under section 73 of the Code, and a class of persons having any kind of interest which is affected by the sale, have been given the right to apply for setting aside the sale. All creditors of a judgment-debtor are in a sense interested in the properties of his debtor for the purpose of realisation of his debts and if we understand the term in a very wide sense their said interest may be said to be affected by the sale of the judgment-debtor's properties in execution of a decree obtained by another creditor. But all such creditors do not appear to have been given the right to apply under the new Code. It is only those creditors who, after obtaining a decree against the same judgment-debtor, have become entitled to a share in rateable distribution, of the assets of the judgment-debtor by putting his own decree into execution and as such can apply for setting aside the sale. Similarity, in the second group of persons entitled to apply, we find only such persons whose interests have been affected by the sale. We have seen that although in the older Codes the expression used was 'any person whose immovable property has been sold' but the said expression had been interpreted by judicial authorities to mean every person who has an interest in the property whether qualified or partial or absolute. It appears that in consonance with such judicial interpretation the now expression 'any person whose interests are affected by the sale' has been introduced in the present Code. A "person entitled to share in rateable distribution of assets" is interested in the property sold, as has been pointed out above, for the purpose of recovery of its debt but has no existing interest in the property itself. If the legislature wanted to mean by the word 'interest' as used in the expression 'whose interests are affected by the sale' any kind of interest not necessarily an interest connected or having some kind of link with the property, then, it appears to us, the expression 'any person entitled to share in rateable distribution' would be absolutely redundant, because on such wide interpretation such a person would have been covered by the former expression. These interests may, however, not only be proprietary but may be any kind of interest whether proprietary, possessory or pecuniary. These interests must, however, be such as are affected by the sale, that is to say, the interests must have some kind of direct and positive, and rot hypothetical or conjectural, relation with the property sold.</u>

<u>16. The learned Judges of the Dacca High Court do not appear to have endorsed the proposition stated by the High Courts of Madras and Calcutta in the cases of Vaidyaratta Vs. Indian Bank Ltd. 1955 Mad 486 and Basanta Kumar Roy Vs. Charu Chandra Pal A.I.R. 1958 Cal. 543: 62 C.W.N. 132, respectively that, such interests as they are affected by the sale must be existing or present in the property sold, on the view that such an interpretation would unreasonably restrict the. Meaning of the expression any person whose interests are affected by the sale and would not cover the case of pecuniary interest. The learned Judges have also referred to a number of decisions which, according to then, lave held that in order to maintain an application for setting aside a sale a person need not necessarily have existing or present interest in the auction sold property have concluded there-from that a person whose pecuniary interest is affected is competent to make such an application. The disagreement expressed by the learned Judges seems to be based upon some misapprehension about the real import of the said decisions, which have held in the same way as the learned Judges that the interests as mentioned in the relevant Rule of the Code are of wider significance and include also pecuniary interest, but the learned Judges do not appear to have noticed that such a conclusion is not antithetical to such pecuniary interest being existing and present in the property at the time of the sale and being directly affected by such a sale.</u>

<u>17. On a perusal of the provision of the Code, as contained in Order 21, rule 90, it is clear that the meaning of the word 'interests' mentioned therein may indeed be very wide and may be kind of interests, but in order that such an interest may be affected by the sale sought to be set aside, it must be existing or present in the property, otherwise it cannot be affected by the sale. The preponderance of the judicial views in the sub-continent seems to be in accord with this view.</u>

18. The Calcutta High Court appears to have consistently given its support to the view that the interest which may be affected by the sale must be some kind of interest, present and existing in the property sold, although sometimes a conflict of views may have arisen as to the kind of interest, which may be taken to be present and existing and be affected by the sale. In one of the early decisions after the enactment of the Code of 1908, a Division Bench of the said Court held in the case of Jogendra Nath Chatterjee Vs. Manmatha Nath Gbosh, 17 C.W.N. 80 that the interest of a creditor, who effected attachment of the property before judgment but bad not obtained a decree, could not be said to be such interest as was affected by the sale, held subsequently in execution of decree obtained by another creditor, although such an attaching creditor could have been regarded to have such interest if he could secure a decree before the sale.

19. A judgment-creditor attaching the property of his debtor which was subsequently sold in execution of another decree was held to have had interest which was affected by the sale in another case of the Calcutta High Court, viz., Dhirendra Nath Vs. Kamini Kumar I.L.R. 51 Cal. 495; 28 C.W.N. 899: A.I.R. 1924 Cal. 786, Suhrawardy, J. explained the principle of the decision in the following words:

"The corresponding words in section 311 of the Cede of 1882 were, 'any person whose immovable property has been sold'. The change of wording in the new Act indicates that the legislature thought it proper in view of the decision in Asmatunnissa Begum Vs. Ashruff Ali, I.L.R. 15 Cal. 488 (F. B.) to widen the scope of the Section. It may be profitable to note the words that occur in Rule 90, namely, 'a person whose interests are affected by the sale' are even wider than the words that are to be found in rule 89, namely, any person either owning such properly or holding an interest therein by virtue of a title acquired before such sale.' This clearly shows that the person who has got a vestige of title in the properly sold may apply under rule 89 to have the sale set aside. But a person who is entitled to apply under rule 90 to have the sale set aside may be a person whose interests are such (not necessarily in the property) as may be affected by the sale. It cannot be said that an attaching creditor has to interest in the sale of the property, or, I may go further; in the properly itself".

20. In the case of Hiralal Saha Vs. Akshary Kumar Saha, 37 C.W.N. 766; A.I.R. 1933 Cal. 815, it was held that the contingent liability of a defaulting auction purchaser who was called upon to put in the deficiency in the sale price on resale of the properly under Order 21, Rule 71 of the Code was an interest which had been affected by the sale and that such a defaulting auction purchaser had locus standi to apply for setting aside the subsequent sale.

21. A view, contrary to what was stated in the case of Jogendra Nath Vs. Manmatha Nath, was expressed in the case of Saehi Gopinath Vs. Kukrai Protab Chandra Saha, 38 C.W. N. 172 where it was observed that the interpretation given in the said case was narrow, and a creditor who had effected attachment of the properly of the debtor before judgment was held to have an interest affected by the sale. The earlier case was, of course, distinguished on the ground that in the latter case the attaching creditor, after all, obtained decree after the sale.

22. In three Single Judge decisions in 40 C. W. N. by the self same Judge, R. C. Mitter, J. namely, BaitIya Nath Vs. Hemanta, 40 C.W.N. 759, Bulanda Bashini Vs. Praia Gobinda, 40 C. W. N. 1334 and Gobinda Prasad Vs. Brindaban Chandra, 40 C.W.N. 1338, a decree-holder attaching the properly before its sale in execution of another decree or a creditor attaching a property before judgment and subsequently securing a decree before the sale were held to have had some interest in the property sold, which was affected by the sale. In the last mentioned case, reference was made to the decision in the case Sachi Gopinath Vs. Kukrai Protap Chandra, but the learned Judge observed that he was not expressing any opinion as to its correctness as the decree was obtained in the said case after the sale. If the interest of an applicant under order 21, Rule 90 of the Code in the property sold shall have to be affected by the sale, such an interest shall have to be existing at the time of the sale. From the said premise, it is difficult to find any distinction between a case where a creditor effecting attachment before judgment has obtained a decree after the sale and a case where such a creditor did not obtain any such decree.

23. As it appears from a consideration of the decisions of the Calcutta High Court referred to above, the interest contemplated in Order 21, rule 90 of the Code is a kind of existing interest in the properly, but such interest in the property may of course be of any kind, and should not be confused with proprietary or possessory interest only. It may be any kind of right or liability connected with or arising from the properly sold: It must have some kind of nexus with the property. The view of the Madras High Court also generally seems to be in the same line.

24. A Full Bench of the High Court of Madras held in the case of Ayyappa Vs. Kasiperumal Mayakar, 1939 Mad. 374: A.I.R. 1939 Mad. 250, that a creditor who had obtained an attachment order before judgment of the property which had been sold in execution of a decree obtained by another creditor was a person whose interests were affected by the sale: This view seems to be contrary to what was held in the Calcutta case of Jogendra Nath Vs. Manmatha Nath, and followed in some other cases where it was held that an attaching creditor cannot be deemed to have any interest in the property, until he had secured a decree. But the Madras view seems to be Iron cogent than the said Calcutta view on this point. What was decided by the Full Bench in the said case, was that the words, 'a person whose interests are affected by the sale' must be taken to include not only persons having proprietary or possessory title in the properly, but also any person whose pecuniary interests are directly and immediately affected by the sale. The close connection of the interest of an attaching creditor with the property sold, as was considered by the Full Bench to have been affected by the sale in the said case, is obvious. A Division Bench of the Madras High Court held in the case of Murugappa Chattira Vs.
