Kunnammai Achi and others A.I.R. 1959 Mad, 76, following the principle laid down in the said Full Bench decision that a creditor who had obtained a decree against the debtor whose properly had been sold in execution of a decree obtained by another creditor, but did not attach the property of his debtor had no interest which could be said to have been affected by the sale. Rajamannar, C. J. explained the view of the Bench in the following words:

"The words are indeed very wide and on a literal construction of the words not only decree holders but even ordinary creditors who have not yet sought to enforce their claims can be said to be affected by the sale of any of the properties of their debtor. Indeed, anyone who has a prospective claim which can be satisfied by a sale of the properties of a person against whom he has the claim can be said to be a person whose interests are affected by the sale of such property.

We have no hesitation in holding that this wide construction was not contemplated by the words. The interests which are alleged to be affected by the sale should be interests which are directly and immediately likely to be affected and not interests which may hypothetically and remotely be affected by the sale."

25. This view was approved by a later Full Bench of that Court in the case of T.S. Saliappan Vs. Subhiah Pilla and others AIR. 1963 Mad 156 which held, overruling an earlier decision in the case of Official Receiver Vs. Verrappa Chettiar and others, A.I.R. 1953 Mad 199, that an interim Receiver, appointed under section 20 of the Provincial Insolvency Act, of the properties of a debtor after the sale of one of his properties in execution of a decree against him, but before the confirmation of the said sale, was competent to apply for setting aside the sale. The basis of this decision, however, does not appear to be that an interim 'Receiver appointed under The Provincial In-solvency Act after the sale is a person whose interests have been affected by the sale. The Full Bench rather appears to have endorsed the view expressed in the case of Official Receiver Vs. Veerappa Chettiar to the effect that a creditor as such cannot be said to be directly and immediately affected by the sale at the instance of a decree-holder of their debtor and a Receiver who would under certain circumstances represent his interests can in no sense be said to be interested in the sale. The reasoning of the Full Bench in support of its decision has been explained by Ram Chandra lyer, C. J., in delivering the judgment of the Bench in the following words at page 159 of the report:

"The debtor had undoubtedly the right to file the application to save his properly from being taken away by an irregular sale; he could also have been in possession of the property, as the quest on of setting the sale would arise only before its confirmation. When the insolvency Court removes from such possession and commits it to the charge of the Receiver, there is at least an implied direction to him to preserve it till the disposal of the insolvency petition. The direction to hold charge of the properly carries with it the direction to file an application to set aside the 'sale, as otherwise the order of the Court would be rendered nugatory and of no avail. The interim Receiver's right to file the application, therefore arises by virtue of the order of the insolvency court and not by virtue alone of any independent right of his."

26. The same view as to the locus standi of a simple creditor of a debtor whose property was sold in execution of a decree obtained by another creditor has been affirmed in the case of S.K. Sundaram Vs. M. Joshi Rajamannar Chettiar and others, A.I.R. 1973 Mad. 166.

27. It is interesting to notice here the controversy which was raised in respect of the interpretation of this provision, while the Courts had to consider the question whether the auction purchaser was a person, within the meaning of the said provision, 'whose interests are affected by the sale'. While construing section 311 of the Code of 1882, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council held in the case of Birij Mohan Thakur and another Vs. Rai Uma Nath Chowdhury and others, L. R. 19 I. A. 154 I. L. R. 20 Cal. 8 that an auction-purchaser was not a person competent to apply for setting aside the sale under the said provision. Under the Code of 1908, the Patna and Madras High Courts took conflicting views on the question in the cases of Khetra Mohan Datta Vs. Sheikh Dilwar, (1918) 46 I. C. 614: 3 Pat L. J. 516; 5 Pat L. W. 151 and Bhavirichetti Gapala Krishnayya Vs. P. P. Sanjeeva Reddy (1920) 55 I. C. 333: M. L. J. 228 respectively without, however, much discussion. In a later Patna case Kartick Chandra Vs. Nagendra Nath A.I..R. 1924 Pat 319 a Division Bench of the Patna High Court, in following its earlier view and disagreeing with the Madras view, made the following observation:

"Interests affected by sale' means interests in the property existing before the sale and which have been adversely affected thereby. In this view of the case, the appeal of the auction purchaser cannot be entertained..."

28. The Allahabad High Court sought to give a wider interpretation in the case of Ravi Nandra Prasad Vs. Jagannath, I.L.R. 47 All 121: A.I.R. 1925 All 458 in holding that an auction purchaser was a person whose interests were affected by the sale. Walsh, J. (Sulaiman, J. concurring) made the following comment in interpreting the provision.

"It is impossible to use a wider term than `a person's interests'. In the ordinary use of the word in English language it is a term covering every sort of interest recognised by law: ...If the expression were `interest in the properly' it would of course be confined to an interest in the property antecedent to the sale. But that is not the expression, and to my mind the actual expression in the rule is free from ambiguity or difficulty of any kind and ought to be construed as meaning what it says".

29. A Single Judge of the Calcutta High Court (D. N. Mittor,"J) differed with the aforesaid" view of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Surendra Nath Das Vs. Alauddin Mistry, A.I.R. 1928 Cal. 828 in holding that an auction purchaser had no locus-standi to apply under Order 21, rule 90 of the Code and expressed his view in the following words:

"It is the sale to the auction purchaser which is to affect the interest and that the interest must have 'existed before the sale which affects the interest. It is true that the words, `persons whose interests are affected by the sale' are of wider import than the words, of the Code of 1882, viz' person value immovable property has been sold'. The latter expression was construed to mean any, person whose interests are affected by the sale' by a Full Bench of this Court in the case of Asmatunnissa Begum Vs. Ashruff Ali (1888) 15 Cal 488 (F. B.) and the legislature has adopted these words in the Cede of 1908. It is necessary to look into the previous history of the legislation in order to determine whether the legislature intended to make such a violent departure from the provisions of the Cede of 1882 so as to include an auction purchaser within the expression 'person whose interests are affected by the sale."

30. Broadway,  J, of the Lahore High Court (Shadilal C. J., concurring) noticed in the case of Nihal Chand Ckpal Goal das Vs. Pritam Singh and another A.I.R. 1932 Lah. 468 the conflicting views of the various High Courts, the Calcutta, Patna and Rangoon High Courts on the one and the Madras and Allahabad High Courts on the other, on the question whether the auction purchaser had such interests as were affected by the sale and expressed themselves in favour of the former view.

31. The Patna High Court however appears to have revised its earlier view in the Special Bench case of Mahadeo Ram Vs. Mohan Vikram A. I. R. 1933 Pat. 435 where the majority of the Judges, viz., James and Agarwala, JJ, endorsed the Allahabad view, while Kulwant Sahaya, J, expressed the dissenting view, after a review of all the earlier cases, that the person competent to apply under Order 21, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure was such a person as had an interest in the property before its sale.

32. A Single Judge of the Bombay High Court (Divitia, J) also expressed himself in favour of the view of the Calcutta, Lahore and Rangoon High Courts and the former view of Patna High Court in the case of Bala Krishna Vs. Sakharam, A.I.R. 1936 Bom 311 and held :

"The expression, 'affected by the sale' means affected by reason of the property being sold, that is by reason of the fact that a person has interest in the property which would be affected if it is sold.

33. But the Nagpur High Court adopted the Allahabad view in the case of All India Railwaymen's Benefit Fund Ltd. Vs. Ramchand, A. I. R. 1939 Nag. 179 holding that "the auction purchaser has an interest to be protected just as the decree holder or the judgment debtor". Thereafter the Calcutta High Court had again an occasion to examine this question in the case of Baidyanath Mallik Vs. Radharani, 50 C. W. N. 394 where Clough, J expressed the view as follows:

"It seems to me that the crucial question is whether the word 'interest' means interest in the property or interest which may be altogether apart from the property sold. It has been held by Suhrawardy and Page, JJ in Dhirendra Nath Roy Vs. Kamini Kumar Pal that the phrase 'a person whose interests are affected by the sale' is not limited to persons who have possessory or proprietary interest in the property, and that a pecuniary interest is also within the contemplation of the Section; in that case the interest concerned was an interest in the property, the appellant being a person who had affected a prior attachment on the property, I have not been referred to any case of this Court which supports the suggestion that the word "interests" can refer to interests other then interests in property. If "interest" does not mean interest in the property then the important word is the word "affect". Upon plain English, it seems to me difficult to find that a person's interest in the property can be affected by a sale, if, prior to that sale, he had no interest in it at all. It seems to me that Miller, J, (i.e., in Surendra Nath Das Vs. Allauddin Mistry) is right when he holds that an auction purchaser who had no interest in the property prior to sale is not within the words of Order 21, Rule 90."

34. A Division Bench of the Kerala High Court of the India jurisdiction, after nothing the conflicting views of the different High Courts of the sub-continent on the question of a locus-standi of an auction purchaser, in the case of C. P. K. Kattagil Vs. K. P. Sathiram Nayar, A.I.R. 1970 Kerala 95 found it difficult to agree with the reasoning of the Nagpur and Allahabad views and held that an auction purchaser was not a person whose interests were affected by the sale.

35. An analysis of the various judicial views as to the correct import of the prevision of Order 21, rule 90 of the Cede, stews that the most of the authorities are of the view that although the said provision is capable of being given a very wide interpretation and the word 'interests' may be any kind of right or liability, proprietary, possessory or pecuniary, nevertheless in order that such interests may be affected by the sale sought to be set aside, they must be preexisting in or closely connected with the properly at the time of the sale.

36. The Calcutta High Court had to consider precisely the question which is before us, viz. whether a share holder of a Company has a locus standi to apply under order 21, Rule 90 of the Cede of Civil procedure to set aside a sale, in the case of Easanta Ktrar Roy Vs. Charu Chandra Pal, 62 C. W. N. 132 : A. I. R. 1958 Cal. 543 and in connection with the consideration of the said question construed the said provision of the Cede again in the following manner:

"However wide may be the meaning of the expression 'any person whose interests are affected by the sale', in order 21, Rule 90 of the Cede of Civil Procedure, such person must have an existing, or present interest, which is affected by the sale of the property. The existing or the present interest must be in the properly which is sold".

37. The Calcutta High Court once again had to examine the same question, namely, whether the interest of a share-holder of a Company is affected by a sale of a properly of the company, in the case of Shyamlal Purchit and another Vs. Jagannath Roy and another, reported in A. I. R. 1969 Cal. 424 and after a review of a number of cases Sinha, C.J. expressed the conclusion of the Bench as to the interpretation of the provision of Order 21, rule 90 of the Cede in the following words:

"The words 'or whose interests are affected by the sale 'in Order 21, Rule 90 are no longer confined to an interest in immovable property or in proprietary or possessory rights. The word "interest:' must be given a wide meaning and may include a contingent interest, but the right may be exercised by one who is directly and immediately affected by the sale of an immovable property. Rights which are likely to be affected or interest which may hypothetically or remotely be affected cannot be considered as coming within the four corners of Order 21, Rule 90 of the Code."

<u>38. In our opinion, the provision of Order 21, rule 90 of the Code has been correctly interpreted in the decisions referred to above to mean that the interests contemplated therein must be a kind of right or liability which is existing in, or closely connected with, the property sold at the time of the sale and which is directly and actually, and not hypothetically or remotely, affected by the sale.</u>

39. Now the question is whether the interest of a share-holder of a private limited Company is such an interest as can be said to be affected by the sale of a property of the Company within the meaning of Order 21, rule 90 of the Cede of Civil Procedure, as construed above.

40. As has been already noticed, in three decisions of the Indian Jurisdiction, viz Vaidyamatha Vs. Indian Bank Ltd. A.I R. 1955 Mad. 496 Basanta Kumar Roy Vs. Charu Chandra Pal, 62 C. W. N. 132: A.I.R. 1958 Cal. 453 and Shyamlal Purchit and another Vs. Jagannath Roy and another A.I.R. 1969 Cal. 424, it has been held that the interest of a share-bolder is not the kind of interest which may be said to be affected by the sale of a properly belonging to the Company.

41. Relying upon the decision of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Charanjit Lal Chowdhury Vs. Union of India, A.I.R. 1951 S.C. 14, the Madras High Court held in the above named case of Vaidyanatha Vs. Indian Bank Ltd as follows:

"A share-holder is no doubt interested in the property of the Company in which he holds share if the properly is not looked after and administered, the share-holder would naturally suffer in his pocket. But this does not mean that every share-holder who apprehends that the property of Company is being mismanaged or is even fraudulently disposed of is entitled to co me to Court in the manner the petitioner has done.

It is easy to see that if such a cause were permitted, the business of the Company can be brought to a complete stare, still, when differences of opinion exist among the members of the Company. One legal effect of incorporation is to vest the ownership of the property in the Company, which acquires a separate legal existence. The property has to be managed by the directors, subject to the control of share-holders and the provisions of the constitution of the Company.

42. The Calcutta High Court expressed the following view as to the legal position of a share-holder with respect to the assets of the Company in the case of Basanta Kamar Vs. Charu Chandra Pal:

"A corporator is not the Corporation which is a distinct legal person. In the assets of a Corporation, the share-holders have no legal or equitable share" and held can the said basis:

"The legal position of a share-holder being as herein before indicated, the appellant had no interest in the auction sold property which was adversely affected by sale."

43. In the case of Shyamlal Vs. Jagannath of the Calcutta High Court, Sinha, C.J. (A. K. Mukherjee concurring) after a review of a number of decisions of the sub-continent summarised his conclusions in the following manner:

"(1) In the case of a public limited, Company registered under the (Companies) Act, the Company is a separate entity from its share-holders. It is the Company which is the owner of the assets, including immovable properties and not the share-holders.

(3) As long as the Company continues to exist, that is to say, before its dissolution, no share-holders can be said to have any interest in the properties and the assets of the Company in the sense that a wastage or frittering away of the assets might affect their rights, to enjoy the profits and eventually the distribution of the Company's assets in a winding up. This however is too remote an interest and cannot: be included with-in the definition, of 'interests' within the meaning of Order 21, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure."

Strong reliance has been placed upon these decisions on behalf of the learned Counsel for the respondents.

44. As mentioned above, learned Counsel for the appellants has cited the. decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Commissioner of Income Tax Vs. K.V. Miller (1959) 11 MR (SC) 430--PLD 1959 SC 219, in support of the proposition that it is ultimately the interests of the share-holders which are involved in the assets of the Contrary and has placed his reliance on the following observation of the Chief Justice Muni, who delivered the judgment of the Bench at page 231:

"The assets of the company are owned by it and not by its share-holders but the company is constituted for the purpose of earning profits and the share-holders are not only entitled to a rateable distribution of its assets on its being wound up, but also indirectly control the management of the company by appointing the Directors What is of the vital importance, however, is that a company is brought into existence and exists for the sole purpose of earning profits and gains and it earns them not for itself but for the benefit of the share-holders. To earn profits for its share-holders being the raison d’etre of the company, a company would be defeating the object of its own existence if Croesus like it filled its coffers with gold and did not distribute it as dividends to its share-holders."

45. In the said case, the Supreme Court of Pakistan was faced with the question whether dividends paid to the share-holders out of the income of a company, which was exclusively engaged in agriculture, were themselves agricultural income so as to be exempt from any tax and it has answered the said question by holding that the income which is agricultural income in the hands of a joint stock company does not cease to be agricultural income when it is distributed to the share-holders by way of dividends. The ratio of this decision is that the income of the company and the dividend income of the share-holders of the said company are derived from the identical source, namely, agriculture and as such the share-holders income as well as agricultural income are exempt from any tax.

46. It is not necessary for our purpose to examine the correctness of this view, as it was mainly concerned with the construction of certain provisions of the Income-Tax Act, but as the learned Chief Justice made certain observations as to the legal character of the relation between a company and its share-holders, which has some relevance to our present enquiry and on which learned Counsel for the appellants has placed reliance the said aspect of the decision acquires consideration.

47. Mr. M.H. Khondkar, learned Counsel for the respondents, has referred in this connection to a decision of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Bacha F. Guzdar Vs. Commissioner of Income-tax, A.I.R. 1955 S.C. 74, which has taken a contrary view as to the nature of the income in the hands of the share-holders paid as dividends out of what was agricultural income of the company, and this view has been based on the definition of 'agricultural income' which emphasizes, according to the said Court, the necessity of the recipient of the in-come having a direct, and immediate, rather than an indirect and remote, relation with land. In analysing the relation of a share-holder with the company, the Supreme Court of India has referred to the well recognised principle that the company is a jurisdiction person and is distinct from its share-holders and that it is the company which owns the property and not the share-holders, and also made the following statement at page 77 of the report:

"A share-holder has got no interest in the property of the company though he has undoubtedly a right to participate in the profits, if and when the company decides to divide them. The interest of a share-holder 'vis-a-vis' the company was explained in the `Sholapur Mills Case Charanjit Lai Vs. Union of India, 1951 S.C. 41 at pp. 54, 55(B). That judgment negatives the position taken up on behalf of the appellant that a share-holder has got a right in the properly of the company. It is true that the share-holders of the company have the sole determining voice in administering the affairs of the company and are entitled, as provided by the Articles of Association, to declare that dividends should be distributed out of the profits of the company to the share-holders but the interest of the share-holder either individually or collectively does not amount to more than a right to participate in the profits of the company."

48. The case of Charanjit Lai Vs. Union of India, A.I.R. 1951 S.C. 41 which has been referred to in the above quoted observation it interesting and has some bearing upon our present enquiry. The petitioner in the said case was a share-holder of a limited company, who made an application under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, challenging the validity of an Ordinance and an Act of the Parliament which subsequently replaced the Ordinance under which a set of Directors were appointed by the Bombay Government in place of the Directors of the Company, for the purpose of taking over the management and administration of the Company on the ground, inter alia, that the petitioner's fundamental right to hold, acquire or dispose of his property, as guaranteed under Article 19 (1) (f) of the Constitution, had been interfered with. The majority of the Judges held that the company being a distinct legal entity different from its share-holders, who had no right in the property of the company, the Act under challenge did not infringe the fundamental right conferred on a share-holder by Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. Fazal Ali, J, while agreeing with the majority view, clearly stated that the petitioner whose only property was his share was not competent to challenge the validity of the Act by way of enforcing his fundamental right relating to property, as the said Act 'purported to affect the right; of the company in respect of its property, and not that of the share-holder and it is pertinent to quote his observation at page 44 of the report:

"The Company and the share-holders are in law separate entities, and if the allegation is made that any has belonging to the Company has been taken possession of without compensation or the right enjoyed by the Company under Article 19(1)(f) has been infringed, it would be for the Company to come forward to assert or vindicate its own rights and not for any individual share holder to do so,"

49. Mukherjee, J. who delivered the learning judgment on behalf of the majority (viz, Kania, C.J. Fazal Ali, J and himself) stated the law as to the competence of a share-holder to invoke the jurisdiction of the Court for relief in respect of the property belonging to the Company in the following manner at page 52 of the report:

"An incorporated Company can come up before this Court for enforcement of the fundamental rights and so may the individual share-holders to enforce their own; but it would not be open to an individual share-holder to complain of an Act which affects the fundamental rights of the Company except to the extent that it constitutes an infraction of his own rights as well. This follows logically from the rule of law that a corporation has a distinct personality of its own with rights and capacities, duties and obligations separate from those of its individual members. As the rights are different and inhere in different legal entities, it is not competent to one person to seek to enforce the right of another, except where law permits him to do so."

50. It may be stated that the Minority view represented by Patanjali Shastri ard S.R. Das, JJ, did not differ with the majority view on the question of a share-holder's incompetence to enforce his fundamental right as to property in respect of the property belonging to the Company, but differed as to the applicability of the fundamental right of equality as provided in Article 14 of the Indian Constitution. S.R. Das, J, rather considered the question in details and came to the same conclusion in holding that there had been no infringement of fundamental right of the share-holder under Article 19(1)(f) and therefore the share-holder could not question the constitutionality of the Ordinance or the Act on that ground.

<u>51. It is now well-settled that an incorporated Company has got the fundamental attribute of corporate personality which is entirely distinct from that of its members and property of the Company is distinct from that of its members, whose only properties are their share-holdings. But Mr. Syed Nasiruddin, learned Counsel for the appellants, has relied, in support of his contention that the interest's of a share-holder are affected by the sale of a Company's property within the meaning of the Rule off he Code of Civil Procedure upon the observation of the Chief Justice Munir made in the case of E.V. Miller, which has already been referred to, that the share-holders have the ultimate control over the management of the Company, the directors being, in substance, their agents or delegates and that they are the ultimate beneficiaries of the income of the Company.</u>

<u>52. It is, no doubt true that the directors of the Company are appointed by the general body of share-holders in the manner prescribed by law and the share-holders way exercise a kind of control by adopting resolutions in General or Extra-ordinary meetings of the puny, but it will not be correct to say that they are the agents or representatives of the share-holders as such. The general body holders acting in a General meeting is to be distinguished Iron individual share-holders.</u>

53. In the Fliteroft's case, (1882) 21 Ch-R1 519 (C.A.) however, which has been cited on behalf of the Respondents, the distinct personality of the Company was emphasised and the limitation of the powers of the directors and of the share-holders in general meting were pointed out, when it was held that neither the directors nor the general meeting of the share-holders had the right to declare dividend out of the capital of the Company. Jessel M.R. made the following observation in the judgment of the Court of Appeal at pp 533-534 of the report:

"A limited Company cannot in any other way make a return of capital, the sanction of a general meeting can give no validity to such a proceeding, and even the sanction of every share-holder cannot bring within the powers of the Company an act which is not within its powers The creditor has no debtor but that impalpable thing, the Corporation, which has no property except the assets of the business. The creditor, therefore, I may say, gives credit to that capital, gives credit to the Company, on the faith of the representation that the capital shall be applied only for the purpose of the business, and has therefore a right to say that the Corporation shall keep its capital and not return it to share-holders, though it may be a right, which he cannot enforce otherwise than by a winding up order. It follows then that if directors who are quasi trustees for the Company improperly pay away the assets to the share-holders they are liable to replace them. It is no answer to say that the share-holders could not compel them to do so. I am of opinion that the Company could in its corporate capacity compel them to do so, even if there were no winding up".

55. The House of Lords gave its seal of approval on the principle of the distinct personality of a limited Company, different from that of its share-holders, for the first time in the well-known case of Salome Vs. Salome & Co. (1897) A.C. 22 and Lord Macnaghten explained the law in his speech before the House in the following words at page 51 of the report:

"The Company is at law a different person altogether from the subscribers to the memorandum ; and, through it may be that after incorporation the business is precisely the same as it was before, an the same persons are managers, and the same hands received the profits, the Company is not in law the agent of the subscribers or trustees for them. Nor are the subscribers as members liable, in any shape or form, except to the extent in the manner provided by the Act."

56. As has been commented by L.C.B. Gower in his "the Principle of Modern. Company Law" (1957):

"Since Salome’s case the complete separation of the Company from the share-holders has never been doubted  there are cases in which the legislature and, to a very small extent, the Courts have allowed the veil of incorporation lifted, but in general it is as opaque and impassable as an Iron Curtain."

<u>57. A Company, however, is an artificial person and must act through some natural agent. The institution of a board of directors who are appointed by the general meeting of the share-holders has therefore been created for the management of, and carrying out the affairs or, the Company. It appears that in England until the end of the nineteenth century the validity of the principle that the general meeting was the company, whereas the directors were merely the agents of the Company subject to the control of the Company in general meeting, has been generally assumed. The board of directors of a Company has gradually developed in to a distinct entity, as we find in the following observation made by Green, L.C. in the case of Shaw & Sons (Salford) Ltd. Vs. Shaw (1935) 2 K.B. 113 C.A. :</u>

<u>"A Company is an entity distinct alike from its share-holders and its directors. Some of its powers may, according to its articles be exercised: by its directors, certain other powers may be reserved for the share-holders in general meeting if powers of management are vested in the directors they and they alone can exercise those powers. The only way in which the general body of share-holders can control the exercise of the rovers vested by the articles in the directors is by altering the articles, or if opportunity arises, under the articles, by refusing to reelect the directors of actions they disapprove. They cannot themselves usurp the powers which by the articles are vested in the directors any more than the directors can usurp the powers vested by the articles in the general body of share-holders."</u>

<u>59. The position that emerges out of the development of the Company law is that it is either the board of directors of a Company or the general meeting of the share-holders which can act on behalf of the Company under certain circumstances. A share-holder has no proprietary interest in the property, of the Company nor his interest in his own property, viz his share-holding, is directly affected by the sale of a property of the Company. If the board of directors do not act, the majority of the members may be allowed to prosecute an action in the name of the Company under certain conditions. The general right of action in case of such a loss of property belongs to the Company itself and the Company can act only through its board of directors. In certain exceptional 'circumstances an individual share-holder or several share-holders may be permitted to initiate proceeding to redress certain illegality.</u>

<u>60. We have already noticed that a proceeding before an executing Court for setting aside a sale held by it is a kind of summary proceeding in which the question as to fraud or irregularity in respect of the processes of the said Court are determined on the basis of the records of the execution case and the evidence that may be produced relating to the processes issued therein. The right to institute such a proceeding has understandably been restricted to these categories of persons, who are directly interested in the sale of the property, which is sought to be set aside. The first two categories, namely, the decree-holder or the persons who are entitled to rateable distribution of assets have no direct interest in the properly sold but are in in a high sale price of the property. The third category comprises those who have some existing interest in the property, which is directly affected by the sale.</u>

61. Having regard to the principles of the Company law and the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, as have been noticed above, there appears to be little difficulty in conducting that a share-holder of a Company has no direct interest in the property of the Company, which may be affected by a sale of such a property in a Court auction so as to entitle him to bring an action for selling aside the said sale under Order 21, Rule 90 of the Code.

<u>62. This is also in accord with the well-known principle of Company law, which is commonly know as the rule in Foss Vs. Harbottle (1843) 2 Hare 461, Jenkins L.J. restated the said rule in the case of Edwards and another Vs. Halliwell and others (1950) 2 All. KR. 1064 (C.A.) thus:</u>

<u>"The rule in Foss Vs. Harbottle, as I understand it, comes to no more than this. First, the proper plaintiff in an action in respect of a wrong alleged to be done to a company or association of persons is prima facie the company or the association of persons itself. Secondly, where the alleged wrong is a transaction which might be made binding on the Company or association and all its members by a simple majority of the members, no individual member of the Company is allowed to maintain an action in respect of that mater for the simple reason that, if a 'majority of the members of the Company or association is in favour of what has been done, then cadit questio. No wrong had been done to the Company or association and there is nothing in respect of 'which any one can sue. If, on the other hand, a simple majority of the members of the Company or association is against what has been done, then there is no valid reason why the Company or association itself should not sue."</u>

<u>63. According to this rule, when a property of the Company has been wrongly or illegally sold in a Court auction, it is the Company itself, and not the individual share-holders, which shall be the 'plaintiff in an action brought to undo the wrong and recover the properly, as individual share-holders have no cause of action in such a case. There may of course he a case where the personal rights of a share-holder have been infringed or about to be infringed. In that case such a share-holder has undoubtedly a cause of action entitling him to bring an action for necessary redress. Apart from that, certain exceptions to the rule in Foss Vs. Harbottle have been recognised in the administration of Company law when individual share-holders have been permitted to bring what is known in American Courts as 'derivative action'. Such an action is really one on behalf of the Company to enforce rights derived from it but may be permissible, as, because of certain circumstances, it is impracticable for the Company to bring such an action.</u>

64. The law on this matter as practised in England has been stated in Halsbury's Laws of England (3rd Edition), Volume 6 at pages 445-46, paragraph 863, in the following words:

"In an action to redress a wrong done to a Company or to recover moneys or damages alleged to be due to a Company, the Company is the only proper plaintiff by direction of the Company or its Directors. Where the members complaining represent the majority of the Company, the action may be brought in the name of the company, even though the directors object. The Court may allow the matter to stand so that a meeting of the Company can be held to that whether the action should proceed in the name of the Company. At such a meeting the votes of the persons complained of cannot be excluded. Proceeding may be brought, however, by any member or members in his or their own name or names, where such authority cannot be obtained and the act complained of is of fraudulent character or oppressive or is ultra-vires of the company or is criminal or where the result would otherwise be that the Company was carrying out by an ordinary resolution something which could only be properly carried out by a special resolution or by another resolution requiring a prescribed majority.

In such a case the plaintiff should distinctly allege the true nature of the act complained of and the impossibility of getting the company to impeach its …………

In all such cases the company must be made a defendant. If directors are them-selves the wrong doers, it is proper to add them as defendants.

<u>65. It seems to be clear that under the general principles of Company law ordinarily an individual share-holder of a Company has no right of action in case of loss of a property belonging to the company. He may, however, be deemed to have such a right in case of fraud or collusion committed by the directors or the persons in control of the company. Such a right is to be exercised obviously on behalf and for the benefit of the company and that on proof of the circumstances giving rise to such a right.</u>

<u>66. Tested from this principle of the Company law also, it is obvious that a share-holder is not directly concerned with a wrongful or irregular sale of a property of the Company and his interest in case of such a sale is indirect and remote. Under this principle, he has no doubt a conditional right of action, but that can be established only in a properly framed suit, in which the company and the directors are necessary parties. The executing Court trying a miscellaneous proceeding, as is contemplated in Order 21, Rule 90 of the Code cannot certainly be considered to be a proper forum for deciding a dispute of this nature, which requires elaborate investigation in matters which are not germane to such a miscellaneous proceeding.</u>

<u>67. From all these considerations as referred to above, we are of the view that a share-holder of a company is not a person whose interests are affected by sale of a property of the company within the meaning of Order 21, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and that he is not competent to apply under the said provision.</u>

68. Learned Counsel for the appellants has also contended, relying upon a Single Bench decision of the Pinjab High Court of the Indian jurisdiction in the case of the Punjab Mercantile Bank Ltd. Vs. Sardar Kishan Singh A.I.R. 1963 Punjab 230, that even if the appellants had no locus-standi to file an application under the specific provision of the Cede to set aside the sale, the Court had ample reserve of inherent powers to satisfy itself suo-motu that its process had been abused and that because the source of information happened to be a person who had no locus-standi, the Court could not close its eyes and decline to exercise its inherent powers to, set aside the sale. This case, which has been relied upon by the learned Counsel for the appellants, arose out of an application made by a stranger who claimed himself to be an intending purchaser prepared to pay a large sum of money for the auction purchase of the property which was sold for a comparatively paltry amount in account of, as it was alleged, a conspiracy between the auction purchaser and the judgment-debtor. The learned judge made the following observation in course of his judgment:

"Even if the person who brought to light fraud had no locus-standi either under Section 47 or Order 21, Rule 90, the Court had an ample reserve of inherent powers to satisfy itself suo motu that its process was abused. Because the source of information happened to be a person who had no locus-standi the Court could not close its eyes and decline to exercise its inherent powers to set aside the sale on being satisfied that as a result of a conspiracy a fraud had been perpetrated and its process had been abused."

69. The judicial authorities on the question of the scope and extent of the inherent power of a Court for doing a thing in regard to which some specific provisions have been made in the Code do not appear to be uniform, but this Punjab case appears to have gone much further than most of these authorities. It is interesting to note allegation of fraud was made in that case against the decree-holder, namely, the official Liquidator of the Bank, who had been in charge of the conduct of the execution proceeding. Rather, if anybody was prejudiced. according to the finding of the Court, on account of the sale being held for a paltry amount as a result of the conspiracy between the auction purchaser and the judgment debtor, it was the decree-holder, who however, does not appear to have chosen to raise any objection to such a sale. The Court intervened in exercise of its inherent powers at the instance of an intending auction-purchaser, who sought to make out a case that the sale took place on a date earlier than the advertised date. This case of the intending purchaser was not accepted by the Court and there was no finding to the effect that the said person was prevented by any conspiracy or fraud from putting in a bid at the time of the auction. The learned judge took the view that the official Liquidator, the decree-holder, occupied the position of trust and represented the creditors, whose interests should not be allowed to suffer because of the inaction of the official Liquidator. It does not appear that either the auction purchaser or the judgment debtor having participated in the proceeding misled the Court in any way and a mistake was committed in consequence thereof, causing injustice to any of the parties. Nevertheless, the learned judge disregarded the specific provision of the Code and exercised its inherent powers in setting aside the sale merely on the view that some prejudice had been caused to some persons because of the sale being held at a low price. It is evident that the scope of the inherent jurisdiction of a Court was sought to be enlarged in this case, contrary to the established principle, for the proper appreciation of which reference may be made to some of the decided cases.

70. In dealing with the question whether a court has inherent jurisdiction to set aside a consent decree, which was obtained by practising fraud upon the court, the High Court of Bombay held in the Hanumant Gouda Vs. Charchi Giri Gouda Yogen Gouda, LL.R 34 Bom 408: 5 I. C. 689, that it was an inherent power of every court to correct its own proceeding where it had been misled.

71. This view of the Bombay High Court was followed by the Calcutta High Court in the case of Peary Chowdhury Vs. Sonoory Dass, 19 C.W.N. 419: AIR. 1915 Cal. 612 where the said High Court upheld, an order of the District Judge setting aside a similar consent decree in exercise of his inherent; powers and observed that not only the court had such powers but that it was its duty to set aside the decree obtained by fraud practised upon the Court, when appraised of it.

72. Rankin, C. J. however, expressly held, delivering the judgment cf a Bench in the case of J. C. Galstaun Vs. Pramatha Nath Roy, 57 Cal. 154: 33 C.W.N. 883, that the provision of section 151 of She Code could not be invoked for the purpose of the setting aside of a consent decree obtained by practising fraud, as the remedy by way of a suit was not available to the parties.

Another Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court (Mookerjca and Ruxburgh, JJ) expressed the same opinion in the case of Suresh Chandra Vs. Jogesh Chandra 43 C.W.N. 969.

73. A Single Judge of the same High Court, Henderson, J, appears to have taken a contrary view in the case of Akina Bibi and others Vs. Mohammad Ali Shah and others, 45 C.W. N. 392, relying upon the decision in the case of Peary Chowdhury Vs. Sonoory Dass 19 C.W. N. 419 and held that the cases involving fraud upon the court were an exception to the general rule that Sect ion 151 of the Cede had no application when there was another remedy by way of suit.

74. But a Division Bench of the Madras High Court in considering the question as to the extent of the inherent powers which could be invoked for setting aside the sale on the ground of fraud in the case of Bajjanna Vs. Critappa, A.I.R. 1947 Mad. 268, disapproved of the exercise of such powers for setting aside a sale en the view that the court could not presume the existence of the inherent powers to do that for which a statutory provision had been made. The said Bench expressed its view in the following words:

"Assuming that there was a fraud en the Court for which the decree Felder was responsible, that was a matter which could, give the petitioner a ground for an application under Order 21, Rule 96 of the Cede of Civil Procedure to set aside the sale prima facie, therefore, it is not a ground with reference to which the Court should presume the existence of any inherent poor to remedy the wrong done. The Court having been given a specific remedy, the Court cannot be presumed to have an inherent power overlapping or running parallel to the procedure laid down in the Code."

75. On the other hard Harris, C. J. (Sarkar, J. concurring) of the Calcutta High Court followed the rule laid down in the case of Peary Chowdhury Vs. Sonoory Dass in setting aside an execution sale in the case of Peary Krishna Vs. Mohan Lal A.I.R. 1950 Cal. 282, on the view, that a court had inherent power to correct its own proceeding when it had been misled by fraud of one of the parties. it was held in the said case that the court, which held the sale, having had no jurisdiction to entertain the proceeding in execution of a decree passed by the original side of the Calcutta High Court without a valid order of transfer by the court which passed the decree, the entire proceeding in execution was a nullity and that the court having been misled by the decree-holder in holding the said sale was competent to correct its own error by setting aside the sale in exercise of its inherent powers.

76. In the case of A. P. Ismail Rowthar Vs. Mynoon Bibi and others, A.I.R. 1966 Mad 84, a single Judge of the Madras High Court (Venkatadri, J) appears to have relied upon the above mentioned decision in the case of the Punjab Mercantile Bank Ltd Vs. Sardar Kishan Singh, as well as that in the case of Raghabachariar Vs. Murugesa Mudali A.I.R. 1923 Mad. 635 in observing that the Court had got inherent powers to set aside the sale, whether or not the petitioners had locus-standi to file the application for setting aside the sale. This observation appears to be a mere obiter dictum, as on the facts of the case the learned Judge had found that the petitioner had locus standi.

77. It may be mentioned that in the case of Raghabachariar Vs. Murugesa Mudali 1923 Mad 635 on which reliance was placed in the above mentioned case, a Division Bench of the Madras High Court held that the Court had inherent power to refuse to confirm a sale if it was satisfied that the court had been misled by reason of suppression of certain material facts by the plaintiff, that is, the decree-holder, in fixing the reserve price or in giving him leave to bid at the time of the sale.

78. A Single Judge of the Calcutta High Court (P. Chatterjee, J) refused to set aside a sale which was held for a low price in exercise of the inherent powers of a Court in the case of Basanta Kumar Vs. Mihirlal, A.I.R. 1968 Cal. 664, relying inter alia, upon a decision of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Manilal Mohan Lai Vs. Sajdu Ahmed, A. I. R. 1954 S. C. 349 where it had been held that the Court would not invoke the inherent power to circumvent the mandatory provisions of the Code.

79. A Division Bench of the pre-constitution Bangladesh High Court had to consider the question of the applicability of section 151 of the Code for the purpose of correcting a certain mistake committed by the Court in the case of S. M. Yousuf and another Vs. Khandakar Hafizur Rahman and others, 26 D.L.R. 124 and laid down the law as to the scope and extent of the powers conferred by section. 151 of the Code in the following manner, at page 131 of the report:"

“……Since the powers, as recited in section 151 of the Code are very wide and incapable of any precise definition, it requires great care and circumspection on the part of the Court in their exercise. A long line of judicial decisions has, however, set down certain norms or conditions for the exercise of the said powers, which, according to the said judicial views, are required to be adhered to, because it is such adherence as is likely to advance the cause of justice and prevent abuse of the process of the Court……..

The powers, as contemplated in the said section, are intended to supplement the other provisions of the Code, as a Legislature cannot foresee and provide for every eventuality which may occur, but they are not for the purpose of evading or ignoring the express provisions of the law for inventing a new procedure according to the individual inclination of a particular Judge. Under the cover of these powers, a Court cannot override the express provisions of the law applicable to a particular case. These powers cannot be invoked in. a case which is fully covered by specific provision in the Code or where there is a positive prohibition regarding a particular act or order or where there is an alternative remedy."

80. An exception, however, was made to the proposition laid down above, in case of a mistake committed by a Court or a Court's officer, in the following observation of the Bench:

"Mistake of a Court or Court's officer has always been treated en a different feeling because of the principle actus curia reminem gravabit" an act of the Court shall prejudice no person. If a mistake of a Court, which was not deliberate or intentional, is allowed to remain on the record, it may operate to the great prejudice of the parties leading to miscarriage of justice or abuse of the process of the Court. It is precisely to deal with such a case that the inherent power of the Court may be invoked to rectify such a mistake. Certainly all kinds of mistakes of a Court cannot be corrected in exercise of the said power. It is only unintentional and non-deliberate mistakes which may be set right in exercise of the said power".

<u>81. It appears to us that the preponderant judicial view which emerges out of the authorities referred to above and with which we find ourselves in agreement, is that the Court should not presume the existence of inherent power to do that for which specific provision has been made by a statute and should not invest itself with such jurisdiction for the purpose of getting round the express provisions of the law. Unintentional or inadvertent mistake of a Court causing some injustice to a party, however, stands on a different footing and in the case of such a mistake the exercise of inherent power of a Court is not subject to those limitations on its exercise which have been set down by the judicial authorities noticed above.</u>

<u>82. Order 21, rule 90 of the Code, as it stands, empowers a Court, which has held an auction sale, to set aside the sale on an application made, amongst others, by a person whose interests have been affected by the sale, on the ground that there has been material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting the said sale. If the ground for impugning the sale is fraud in publishing or conducting the sale then, according to the terms of the rule, the proceeding is to be initiated by a person as has been named in the said rule and recourse cannot, certainly, be taken to section 151 of the Code for the purpose of evading or circumventing the conditions laid down therein. If the ground of challenge is a kind of fraud other than that contemplated in the said rule, which vitiated the proceeding altogether, recourse to section 151 of the Code will also not be ordinarily appropriate, as a properly framed suit under the general law will undoubtedly be a mere appropriate remedy in such a case. Mistake of a Court or Court's officer causing some injustice to a party is the only circumstance which provides an exception to the proposition stated above and justifies the exercise of the inherent powers to correct such a mistake.</u>

83. We have already pointed out that the exercise of the inherent power to circumvent the conditions of the specific provision of the Code was not properly made in the case of The Punjab Mercantile Bank Ltd. Vs. Sardar Kishan Singh, A.I.R. 1963 Pun. 43, on which reliance has been placed on behalf of the appellants. Let us, however, see whether, independently of the said decision, the appellant can take advantage of the court's inherent powers on showing that the disputed sale was held causing injustice to a party, on account of a mistake committed by the Court on its being misled.

<u>84. The case made out in the instant case was briefly to the effect that, taking advantage of the fact that the Managing Director of the Company was residing in Calcutta and was in complete ignorance of the affairs of the Rupkhatha Cinema Hall; the appellants, who had been put in the meantime in charge of the management of the Cinema Hall, obtained a fraudulent and collusive decree against the Company, Respondent No. 3, in the name of Respondent No. 2, and thereafter got the execution proceeding instituted and, after suppressing all kinds of processes purchased the Cinema Hall with all its paraphernalia for a paltry sum of Tk . 3000/-.</u>

<u>So far as the allegation of fraudulent and elusive procurement of the decree is concerned if cannot be investigated in the proceeding for execution of the said decree.</u>

<u>85. The only other allegation of fraud mad by the appellant was in respect of suppression of processes before the sale was held, which was precisely within the scope of a proceeding under Order 21, rule 90 of the Code. There was no allegation of fraud which had misled the Court and induced it thereby to commit a mistake causing injustice to any of the parties. As a matter of fact, the only point for determination relating to the grounds for cancelling the sale, which was formulated and investigated in the Court of the Subordinate Judge; was in respect of material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting the sale. Under the circumstances, it would not have been permissible for the Court to ignore the terms of the specific provision of the Code and take recourse to its inherent power to set aside the sale.</u>

<u>The result, therefore, is that this appeal is dismissed. There shall, however, be no order as to costs.</u>

End.
