case_source: On appeal from the Judgment and Order dated July, 1, 1969 of the High Court of East Pakistan, Dacca in Civil Rule No. 1687 of 1968.
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, J:- This appeal arises against the judgment and order of a Division Bench of the High Court of East Pakistan Dacca as it then was, which was passed in Civil Rule No. 1687 of 1968 on July 1, 1969.

2. The appellant who claims to be the eldest son of one Md. Amir Ali Mia, was on the death of his father, substituted as the Mutwalli of Salamat Mia Wakf Estate (enrolled as E. C. No. 4028) by an order of the Commissioner of Wakfs, East Pakistan on April 10, 1967. According to the terms of the registered deed of Wakf dated July 1, 1930 one Salamat Mia who is the Wakf, appointed himself the first Mutwalli and on his death his full brother's son Md. Amir Ali Mia was to be appointed the next Mutwalli, and after him the eldest amongst his sons, if religious and of good character, would become the Mutwalli, After the death of the said wakif, Amir Ali Mia became the Mutwalli. He died on April 5, 1967. Five days later, on April 10, 1967 the appellant applied for enrolling himself as Mutwalli.

2. On the same day the respondent No 1, Md. Khurshed Alam, had also sent one application by post to the Commissioner of Wakf to enroll him as the Mutwalli of the said Wakf Estate claiming to be the eldest son of Amir Ali Mia, the previous recorded Mutwalli. On May 3, 1967 the Commissioner of Wakfs rejected his prayer for appointment as Mutwalli on the ground that the late Md. Amir Ali Mia had filed an affidavit wherein he stated that the respondent No. 1, Md. Khurshed Alam, was not his son. No appeal was filed by him against the order dated April 10, 1967 appointing the appellant as the Mutwalli.

3. Thereupon the respondent No. 1 filed another Petition before the Commissioner of Wakfs contesting the appointment of the appellant as the Mutwalli. Notice was issued to the appellant on June 20, 1967 to show cause why his appointment as Mutwalli should not be cancelled and the respondent No. 1 be appointed as Mutwalli. On July, 7, 1967 the appellant filed objection against the prayer of the respondent No. 1 for appointment as Mutwalli on the ground that he was not the son of late Md. Amir Ali Mia. He even went further and asserted that the respondent No. 1 was the son of a prostitute who was still alive and living at Natore.

4. Both the parties appeared before the Administrator of Wakfs who, after hearing them, quite rightly felt that as the question involved as whether the respondent No. 1 was the legitimate son of Amir Ali, it could only be finally decided by a Civil Court. He, therefore, expressed reluctance to interfere with the order of his predecessor who had earlier rejected the claim of the respondent as has been referred to above and by his order dated December 5, 1967 rejected the petition of the respondent No. 1.

5. The respondent No. 1 preferred an appeal (Miscellaneous appeal No, 12 of 1968) against this order under Section 43 of the East Pakistan Wakfs Ordinance, 1962 before the District Judge, Rajshahi, who by the judgment dated September 16, 1968 dismissed the appeal on findings, interalia, (1) that although the late Mr. Md Amir Ali Mia acknowledged the respondent No. 1 as his son, that did not establish that he was legitimate and as such this "acknowledgment is no acknowledgement in the eye of law" (2) that the Administrator considered the documents filed by the parties. (3) that the appeal from the order dated December 5, 1967 was not competent and (4) that the appeal, if taken from order dated April 10, 1967 was barred by limitation;

As the respondent No, 1 got no relief from him, the moved the High Court of East Pakistan under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and succeeded in obtaining the Rule, being Civil Rule No. 1687 and 1968.

6. The learned Judges of the High Court who heard the Rule on July 1, 1969 set aside the orders of the Administrator of Wakfs as well as of the District Judge and ordered that the respondent No 1 was to act as Mutwalli till his status was determined in a properly constituted suit, if any. The learned Judges found inter alia (1) that the order of the Administrator dated April 10, 1967 was no order in the eye of law under Section 43 of the East Pakistan Wakfs Ordinance 1962, (2) that the order dated December 5, 1967 was the one under that section and the appeal to the learned District Judge therefrom was competent and within time, (3) that the learned District Judge did not act as a "persona designata" (4) that acknowledgment by the late Md. Amir Ali Mia of the respondent No. 1 as his son is substantive evidence that the respondent No. I. is his legitimate son and (5) that the appellant if so advised, might file a properly constituted suit to have the status of the respondent No. 1 determined.

Being dissatisfied with the order passed by the learned Judges of the High Court, the appellant filed a petition for special leave to appeal in the Supreme Court of Pakistan.

On December 1, 1969 the Supreme Court of Pakistan granted leave to consider the following contentions raised by the appellant:

7.(1) acknowledgment by itself is no proof of legitimacy,(2) High Court in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction could not set aside the findings of the fact arrived at by the District Judge, and (3) the revisional application before the High Court was not maintainable as the District Judge acted as a "persona designata".

8. Of the three contentions we propose to consider the third contention first since it raises preliminary objection to the jurisdiction of the High Court. Mr. M. H. Khondkar, the learned Counsel for the appellant, vehemently argued that since the District Judge has been mentioned by his designation and not as a Court in Section 43 of the East Pakistan Wakfs Ordinance, 1962 (hereinafter referred to as "the Ordinance") no revision lies against his order before the High Court under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or, in other words, in such circumstances the learned Judges of the High Court should have declined to exercise jurisdiction under that Section, and since they did not do so; their judgment is not sustainable in law. Whether the District Judge constituted a Court or should be viewed as such, or he was a mere 'persona designata' is a question which being undoubtedly of considerable importance has been considered many a time by various Courts. In the former case, his Court being subordinate to the High Court was amenable to its jurisdiction exercisable under Section 113 of the Code. In the latter case, however the position would be otherwise, he not being a Court but a person described by his designation cannot be subjected to any order of the High Court under section 115 of Code.

9. If Mr. Khondker succeeded to establish the preliminary point, the impugned judgment of the High Court is liable to be set aside and the result would be that the appellant would remain the Mutwalli of the wakf Estate as was decided by the learned District Judge, provided, of course, his decision was within the scope of his powers conferred by Section 43 of the Ordinance. The learned Counsel', therefore; first attempted to substantiate his contention that the District Judge was not a Court but a 'persona designata' from whose order no revision lies under Section 115 of the Code. In support, he cited the following decisions:-Must. Dirji Vs. Smt. Goalin, AIR 1941 Patna 61 (F.B) : Afsaruddin Vs. Wazed Khan and another, (1952) 4 DLR 442; Azizul Huq Vs, M/s. Hanif Ltd. and others, (1955) 7 DLR : 287; Aswad Mia and another Vs. Shahidulla Mia, (1958) PLR Dacca 1163; Anil Das and others Vs. Mustaque Ahmed, (1966) 18 DLR 86 IDBP (Bangladesh) Vs. KS, Master Industries,(1974) 26 DLR 157 and Bangladesh Fisheries Society Ltd. Vs. Chairman, Labour Court: (1975) 27 DLR 367.

10. As the question whether the District Judge is a 'persona designata' or a Court becomes relevant when he is so described in a particular statute. It would be well to quote the provisions of Section 43 of the Ordinance which, in the present case, raised this controversy. Section 43 runs as follows:

"In the case of any wakf of which there is no Mutwalli or where there appears to the Administrator to be an impediment to the appointment of a Mutwali in terms of the deed of wakf or where the successor to the office of Mutwalli is a minor, a person of unsound mind or a person adjudged insolvent by a competent. Court of law, the administrator may for such period as he deems fit, appoint a person to act as Mutwalli with notice to all the persons interested in the wakf. Any person aggrieved by such an appointment may, within three months iron the date of receipt of the notice, appeal to the District Judge and the decision of the District Judge shall be final.

11. These provisions, as will be seen, do not mention the Court of District Judge, but describes him by his official designation. Now, before it can be determined whether he is a Court or a mere 'persona designata' , it would be necessary to find what a Court is. Ordinarily, a Court means the place where justice is administered, but this word also means the person or persons who administer justice. When used in the latter sense, its essential attribute is the exercise of judicial functions by such person or persons. This, in turn, requires us to consider what are judicial functions, and also the processes involved in a judicial decision, but as they have already been considered and defined in judgments cited before us, no fresh attempt to define them is, however, necessary. As observed by Fazi Ali J:—

"Judicial function means the function of "deciding litigated questions according to law" deciding them not arbitrarily but on evidence and according to certain rules of procedure which ensure that the person, who is called upon to decide them, acts with fairness and impartiality. It is often said that two of the important features of a Court are (1) that the proceedings before it are normally conducted in public and (2) that it is conducted in. the presence of the parties concerned.

(Vide AIR 1941 Patna at p. 65)

In this case the question was whether Commissioner appointed under the Workmen's Compensation Act was a Court.

<u>12. Since in this connection another Latin expression 'persona designata' referred to earlier, has been considered in determining the question whether District Judge named in the statute as such exercises his powers as a Court or not, we may also consider its meaning before we refer to what a judicial decision or a court is. The expression 'persona designata' means a person described in the statute or legal instrument by his official designation or as a member of a class" (Vide AIR 1941 Patna 65 at 68) In Osborn's Concise Law Dictionary, 4th col; at P.253 this expression has been defined as "a person who is pointed out or described as an individual, as opposed to a person ascertained as a member of a class, or as filling a particular character." In Partha Saradhi Naidu V. Kateswarn Pao, AIR 1924,  Madras 56 (F.B) Schwabe C. J. defined 'persona designata' as persons selected to act in their private capacity and not in their capacity as Judges. This expression has not, however, been used in the provisions of Section 43 of the Ordinance, as also it does not occur in similar provisions of law elsewhere. None the less, in interpreting such provisions where powers have been conferred upon persons who, though officers of the Court, have been mentioned by their designation, such as District Judge. Chief Judge of the Small Cause Court, Commissioner etc. The question which arose was whether an officer so named in the statute exercises the powers of a Court or is a mere persona designata'. As observed by Fazi Ali J,</u>

<u>"If he is invested with the rowers as a Court, the necessary implication is that the jurisdiction of the Court is enlarged and its decision is subject to all the incidents of such jurisdiction: if the powers are conferred on him not as a Court, he is a mere 'persona designata' and his decision will not be subject to the incidents of such jurisdiction as the court ordinarily exercises.</u>

<u>(Vide AIR 1941 Patna P. 65)</u>

13. Further, in the opinion of the learned Judge there is no real antithesis between the expression `persona designata' and a Court, in other words, even a persona designate may be a Court :

“Whether he is a Court or not depends upon his powers and the functions which he has to discharge, It is not inconceivable that in some cases when an Officer of a Court, say the District Judge, is called upon to decide a certain matter not as a District Judge, but as a 'persona designata' he may still be a Court by reason of some special provision in the statute which authorised him to decide the matter. The statute may expressly say that he will be deemed to be a Court or that his decision will be subject to appeal or revision by a superior Court."

<u>(Vide AIR 1941 Patna P. 65)</u>

14. We may there also refer to the following well-known exposition of what a judicial decision is made by Scott C. J. in Cooper Vs. Wilson, (1937) L.R. 2 KBD. 309.

"A true judicial decision pre-supposes an existing dispute between the two or more parties and then involves four requisites (1) the presentation (not necessarily orally) of their case by the parties to the disputes (ii) If the dispute between them is a question of fact the ascertainment of the fact by means of evidence adduced by the parties to the dispute and often with the assistance or argument by or on behalf of the parties on the evidence, (iii) if the dispute between them is a question of law the submission of legal argument by the parties and (iv) a decision which disposes of the whole matter by a finding upon the facts in dispute and an application of the law of land to the facts so found, including where required a ruling upon any disputed question of law. A quasi judicial decision equally presupposes an existing dispute between two or more parties and involves (i) and (ii) but does not necessarily involve(iii) and never involves (iv)"

15. As early as 1952, Ibrahim, J. of the Dacca High Court, while considering the provisions of Section 18-C of the Bengal Local Self Government Act, 1885, had to consider whether a District Judge or Sub-judge deciding election cases are courts within Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In deciding the District Judge or a Subordinate Judge whose decision was made final was a Court subordinate to the High Court the learned Judge reviewed a number of decisions of the different superior Courts in the Indian sub-continent which need not be considered afresh by us, and reached the conclusion that "if the function is a judicial function, then he is a court, though he is described not as court but by official designation". (Vide, Afsaruddin Bhuiyan V, Wajed Ali Khan, (1952) 4 DLR 442).

16. In this connection the learned Judge considered at length the meaning and the content of the word 'Court' and observed as follows:

“Court means two things: a place where justice is administered and a person who administers it. He must invariably be appointed by the State; for the administration of justice is an exclusive affair of it. The court is no forum for decision of hypothetical questions. The Judge deals with actual disputes, and his duty is not to report but to decide. He has no interest in the proceeding before him except the interest of justice. He decides cases not initiated by him but by the interested parties who have a right to be heard. The proceeding is held in their presence and is normally open to the public. He decides not arbitrarily, not according to any law made by him but according to the law, both substantive and adjective, laid-down by the statutes, and on 'evidence which the parties have the right-to-adduce. He cannot refuse to exercise his jurisdiction, and to enable him to exercise it, he is armed with powers to compel the attendance of witnesses and the production of documents and material objects, and to execute his orders. His decisions are given by judgments which set forth the reason, and which are, subject to alternation by any Court of superior jurisdiction, final and binding. But what constitutes the distinctive feature of the Court is that its function is judicial. Judicial function is different from all other functions. The subject of judicial function is to determine jural relation." (Ibid, at. P. 44).

In support of these specific conclusions the learned Judge relied on the following observations : "An enquiry is judicial if the object of it is to determine jural relation between one person and another or a group of persons or between" him and the community generally "and' even a judge acting without such an object in view is not acting judicially." (vide, Queen Empress Vs. Tuja and others, ILR 12 Bombay 36). The main considerations for the decision are found in the following observations of the Court : "The question raised by the election petition is a very substantial question of right and the Judge is not required to report or to give an opinion, but to decide. Opinion involves both interpretation and application. Under this Act, the decision is required to be in the form of a declaration and the declaration shall be whether the election is valid or void. Such a declaration can be given only by a Court". (Vide (1952) 4 DLR 442 P. 448).

17. Besides, the District Judge was given the power to summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses as compel them to produce documents and articles in their possession or power and to give evidence.

18. In Azizul Huq. vs. S. M. Hanif (1955) 7 DLR 287, the expressions "District Judge" used in Section 29 of the East Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1953 were considered by the Dacca High Court. The question was whether the District Judge who was invested with a power of transfer of appeals, even though that power of transfer is restricted to such judicial officer as may be appointed by the Government, is a court or a 'persona designata', Mention was made that there was no provision in the Act which either expressly or by implication denied the revisional power of the High Court under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, though it was provided that the decision of the District Judge shall be final. In deciding that the District Judge was acting as a Court and not a 'persona designata' a number of decisions were considered among which the case of Walled All vs. Haji Abdul Wahed, (1954) 6 DLR 206, a decision of a single Bench of the Dacca High Court which held that the "District Judge" as mentioned in Section 29 of the East Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1953 was not a court but a 'persona designata', was over-ruled.

19. In this connection reference may he made to the case of Aswad Miah and another vs. Shahidullah Miah and others, 1658 PLR Dacca 1163 but as this decision does not concern the determination of the question whether a person named in the statute is a court or a 'persona designata', it is not necessary for us to consider the same. It may, however, be mentioned that a long line of decisions was considered in this case regarding the attributes of a Court as well as what are the elements of a judicial decision. In deciding whether a Collector who holds sale for arrears of revenue under the provision of the Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act, 1859 acts as a Court or not, some tests for determining whether a tribunal is a Court or not were formulated in this case.

20. In Anil Das vs. Mustaque Ahmed (1965)17 DLR 86, the question was whether the District Judge who was authorised to hear appeal from an order of eviction passed by a Magistrate under Section 2 of the East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance, 1964 was to exercise judicial function and as such to act as a Court. It was held that as in hearing the appeal the District Judge was to decide the dispute between the parties, to consider the materials on record, conclusions reached by the Magistrate and to scrutinise judicially materials e n which these conclusions are based, he cannot be viewed as holding a departmental inquiry. It was held that as he fulfills these well-known characteristics of a Court; the District Judge is a court amenable to the jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

21. Recently, in the case of IDBP vs. Master Industries (1974) 26 DLR 157, the question whether District Judge as mentioned in Section 39 of the Industrial Development Bank of Pakistan Ordinance, 1961 was a Court or a 'persona designata' was considered by Bhattacharya J. (of the High Court Division, as he then was) who, after considering many decisions, including the aforesaid ones, made the following observations:

“It is clear that the District Judge who is a part of the ordinary judicial system of the country becomes seized of a dispute under Section 39 of the Ordinance which arises out of an assertion of a legal right pertaining to enforcement of a security respecting repayment of a loan. Such a dispute can be litigated in the ordinary courts of country in accordance with the ordinary judicial procedure. For the purpose of expeditious settlement of a claim and in order to avoid delay which is inevitable under the ordinary procedure, a special procedure has been devised in Section 39 of the Ordinance. Nevertheless, the District Judge has to investigate the claim in accordance with the ordinary judicial procedure as provided in the Code of Civil Procedure and determine the dispute judicially by giving a binding decision in the case. The District Judge in disposing of the dispute has to finally determine the rights of parties pertaining to the dispute subject to the scrutiny of the High Court in an appeal, if so preferred" (at PP. 169-170).

22. Again, in Shamsul Huq Sikder vs. Election. Tribunal and others (1975) 27 DLR 392, the same learned Judge, had to consider whether the Presiding Officers of Civil Courts who have been appointed as Election Tribunals exercised the powers of the Court. In giving a negative answer the learned Judge observed:

“Exercise of judicial power of the State is the determining factor for investigating body with the character of a court and that a tribunal exercising a judicial power does not mean merely that it is acting with fairness and impartiality on a proper consideration of all relevant materials after giving an opportunity to all contending parties to present their respective cases. In order the exercise of the judicial power or action judicially may be a sign of acting as a court, it must be acting as a part of the judicial machinery of the Slate charged with the duty of determining the rights of the subject against another or the question of rights between the subject and stale and discharging its functions according to established form of judicial procedure. If we examine the character of an Election Tribunal in the light of this view of law, it will be found that the Election Tribunal does not at all act as a part of the judicial machinery of the State exercising judicial power of the State and as such, in our view, an Election Tribunal cannot be regarded as a Civil Court".

23. In one of the cases decided by the Dacca High Court, namely Khwaja Gholam Akbar vs. Madarbari Conciliation Court Union Committee (1968) 20 DLR 160, the question whether the District Judge as mentioned in Section 8 of the Conciliation Courts Ordinance is a persona designata or not was, however, answered in the affirmative, meaning thereby that he is not a Court subordinate to the High Court.

24. Mr. S.R. Pal, Counsel for the respondent No. 1, submitted that reference to District Judge in Section 43 of the Ordinance cannot negative him as a Court and convert him into a private individual. Whether any procedure regulating the manner of discharge of his functions in deciding an appeal under this Section has been laid down or not or whether any power of transfer of such an appeal to an Additional District Judge or Subordinate Judge has been conferred on him or not, these being merely superficial considerations, cannot make him a 'persona designata'. Rather the absence of any procedure shows that the District Judge was to act as a Court. Moreover, when such right of appeal as under this section is given to one of the ordinary Courts of the country, the procedure, orders and decrees of that Court will be governed by the ordinary rules of the Civil Procedure Code.

25. In support, he cited the following decisions: Maung Bo Thaw vs. Ma Pin, AIR 1934 PC 81, Hemsiugh vs. Basant AIR 1936 PC 93 and Adaikappu vs. Chandrasekhar. AIR 1948 PC 12. When a person is claiming an office as under Section 43 of the ordinance, such claim which partakes of civil nature involves a decision requiring the exercise of judicial functions. The learned Counsel also mentioned that District judge as defined in Section 3(17) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 means the Judge of a principal Civil Court of original civil jurisdiction and also referred to the definition in East Bengal Civil Courts Act where also District Judge means a principal Civil Court. According to him, the expression 'persona designata' means a definite person, but District judge is not such a definite person and means that Court of District Judge having jurisdiction to hear an appeal under Section 43, not any District Judge, Mr. Pal, further submitted that excepting the case of Khwaja Gholarn Akbar vs. Madarbari Conciliation Court (1968) 20 DLR, 160 in all other cases cited by Mr. Khondker, District Judge has been held as a Court. The decision reported in 20 DLR 160 shows the lack of proper considerations of the principle which has according to Mr. Pal, been correctly laid down in the decision reported in (1952)4 DLR 442 referred to above.

<u>26. Having considered the decisions cited and submissions made by the learned Counsel we are of the view that the expression "District Judge" as occurs in section 43 of the Wakfs Ordinance means a Court and not a persona designata'. This conclusion which establishes the maintainability of the revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure sterns from the consideration of section.43 of the Ordinance. In hearing an appeal from the order of the administrator of wakfs made under this section, the District Judge is required to decide a dispute regarding the right to the office of Mutwalli claimed by two or more parties. This he can only do after hearing them and taking such evidence as may be considered necessary and also after hearing legal arguments on both facts and law which he is supposed to interpret and apply. Though his decision has been made final, which precludes any further appeal from his decision, such finality as attaches thereto does not oust the revisional power of the High Court, As observed by Amiruddin Ahmed J. of the Dacca High Court in a case involving interpretation of the word 'final'. The word 'final' in relation to the orders of the Court occurring in several statutes has been construed to mean that they are not appealable; nevertheless they are open to revision or reviewed". [Vide. (1955) 7 DLR 287).</u>

<u>The use of the word 'final' in section 43 does not therefore, mean that the District Judge is not amenable to the jurisdiction of the High Court.</u>

27. As to the merits of the case, among the two questions involved, one relates to the legitimacy of the respondent which, if established, would entitle him to the office of Mutwalli as claimed by him and with this question is also connected the controversy which involves the extent of the powers of the District Judge to determine this question in hearing an appeal from the decision of the Administrator of Wakfs under section 43 of the Ordinance. If it be found that the District Judge had no power to decide this question even provisionally, his findings thereon should have been set aside by the High Court and the parties should have been directed to get the question of legitimacy settled by a competent civil court as directed by the Administrator of Wakfs. We may now, therefore, consider whether the Judge should have proceeded to consider the question of legitimacy.

27 A. Proceeding to consider the connected controversy first, if it is answered by us in the negative, there is no need to consider the question as to legitimacy referred to above. On a reference to the previsions of Section 43 of the Wakfs Ordinance quoted above, it appears that an appeal to the District Judge has been provided against the decision of the Administrator of Wakfs appointing someone to act as Mutwalli. Some confusion, it needs be mentioned, seems to exist as regards the scope of the power of the Administrator of Wakfs regarding the appointment of a Mutwalli under this Section.

<u>28. This Section does not confer upon him the power to remove a Mutwalli but only enables him to appoint someone as Mutwalli when there is some obstacle or difficulty in appointing someone as such due to the circumstances mentioned therein. Actually, the Administrator's power to remove a Mutwalli is regulated by Section 32 of the Wakfs Ordinance.</u>

29. Before the High Court the point raised on behalf of the appellant was that the order under which the appellant was inducted into the office of the Mutwalli was merely an order of substitution within the meaning of Section 51 of the Wakf Ordinance and was not an order of appointment under Section 43 and that as such the appeal before the District Judge by the respondent was incompetent. It may be recalled that the first order of the Administrator of Wakfs which was passed on April 10, 1967 expressly mentions substitution. The precise order made is as follows:-

"In reply to the above name an affidavit from the late recorded Mutwalli Moulana Amir Ali Meah and a substitution petition from his son Moulvi Amir Sultan Ali Hyder placed may please be seen. It appears from the substitution petition that the recorded Mutwalli Moulana Amir Ali Meah is dead. The applicant being eldest and religious and man of characier has applied for Mutwalliship in place of his deceased father according to the provisions of this deed.

In this connection consulted wakfs deed and it appears at marked A and B the wakfs deed that after-the death of the recorded Mutwalli Moulana Amir Ali Meah, among his sons who is eldest religious and man of character shall be next Mutwalli.

Accordingly, the applicant Moulana Amir Sultan Ali Hyder may be substituted as Mutwalli in place of late Moulvi Amir Ali Meah.

Sd/- Illegible,

10-4-67.

This order was not passed either in presence of the respondent No. 1 or to his knowledge. As a matter of fact, the respondent No. 1 who did not know of the aforesaid order sent the following application on April 10, 1967 to the Wakf Commissioner for appointing him as Mutwalli.

"To

The Commissioner of Wakfs, Government of East Pakistan, Dacca.

Sir,

I beg most respectfully to state that my father Md. Amir Ali, Mutwalli of Salamat Hossain Wakf Estate has expired on 5-4-67 in the Rajshahi Medical College Hospital, In accordance with the terms of the wakfs deed I shall be enrolled as the Mutwalli of the Salamat Hossain wakf estate being the eldest son of the deceased Amir Ali.

I pray, therefore, that your honour would be graciously pleased to enroll me as Mutwalli of the wakf estate and pass such other or further orders as your honour deem fit and proper and for which act of kindness as in duty bound I shall ever pray.

Yours most obediently

Sd/-Md. Khurshed

s/o. late Amir Ali Prop : Sahi Karachi Hotel, Saheb Bazar,

P.O. Gorma, District : Rajshahi.

Dated the 10th April 1967.

This application was rejected by the wakf Commissioner on June 5, 1967. This order reads as follows:

To

Mvi. Khurshed Alam

Prop. Shahi Karachi Hotel, Saheb Bazar P.O. Ghoramara, Rajshahi.

With reference to his petition dated 10-4-67 on the above subject, he is in-formed that his claim for Mutwalliship stands rejected as the late Mvi. Amir Ali stated swearing affidavit that he (Khorshed Alam) is not his son.

Sd/- R. Khan,

3-5-67.

Sd/- Kafiluddin,

For Administrator of 3-5-67 Wakfs. E,P."

On April 17, 1967 the respondent No. 1 submitted a fresh application for appointment as Mutwalli. This is as follows:

To,

The Commissioner of Wakfs

Government of East Pakistan, Dacca.

Sir,

In enclosing herewith a true copy of my petition dated 10-4-67 I beg to state that I despatched the above with registered post but as yet I have not received the acknowledgement, In the meantime I had in my mind to go personally before-your-honour with the relevant papers but due to serious illness of my daughter I could not avail. Perhaps your-honour is in receipt of the same in the meantime. Inshaallah, I will go to meet your honour within short time.

This is for favour of your information and kind consideration.

Your most obediently

Sd/- Md. Khurshed Alam

s/o. Late Amir Ali

Prop : Shahi Karachi Hotel P.O. Ghoramara, Dist. Rajshahi.

Dated the 17 April, 1967.

30. When this application of respondent No. 1 for appointment as Mutwalli of the Wakf estate was being considered by the Administrator in presence of the appellant, he felt that as the contest between them for appointment as Mutwalli involved the question whether respondent No. 1 was the legitimate son of Amir Ali, it could only be finally decided by a Civil Court. He further ordered that appellant should continue as the Mutwalli. The order which was made on 5-12-67 is as follows:

"Both the parties filed petitions  for appointment as Mutwalli. Amir Sultan Ali Hyder was appointed as Mutwalli and the claim of Mr. Khurshid Alam was rejected by my predecessor. The question of Mr. Khurshid Alam being a legitimate son of Amir Ali can only be finally decided by a Civil Court.

As his claim has been rejected Mr. Khurshed Alam should go to a competent Civil Court for establishing his claim. If he can succeed, then his case will be considered here. The Mutwalli should not only be the eldest son of late Amir Ali but also should be religious minded and of good character."

31. In repelling the contention referred to above, the High Court has pointed out that section 51 of the Ordinance does not provide for making an order for substitution of the successor of a deceased Mutwalli. It merely enables the successor or any other person to give information to the Administrator that a vacancy has occurred due to the death of Mutwalli. The High Court held that the order of the Administrator appointing the appellant as Mutwalli till the decision in a civil suit which may be instituted by the respondent was an order of appointment of Mutwalli under Section 43 of the Ordinance.

32. In granting special leave to appeal the Supreme Court seems to hold the view that the High Court was not wrong in so deciding. It, therefore, did not grant leave on this point. The High Court appears to have been correct in treating the order in question as an order of appointment of a Mutwalli under section 43 of the Ordinance. The Order dated April 10, 1967 mentions substitution of the appellant as Mutwalli in place of his deceased father, the final order was passed as a result of intervention by the respondent on December 5, 1967. From the order on this date which has been quoted above, it is, however, clear that the appellant was appointed Mutwalli provisionally as the order itself was to remain in force only until the question of legitimacy was finally decided by a competent Civil Court at the instance of the respondent.

<u>33. According to section 51 of the Ordinance, if there is any change in the management of an enrolled wall' which may be occasioned by the death or retirement or removal of Mutwalli, the prospective Mutwalli is to notify the change to the Administrator. In the absence of a dispute the latter is not required to make any formal order of appointment of a Mutwalli, as successor to the deceased, retired or removed Mutwalli. Only when a dispute exists the Administrator is to act under section 43 or 44 of the Ordinance. In the present case as already observed, the Administrator does not appear to have appointed the appellant as Mutwalli finally. He was to continue as a Mutwalli till the decision of a suit which the respondent might institute. The order of the Administrator was to all intents and purposes an order of appointment under Section 43 of the Ordinance.</u>

34. Of the two contentions upon which the Supreme Court granted leave, the first relates to the question whether acknowledgment by itself is a proof of legitimacy. As to the question whether the respondent is the oldest son of the deceased Mutwalli, the Administrator, the District Judge and the High Court seem to have been of the view that this should be decided finally by a Civil Court of competent jurisdiction in a properly framed suit and that till such decision is made, one of the rival claimants who has prima facie a better claim should be appointed as Mutwalli for the purpose of section 43 of the Ordinance. The Administrator and the District Judge were of the view that there was no proper evidence to show that the respondent was a son of Amir Ali, the deceased Mutwalli. After referring to certain documents such as the respondent's school certificate, deposition of Amir Ali in a criminal case, previous Mutwalli's letter, a Cabinnama, a certificate of the Commissioner etc. in which the respondent was acknowledged by Amir Ali as his son, the District Judge observed that the acknowledgement did not show that the respondent was acknowledged as a legitimate son. Such acknowledgement is no acknowledgment in the eye of law, he observed. He relied on an affidavit sworn by Amir Ali before his death stating that the appellant was his eldest son. This, according to the District Judge, set at rest all disputes regarding the claim of the respective parties. He, therefore, held that the respondent Khurshed Alam dismally failed to prove that he was the righful claimant of the office of the Mutwalli. Incidentally, it may be mentioned that he did not however, consider whether acknowledgment once validly made can subsequently be disclaimed by the acknowledger.

In spite of such a firm finding the District Judge affirmed the impugned order dated December 5, 1967 which gave the respondent the right to establish his clam in a Civil Court of competent jurisdiction.

35. It appears that before the High Court also elaborate arguments were advanced on both sides on the legitimacy issue. After considering the arguments and the decisions cited before them, the learned Judges of the High Court approved the following principle enunciated by Mahmood J, in the case of Muhammad Alladad Khan vs. Muhammad Ismail Khan ILR 10 Allahabad. 289;

"Although, according to the Muhammadan Law, Ikrar or acknowledgment in general stands upon much the same footing as an admission as defined in the Evidence Act, acknowledgments of parentage and other matters of personal status stand upon a higher footing than matters of evidence, and form a part of the substantive Muhammadan Law, So far as inheritance through males is concerned, the existence of consanguinity and legitimate descent is an indispensable condition precedent to the right of succession, and such legitimate descent depends upon the existence of a valid marriage between the parents. Where legitimacy cannot be established by direct proof of such a marriage, acknowledgment is recognised by Muhammadan law as a means whereby marriage of the parents or legitimate descent may be established as a matter of substantive law. Such an acknowledgement always proceeds upon the hypothesis of a lawful union between the parents and the legitimate descent of the acknowledged person from the acknowledger, and there is nothing in the Muhammadan law similar to adoption as recognised by the Roman and Hindu systems, or admitting of any affiliation which has no reference to consanguinity or legitimate descent. A child whose illegitimacy is proved beyond doubt, by reason of the marriage of its parents being either disproved or found to be unlawful cannot be legitimated by acknowledgment. Acknowledgment has only the effect of legitimation where either the fact of marriage or its exact time, with reference to the legitimacy of the child's birth, is a matter of uncertainty."

36. The learned Judge of the High Court also referred to the case decided by Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, namely, Saddique Hussain Khan vs. Hashim Ali Khan, 43 IA 212, wherein it was held that an acknowledgment by a Mohammadan that a person is his son is substantive evidence that the person is his legitimate son and that the onus of disproving his status is upon the person who alleges his illegitimacy. Relying on these observations of the Judicial Committee, the learned Judges of the High Court observed that as in the present case the allegation as to illegitimacy of the respondent No. 1 was made by the appellant he has to discharge that onus by proving his case in a properly constituted suit and the respondent No. 1 could not be relegated to a suit.

<u>37. The Muhammadan law does not recognise legitimation and acknowledgment cannot create or confirm the status of a legitimate son in favour of or upon a person, who as a matter of a fact, is not or is disproved to be the legitimate son of the acknowledged. But in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, an acknowledgment raises a presumption, the rebuttal of which is the burden of the person who disputes it and such a presumption can be rebutted only on the proof that the acknowledged person is not or cannot be the legitimate son of the acknowledger.</u>

38. The dictum of Mahmud J, on the question of acknowledgment in the Allahabad case and the view of law on the said question as expressed in the decision of the judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Saddique Hossain Khan vs. Hashem Ali Khan where referred to with approval in another decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Syed Habibur Rahman Chowdhury vs. Syed Altaf Ali Chowdhury. L.A. 48 IA 114 26 CWN 81 ILR. 48 Cal 856: AIR 1922 PC 159, where the law on the question was explained in the following words:

".. Legitimacy is a status which results from certain facts. Legitimation is a proceeding which creates a status which did not exist before. In the proper sense there is no legitimation under the Muhammadan law……….

By the Muhammadan law a son to be legitimate must be the offspring of a man and his wife or of a man and his slave; any other offspring is the offspring of zina, that is, illicit connection, and cannot be legitimate. The term 'wife' necessarily connotes marriage; but, as marriage may be constituted without any ceremonial, the existence of a marriage in any particular case may be an open question. Direct proof may be available, but if there be no such, indirect proof may suffice. Now one of the ways of indirect proof is by an acknowledgment of legitimacy in favour of a son. This acknowledgment must be not merely of sonship, but must be made in such a way that it shows that the acknowledge meant to accept the other not only as his son, but as his legitimate son. It must not be impossible upon the face of it, i. e. it must not be made when the ages are such that it is impossible in nature for the acknowledger to be the father of the acknowledge, or when the mother spoken to in an acknowledgment, being the wife of another, or within prohibited degrees of the acknowledger, it would be apparent that the issue would be the issue of adultery or incest.

The acknowledgment may be repudiated by the acknowledge. But if none of those objections occur, then the acknowledgment has more than a mere evidential value. It raises a presumption of marriage a presumption which may be taken advantage of either by a wife claimant or a son claimant. Being, however, a presumption of fact, and not juris et de jure, it is, like every other presumption of fact, capable of being set aside by contrary proof.

The result is that a claimant son who has in his favour a good acknowledgment of legitimacy is in this position. The Marriage will be held proved and his legitimacy established unless the marriage is disproved. Until the claimant establishes his acknowledgment the onus is on him to prove marriage. Once he establishes an acknowledgment, the onus is on those who deny a marriage to negative it in fact".

39. Mr. Khondker, Counsel for the appellants, placed the Allahabad Judgment in full as well as the judgment of the Judicial Committee of the privy Council in the case of Saddique Hossain Khan vs. Hashem Ali Khan (43 IA 212) before us and also made lengthy submissions on the principle stated therin, but it appears that the High Court has correctly enunciated the law as to the acknowledgment being substantive proof of legitimacy and having the effect of raising the presumption of legitimacy. The finding of fact that the respondent could not prove that he was the legitimate son of the deceased Mutwalli, based as it is on a wrong view of law as to the effect of acknowledgment in establishing legitimacy in Muslim law was, therefore, correctly reversed by the High Court.

<u>40. The principle which seems to be well established is that an acknowledgment has the effect of raising presumption of legitimacy excepting where illegitimacy is proved beyond doubt by reason of the marriage of its parents being either disproved or found to be unlawful. Having regard to this principle the High Court came to the conclusion that prima facie, in view of the earlier acknowledgment by Amir Ali, respondent should be accepted as the legitimate eldest son of Amir Ali until the contrary is proved in a Civil Court of competent jurisdiction and that as such the respondent had better claim to be appointed as a Mtuwalli under Section 43 of the Ordinance, The High Court did not, it appears, arrive at any conclusive finding on the question but held that on the correct view of law respondent shall be presumed to be the eldest son till such presumption was rebutted in a properly framed suit.</u>

<u>41. In the facts and circumstances of the case, consistently with reason and justice, the Administrator should have chosen the claimant who has prima facie better claim to the office of the Mutwalli. It may also be very well contended that perhaps it would have been proper if the Administrator chose a completest anger for the office and referred both the rival claimants to a Civil Court for establishing their respective claim. Since, however neither the Administrator nor any of the Courts below considered the propriety of such a course and the order granting special leave did not raise such a consideration it is not necessary or proper for us to consider the adoption of the possible alternative course.</u>

<u>42. In exercising the power of appointment of a Mutwalli under section 43 of the Ordinance the District Judge as the appellate authority has the same power as the Administrator to appoint any of the contending parties as such but in doing so they were to apply their judicial mind in judging the relative merits of the rival claimants.</u>

43. As was quite rightly decided by the High Court, the Administrator should have, on the facts of the case, appointed the respondent, and not the appellant as Mutwalli, this is because the former was acknowledged by the deceased Mutwalli as his son who should, therefore, be treated as the eldest son and as such entitled to succeed, in terms of the wakf deed, to the office of the Mutwalli, until it is established in a properly framed suit that in spite of such acknowledgement there have been in fact no marriage between the mother of the respondent and the deceased Mutwalli or that such marriage, if at all, was unlawful.

44. The second question on which the Supreme Court granted leave concerns the limits of the powers of the High Court exercising jurisdiction under section 115 C. P. C. According to Mr. Khondker, Counsel for the appellant, High Court in deciding the applications under Section 115 C. P. C. improperly reversed the findings of fact relating to legitimacy and acknowledgment arrived at by the District Judge. He cited the following decisions as to the scope of the High Court's revisional power under the aforesaid section: S. N. Veugatagiri Vs. Hindu Religious Endm. Beard reported in (1949) 1 DLR 81: Ranjan Khan Vs. Obaidul Huq. reported in (1976) 28 DLR (AD) 57; and Shahzada Muhammad Umar Beg Vs. Sultan Mahmood Khan and another reported in PLD 1970 SC 139.

45. As in analysing the scope of the powers of the District Judge to appoint a Mutwalli conferred upon him by Section 43 of the Ordinance, we have found that le should have, in exercising such power, appointed the one among the rival claimants who has better claim to the office of the Mutwalli and that he failed to do so on misapprehension of the legal effect of the acknowledgment of the respondent by the deceased Mutwalli as his son, the inevitable conclusion which these findings lead us to is that the District Judge had, in an irregular exercise of his jurisdiction, held that the respondent dismally failed to prove that he was the rightful claimant to the office of the Mutwalli. His findings were, therefore, rightly reversed by the High Court.

We, therefore, find no reason to interfere with the decision of the High Court.

Before parting with the case is, however, necessary for us to mention that as the question regarding legitimacy will have to be considered in the suit, if an to be instituted by the respondent, if he so feels, any observations made by us regarding the facts necessary to establish such legitimacy will not be binding on the Courts below.

For the reasons stated above, the appeal is dismissed. We, however, make no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
K. M. Subhan, J. : —This reference by the learned Munsif, 2nd court, Bagerhat is under section 113 read with rule 2 of Order 46 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. From the statement of facts as stated by the learned Munsif, it appears that a miscellaneous case under section 173-174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act was filed for setting aside the sale held on 19-3-52, in Rent Execution Case No. 1308 of 1951 and confirmed on 18-5-52, on the ground of material irregularity in publishing and conducting the same and inadequacy of price and thereby causing substantial injury to the petitioner. The application was filed on 2-11-66. The learned Munsif being confronted with two contradictory decisions of two learned Single Judges of this Court, has referred this matter for a decision.

3. The decisions which were placed before the learned Munsif and contradictory to each other, are in the case of Sarat Sanda Vs. Sumati Bala and others, 18 D.L.R. 293 and in the case of Ledu Mridha and others Vs. Chand Mridha and others, 20 D.L.R. 158. In the decision reported in 18 D.L.R. 293, a learned Single Judge of the Dacca High Court held that a right of action under section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act continues even after the repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act and after coming into operation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the right of action having accrued under the Bengal Tenancy Act and having not been expressly or by necessary implication repealed. The view on this point taken by another learned Single Judge of this Court in the decision reported in 20 D.L.R. 158 was otherwise and the reason behind the view taken by the learned Single Judge in the decision reported in 20 D.L.R. 158 was:

"Before adverting to the merits of the case what strikes me is that both the courts below overlooked the fact that a change had been brought into the whole tenancy system by the State Acquisition Act of 1951. On and from 14th of April, 1956 the relationship between landlord and tenant under the Bengal Tenancy Act ceased to have effect, State by its powers of eminent domain as enacted by the Act acquired all the rights of the previous rent-receivers. A new order has been brought into being. According to provisions of section 44 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act one of the consequences that ensurs is that all the rent-receiving interest shall disappear and all the interest of the outgoing rent-receivers vest absolutely in the Government free of all encumbrances."

<u>4. The basic question; however, remains as to the effect of a repeal and the answer to that must be had from section 6 of the General Clauses Act which runs as follows:</u>

<u>“6. Where this Act, or any Central Act or regulation made after the commencement of this Act, repeals any enactment hitherto made or hereafter to be made, then, unless a different intention appears, the repeal shall not—</u>

<u>(c) affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under any enactment so repealed."</u>

<u>This section 6(c) of the General Clauses Act is in identical terms with section 38(2)(c) of the Interpretation Act, 1889 of England. The effect of section (6)(c)of the General Clauses Act, in our opinion, is that whenever there is a repeal of a Statute, the consequences laid down in section 6 of the General Clauses Act shall follow unless a different intention appears in the repealing Statutes. When the repeal is followed by a fresh legislation on the subject, the court has to look to the provisions of the new Statute for the purpose of ascertaining whether a different intention is indicated. The determining factor is not that the new enactment expressly keeps alive the vested right, but whether it manifests an intention of wiping them out. Section 6, therefore, will be applicable unless there is a manifest intention incompatible or contrary to the proposition of section 6. This view that we have taken, is supported uniformly by decisions of the Indian jurisdiction. Reference in this connection may be made to T.S. Baliah Vs. Rangachari Income-tax Officer AIR 1969 SC 701 and M/s. Munshilal Beni Ram Glass Works Vs. Sri S,R. Singh Asstti Labour Commissioner and others (1970) 1 SCWR 132. The same view was taken by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the case of Akhtar Hossain Vs. State, 29 D.L.R. (S C) 101.</u>

<u>5. The view that was taken in 20 D.L.R. 158 by a learned Single Judge appears to have been taken without taking into consideration of the provision of section 6 of the General Clauses Act. His lordships found that by virtue of section 44 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act; there was a total change as has been observed by his lordship in the reasoning quoted above. His lordship was merely considering that a new order ushered in by the enactment of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, but that was confined only to the relationship between the tenants and the new landlord, that is, the Government. The point that was involved in this case was whether the rights which accrued under the repealed act, could be exercised under the repealing act, was not considered in the light of section 6 of the General Clauses Act and was not argued at the Bar either.</u>

<u>6. The learned Single Judge in the decision reported in 18 D.L.R. in our opinion, took the correct view although without making any reference to the provision of section 6 of the General Clauses Act. The absence of the saving clause in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, in our opinion, should not be a bar to the enforcement of the rights accrued under the Bengal Tenancy Act. In this connection reference may be made to Craies on Statute Law, 5th Edition, page 384 where it has been observed that a mere absence of saving clause, is by itself immaterial when there is absence of such incompatibility in the new enactment. Such clause as this is apparently unnecessary and only inserted ex abundanti cautela and this is now a general cannon of construction as to repeals made after 1889. We have already found that section 6 of the General Clauses Act is in identical terms with section 3 8(2) of the Interpretation Act, 1889 of England.</u>

In the case of Hamilton Gell vs. White, (1922) 2 K B. 422, at page 431 Lord Justice Atkin in interpreting section 38(2) of the interpretation Act, 1889 has said:

“The provision was not intended to preserve the abstract rights conferred by the repealed Act; such for instance as the right of compensation for disturbance conferred upon tenants generally under the Act of 1908, for if it were the repealing Act would be altogether inoperative. It only applies to the specific rights given to an individual upon the happening of one or other of the events specified in the statute."

The same view was taken when the question of rights accrued under the repealing act were sought to be exercised after repeal under the repealing act; in the case of Khushiram Atmaram Jaisinghani and others vs. Custodian of Evacuee Property, West Pakistan and Karachi and others (1965) 17 D.L.R (S.C.) 430 =P.L.D. 1965 (SC) 453 (468) and in the case of Saeed Ahmed vs. The State, (1964) 16 D.L.R. (S.C.) 484=P.L.D. 1964 (S.C,) 266 at page 290.

The view that we have taken is supported by this decision of the superior courts of India and England as we have quoted and is pursuant to the view expressed, though in a different context, by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in 29 D.L.R. (S.C.) 101. In the view of the matter, we hold that the view that was taken by the learned Single Judge in the case reported in 20 D.L.R. 158, was wrong and the view taken in the case reported in 18 D.L.R. 293, is the correct view.

We hold that the application made under section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is maintainable.

The reference is accordingly answered. Let the matter be sent back to the trial court for decision in accordance with the judgment.

A.	T. M. Afzal, J. —I agree.

End.

full_judgment:
This rule, under section 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, at the instance of the defendant is directed against the judgment and decree of the learned S. C. Judge in a suit for ejectment of the tenant on the ground of bonafide requirement.

2. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant was inducted in the suit premises as a monthly tenant at a rental of Taka 15/- per month and the defendant executed an agreement dated 1.11.62 in favour of the plaintiff: The rent was subsequently enhanced to Taka 20/- per month. The plaintiff bonafide requires the premises in question for setting up a business by his son' and for re-construction thereof. The said monthly tenancy was terminated, by the pleader's letter dated 14. 9. 74.

3. The defendant contested the suit contending, inter alia that the suit was not maintainable and that he did not execute any agreement on 1.11.62 undertaking to vacate the premises on demand of the plaintiff. The plaintiff did not bonafide require the premises for his own use or for rebuilding. The plaintiff wanted to eject the defendant and to let out the premises for higher rent and premium. On the side of plaintiff, 5 Witneses including the plaintiff and his son were examined whereas the defendant examined himself.

4. The learned S. C.C. Judge, on consideration of the materials on record granted a decree in favour of the plaintiff holding that "the fact that the plaintiff has got a plan passed from the local Paurashava authority for rebuilding this premises is admitted by the defendant. The plaintiff has also filed the blue print of the plan and that has been marked Ext. C. According to law the very fact is sufficient to prove the bonafide requirement for the premises." The learned S.C.C. Judge further held that the plaintiff required the premises as one of his sons needed provision. The said son is Commerce graduate and married. According to the learned S.C.C. Judge this constitutes "a very good claim" for ejectment of the defendant.

5. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the rule contends that no notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, determining the tenancy was served on the tenant. According to the learned Advocate the suit is not maintainable in the absence of a valid notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. In the plaint, there is Whirl to indicate that a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served on the defendant terminating the alleged tenancy in accordance with law. A statement has been made in the plaint to the effect that a pleader's letter has been served.  In evidence, the plaintiff stated that he served the pleader's letter. There is no denial by the defendant as regards the service of the pleader's letter Curiously, the pleader's letter has not been proved.  There is nothing on record to indicate that the alleged pleader's letter amounted to a notice u/s 106 of the Transfer of Properly Act and that the tenancy was determined by the said letter. The learned S.C.C. Judge is completely silent about the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. There is no finding whether the pleader's letter was served on the defendant and if served; it was a valid service. There is also no finding that the pleader's letter was a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and that was valid and sufficient to terminate the tenancy Thus the contention of Mr. Chaudhury is of substance. Mr. Abdul Hamid, the learned. Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff contends that there is no denial by the defendant that the pleader's letter was served on him. Mr. Hamid points out that the copy of the pleader's letter, postal receipt and acknowledgement are on record. According to him the said copy of pleader's letter amounts to a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and the postal receipt and acknowledgement prove service of such notice. As observed earlier, no averment was made in the plaint that the alleged pleader's letter was a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Properly Act. The absence of denial by the defendant in the pleading and evidence as regards the receipt of the pleader's letter according to the rules of may amount to an admission of the defendant regarding receipt of a letter but it does not absolve the plaintiff from his burden of proving the service of a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and that such letter amounts To a valid and sufficient notice according to law and that the tenancy was legally deter-mined. It appears that the learned S.C.C. Judge failed to direct his attention to this vital question and yet granted a decree in favour of the plaintiff. The materials on record indicate that no attempt was made to bring the alleged pleader's letter in evidence. In the circumstances, there is no escape from the irresistible conclusion that the suit, as framed is not maintainable for want of notice Under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. Mr. Abdul Hamid has, however referred the decision in the case of Shaikh Mahmudur Rahman and another Vs. Amulya Kumar Sarkar and another 19 Dacca Law Reports 743. This case has no manner of application to the question involved in this rule. The case of Nekar Ali Biswas Vs. Nazam Nagar Rashida Bann, 19 D.L.R. 905 is of no assistance to Mr. Humid. In the instance case, no notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is on record and in evidence. Hence the question of slight inaccuracies in the notice does not arise. Similarly the decision in Messrs Memon Trading Co. Vs. Messrs Jajee Gaffar Hajee Habib Janno 17 D.L.R. (Dacca) 677 is wide out of the mark. In this case it was held that a notice to quit should be interpreted liberally and slight inaccuracies do not render the notice illegal. Where there is no notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, the proposition in the case of Messrs Memon. Trading Co. (supra) cannot be applied. For the same reason, the case of Ahmadni Rahman Vs. Sheikh Mafazzal Hossain, 14 D.L.R. 826 has no application in the facts of the instant case. Thus none of the cases cited by the learned Advocate has any relevance.

6. Mr. Chowdhury has raised another question indicating the inherent infirmity of the suit. There is no mention of the month of the tenancy either in pleadings or in evidence. A monthly tenancy is required to be specific according to any Calendar month in the absence of a contract to the contrary. The plaintiff did not adduce any evidence to indicate that the alleged tenancy was referable to a month according to any calendar or contract. Mr. Hamid, on a scrutiny of the plaint's deed of lease and evidence, could not place any material to connect the tenancy with a month according to any calendar or contract. Thus the contention of Mr. Chowdhury that a suit for ejectment of a tenant of an indeterminate monthly tenancy was misconceived, is rot without substance.

7. Mr. Chowdhury next contended that the plaintiff is to prove the bonafide requirement in terms of law. According to Mr. Chowdhury, in order to succeed in a suit tor ejectment of a monthly tenant on the ground of bonafide requirement, the landlord is required to prove a "must have" along with other incidental elements. The plaintiff's case is that the bonafide requires the premises for providing his graduate son with an occupation by starting a business. The further case of the plaintiff is that he intends to make improvement of the premises by constructing a building as per exhibit. B. Mr. Chowdhury does not dispute the order of the S.D.O. and the plan but submits that unless the plaintiff succeeds in proving that he has means to make the contemplated improvement in nature of reconstruction of the building as per the blue-print, the elements constituting "bonafide requirement" are not satisfied. Mr. Chowdhury further contends that the actual reconstruction and setting up of the business is a further requirement to complete the bundle of elements constituting a bonafide requirement in law. According to the learned Advocate the judgment of the learned S.C.C. Judge is empty and does not contain the necessary findings to support the decree. Mr. Chowdhury has referred the case of Jagadish Chandra Sarkar & Ors Vs. Abdul Aziz 7 D.L.R. 314, Mulla Mahbub Ali and others Vs. Jonab Ali 8 D.L.R. 448, Sri Naresh alias Narendra  Chandra Sarkar Vs. Kanailal Roy Choudhury 56 C.W.N. 480. The principle laid down in the aforesaid cases has been consistently followed in the subsequent decisions of the Dacca High Court and also in this Court. Referring to the case of Abdur Rauf & ors. Vs. Mir Muhibur Rahman, 22 D.L.R. 811. where the case of Haji Habibullah Vs. Abdul Hamid 21 D.L.R. 104 was noticed, Mr. Chaudhury, contends, the decision in the case of Haji Habibullah, properly, construed, is not a departure from the principle laid down in the cases referred to above.

8. Mr. Abdul Hamid, referred to the decision in the case of Faziur Rahman Vs. Nayeema Khatun 13 D.L.R. 869, the case of Mullah Mahbub Ali & other (supra) 8 D.L.R. 448 and the case of Abdur Rauf & ors. (supra) and the case of M/s. East Bengal Paper Traders Association Ltd. Vs. Md. Waziullah & others, 21 D.L.R. 572 in addition to the case of Jagadish Chandra Sarkar and Abdur Rauf as referred to above. Relying upon these decisions Mr. Abdul Hamid contends that the bonafide requirement is to be construed with reference to the facts and circumstances of each case. The plaintiff proved his case of bonafide requirement for setting up a business to provide his unemployed graduate son. This, according to Mr. Hamid; amounts to sufficient compliance of the requirements of law. In the case of Failur Rahman (supra) the facts are distinguishable. Asir, J. construed bonafide requirement to mean bonafide necessity. In the case of Mulla Mahbub Ali (supra) Rahman, J, held that there must be a genuine present need which must not merely be a desire for the premises but at the same time it does not go to the extentof absolute necessity. In the case of Abdur Rouf & others Nurul Islam, J. was of the view that bonafide requirement means not merely an assertion as to the requirement of the house by the plaintiff but something more. He has also to prove by evidence that he needs the house for the use of the same. The case of M/s. East Bengal Paper Traders' Association Ltd. has no application in the facts of the present case.

9. In the case of Mst. Shamsher Messa Sakeba Banoo and others. Vs. A. H. Mohsenuddin Ahmed and others 27 D.L.R. 643 Bhattacharya, J. as his Lordship then was; considered the terms "require" and "bonafide" and dealt with the concept of bonafide requirement in the following manner:

“The use of the term 'require' certainly indicates something more than a mere wish or fancy and it involves an element of need, that is to say, it also has an objective import. The use of the qualifying word (bonafide along with the word 'require' tries to limit the scope of the subjective aspect of the land-lords' feeling of need for the house, although the word `bonafide', the equivalent of which is 'honesty' is essentially a subjective concept. The Legislature seems to convey by using the words `bonafide require' a kind of genuine feeling of need and not a colourable pretext. Chunder, J of Calcutta High Court, in interpreting a similar expression in an analogous West Bengal Act has observed in the case of Sri Naresh alias Narendra Chandra Sarkar Vs. Kanai Lal Roy Chowdhury, 56 C.W.N. 480 that there is an clement of `must have' in the need of the landlord and this want or need of the house must be genuinely felt by him. The principle laid down in the aforesaid case was followed in two single Judge decisions of the Dacca High Court, viz. Jagadish Chandra Sarkar Vs. Abdul Aziz, 7 D.L.R. 314 (Akbar J) and Mulla Mahbub Ali and others Vs. Jarab Ali 8 D.L.R. 448 (Rahman.). The learned Judges however made it clear in those two decisions that the expression `bonafide require' implies a genuine present need but it does not go to the extent of saying that there must be absolute need or absolute necessity. The expression, therefore, connotes an honest feeling of need for the house and in ultimate analysis, it is a question of fact which is to be determined on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case.”

10. Considering the view consistently expressed in the aforesaid decisions, it is evident that the expression `bonafide' require' does not admit of a definition to restrict its import. The constituents illustrate a genuine present need having a corresponding phenomenal content. A bonaficle requirement, therefore, is a conceptual fact which is to be determined with reference to the facts and circumstances of each case.

The materials on record do not justify a conclusion that the plaintiff bonafide requires the premises. In the circumstances, the judgment and decree of the learned S.C.C. Judge do not stand on the strength of the materials on record.

Mr. Hamid, referring to a statement in the counter affidavit, submits that the defendant became the defaulter subsequently and as such the plaintiff is entitled to, a decree for ejectment. The suit was not for ejectment on the ground of default. In the circumstances, the submission of Mr. Hamid is of no legal consequence.

For the reasons stated above the Rule succeeds and is made absolute with costs assessed at 5 gold mohors. The judgment and decree of the learned S.C.C. Judge are set aside and the suit is dismissed without costs.

End.
