full_judgment:
This Rule under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against. the Order dated 15.1 t.84 passed by Mr. Abdul Hamad, Munsif, Gurudaspur Upazila, Natore, restoring the Misc. Case No. 58/84-66/84 arising out of Misc. Case No. 21 of 1984 in O.C. Suit. No. 444/83. 

2. The plaintiffs/petitioners instituted a suit being O.C. Suit No. 444/83 in the court of Munsif, Gurudaspur Upazila Natore for declaration of their title and correction of wrong records. 

3. The summons were duly served upon all of the defendants including the present defendant opposite party but they did not take any steps and as such the suit was decreed evade on 12.1.84. 

4. The present defendant opposite party filed an application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the said exparte decree on the averment that summons was duly served at Rajshahi on 21.12.83 but the Advocate for the present defendant opposite patty did not receive any instruction to contest the said suit by filing any written statement. The further case of the defendant opposite party is that the exparte decree is fraudulent. The said application was numbered as Misc. Case No. 21 of 1984. 

5. In the said Miscellaneous Case No. 21 of 1984, 18.3.84 was fixed for depositing the requisite by the defendant opposite party but neither the requisites were pat in nor any step was taken from the side of the defendant opposite party. As a result, the said Misc. Case was dismissed for default by the learned Munsif by his order dated 18.3.84. 

6. The defendant opposite party filed another Misc. Case being Misc. Case N. 58 of i984 under Order 9, rule 4 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the said default order. 

7. The plaintiffs/petitioners filed written objection to contest the said Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1984 stating, inter alia, that the said Misc. Case is not maintainable and the same is barred by principles of estoppel, acquiescence and waiver. The statement about filing petition by the defendant opposite party for time is also false. 

8. The learned Munsif, Gurudaspur Upazila, who heard the case on transfer, allowed the same application, set aside the order of dismissal of the Misc. Case No. 21 of 1984 and restored the same by his order dated 15.11.84. Thereafter the plaintiffs/petitioners obtained the present Rule from this court on 7.1.85. 

9. Mr. Md. Assar Ali, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the learned Munsif committed an error of law resulting in an error in his decision occasioning failure of justice in not holding that the order of dismissal for default of the Misc. Case No. 21 of 1984 wider Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure being appealable under Order 43, rule 1 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1984 is not at all maintainable in law. 

10. The learned Advocate for the petitioners referred to the following decisions in support of his contention. These decisions are 28 DLR 252. 27 DLR. 232, 27 DLR 683 and I DLR 26. In the Case of Azizur Rahman Vs. Janata Bank reported in 28 DLR 252, it was held that:—"The scope of section 151 is often misunderstood by the courts below Section 151 clearly provides for such an application only when the courts find that prevention of abuse of the process of the court is necessary or where for the ends of justice an order on an application is necessary to be made. In the garb of an order being necessary for the ends of justice cannot negative the remedies available under the Code itself. The appeals or for that matter revisions under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure are provided for to meet situations in which some injustice is felt to have been made to party in a proceeding. This phraseology for the end of justice is not an omnibus remedy given to the courts where a final order has been passed to rectify a wrong as may be necessary for the ends of justice. An application under section 151 of the Code should be used in a limited and in a sparing manner and must be avoided in a case where the Code provides for appeal or for revision." In the case of Rajendra Shirai; and others Vs Mahadev Shirali reported in 27 DLR 232, it was held :—"The powers. as contemplated in the section, 151 C.P. Code are intended to supplement the other provisions of the Code as a Legislature cannot forsee and provide for every eventuality which may occur, but they are not for the purpose of evading or ignoring the express pro-visions of the law or for inventing a new procedure according to the individual inclination of a particular judge. Under the cover of these powers a court cannot override the express provisions of the law applicable to a particular case. These powers cannot be invoked in a case which is fully covered by a specific provision in the Code, or, where there is a positive prohibition regarding a particular act or order or where there in alternative remedy". . In the case of Mst. Masuda Khartum & ors. Vs. Maniruzzaman reported in 27 DLR 683, it was held that : "The application for restoration is under Order 9, rule 4 and under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is undauntedly misconceived. Order 9, rule 4 of Civil Procedure Code provides for the plaintiff to bring a fresh suit which is dismissed either for non-service of summons in consequence of plaintiff's failure to pay cost or for non-appearance of both the plaintiffs and defendant. An application under section 151 C.P,C. is not maintainable. Prayer under section 151 was deleted on the application filed by the defendant himself. It is thus not clear under what provisions of law the court has granted the prayer of the defendant restoring the application. It may be presumed that the court purported to act under section 151 C.P C. It appears clear that there were good grounds for restoration of the case under Order 9, rule 13 and therefore there is no need to exercise the power vested in the Supreme Court under section 115 C.P.C." In the case of Musst Mansura Khatun & ors. Vs. Muhammad Raja Meah and ors. reports. in I DLR 26, it was held that: "When a party has got a right of appeal against an order he cannot main-tain an application under section 151 C.P.C. for reversal of that order and that the trial court acted in the exercise of its jurisdiction with material irregularity in entertaining the said application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure". From the decisions quoted above it is clear that when a party had got a right of appeal against the Order he should go for an appeal, he cannot maintain as application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for reversal of the exparte order. In the instant case, the learned Munsif did exercise his jurisdiction with material irregularity in allowing the said application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It was just and proper for restoration of a case under Order 9, r. 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure but it is not just and proper to entertain the application for restoration under Order 9, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure and under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Order 7, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for the plaintiff to bring a fresh suit which is dismissed either for non-service of summons in consequence of plaintiff's failure to pay cost or for non-appearance of both the plaintiff and defendants. In this connection, an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is also not maintainable, because inherent power of the court exists only where there is no express provision of law applicable to the case. The provisions of this section cannot be invoked to defeat the provisions of the Code nor can be invoked to further injustice or to condone gross negligence. The court cannot interfere under section 151 of the Code with appealable order. 

12. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners also referred to an unreported decision of this court being Civil Revision No. 258 of 1984. In this case also it was held that Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is appealable under Order 43, rule 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure and, therefore, for setting aside the order of dis-missal for default or of said application, a court's inherent jurisdiction cannot be invoked under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This decision is also applicable to the instant case and I end that there is substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. 

13. From the facts, circumstances and discussions above I find that this is a fit case tor interference by this Court. 

14. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. Send down the lower Court's records at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarkar, J: When 178 individuals approached this Court, as the petitioners, stating in their petition the following facts; that they are the Members of a registered Co-operative Society bearing registration No. 00889 of 2007 dated 17-6-2007 under the Samabay Samity Ain, 2001 under the name and style of "Gabtali Bricks, Stone, Sand Aroth Babsayee Bahumukhi Samabay Samity Ltd; that they were running their respective businesses individually on the eastern bank of the river Turag in 52.36 acres of land of CS plot Nos. 654, 659, 660, 661, 665, 666, 667, 668, 669, 676 and part of CS plots No. 636, 637, 639 and 649 of Mirpur Mouza, PS Mirpur, District Dhaka for last many years, before the construction of flood protection embankment (shortly, embankment) by the Water Development Board (hereinafter referred to as the WDB) in the area and at the time of construction of the embankment the petitioners were displaced from their business places; that after construction of the embankment, WDB handed over the said 52.36 acres of land to the Dhaka City Corporation (shortly, the DCC) on 3-6-1989 to rehabilitate the petitioners for running their businesses; that the DCC divided the said 52.36 acres of land into 300 plots upon making. a sketch map for the said 300 plots by their engineering department and on 22-7-2005 the DCC invited applications from the real bricks, stone and sand business men who were continuing their businesses therein for allotment of Aroth plots; that the said notice for allotment of plots was published on 22-7-2005 in the "Dainik Janata" and "Dainik Bangladesh; that, thereafter, the petitioners filed the applications for allotment of plots for Aroths in their favour along with Salami (advance money) and, eventually, 70 persons paid Taka 1,50,000 (one lac fifty thousand) each and other 113 persons paid Taka 1,00,000 (one lac) each as Salami which was paid through Pay Order and, accordingly, the DCC on receipt of the Salami money inducted 178 members and handed over the possession of their respective plots to run their businesses and, that is how, the members of the Samity have been owning and enjoying the possession of their respective plots using the Ghats Aroths by giving Salami to the DCC since 2005; that their 52.36 acres of land are in one compact block bounded by at north side: Dhaka-Aricha Highway, at east side: Flood Protection Dam Road, at south side: City Corporation Road (IWTA Landing Road) and at west side: Gabtali Cattle Market and River Turag;

2. That though the DCC took the Salami and handed over possession of the said plots but the DCC did not execute registered deeds of settlement in favour of the petitioners and, taking the advantage of the circumstances, the officials of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka orally asked some of the petitioners to vacate the said plots and Aroths just after 11th of January, 2007, when the petitioners filed petition to the DCC for issuing lease documents and to prevent the attempt of eviction; that thereafter, the DCC requested the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka vide letter dated 22-1- 2007 under Memo No. Estate/952(1) 2006-2007 not to evict the petitioners from their respective Aroths and plots till the settlement of boundary of the lands; that the petitioners filed an application to the Deputy Commissioner who forwarded the said application to the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka for local inquiry and for urgent report, but the Additional Deputy Commissioner neither visited the spot nor submitted any report and the respondents, without disposing of the petitioners applications for lease document of the plots, and Aroths, are now trying to give allotment of the said Aroths and plots to the strangers and, accordingly, on 13-1-2008 at about 3-00 pm some persons on behalf of the respondent Nos. 5 and 6 came to the area with microphone and gave an ultimatum to the petitioners to vacate the case-lands within 7 days, failing which, they shall evict them by force from their respective business plots and threatened to demolish their office and Aroths without giving any personal eviction notice to the members of the Samity; that the petitioners have been aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the threats of respondents for demolishing and evicting the petitioners from their respective plots and Aroths and they do not have any other alternative or equally efficacious remedy provided by law, then, upon a preliminary hearing of the case on 21-1-2008, this Rule' was issued in the following terms;

"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to give proper documents of lease of the respective plots and Aroths of Bricks, stone and sand business for each of the petitioners who paid the Salami to the Dhaka City Corporation for 300 plots covering 52.36 acres of the land of CS Plot Nos. 654, 659, 660, 661, 665, 666, 667, 668, 669, 676, and part of CS plots No. 636, 637, 639 and 649 of the Mirpur Mouza, PS Mirpur, District Dhaka fully described in paragraph 4 of this petition, which has been more clearly shown in the lay-out plan of the Dhaka City Corporation (annexure-C) and/or pass any other order or direction as this Court may deem fit and proper."

3. The DCC (respondent Nos. 1-4) contested this Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter-alia, that the land in question of 52.36 acres was acquired by the WDB through LA Case No. 20/76-77 for the purpose of construction of embankment and after construction of the said embankment, the WDB handed over the said 52.36 acres of land to the DCC on 3-6-1989 and the land of Mouza-Mirpur CS Khatian No. 1106, SA Khatian No. 4, Dag No. 641 and 633 and also the lands of Mouza Mirpur CS Khatian No. 1106, S.A. Khatian No. 4, Dag No. 502 were acquired by the Roads and Highways Department under LA Case No. 32/88-89 and were handed over the same to the DCC on 2-10-1998. Regarding the advertisement for lease of the case-lands in the newspapers and receiving Salami, it is stated that the petitioners in collaboration with some corrupt officials of the DCC had attempted to enter into vague agreements, as there was no approval from the Government to lease out the case land to anybody. It is further stated that no allotment letter was issued to the petitioners and the DCC has never received any rent from the petitioners and, therefore, no contract or lease agreement was executed, no possessions have ever been handed over in favour of the petitioners and no rehabilitation programme for the writ petitioners was ever taken by the 15CC. On 2-2-2010, in the ECNEC meeting a project with the financial aid of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) for setting up a modern slaughtering house in the case land was approved and the period to complete the project was fixed to be December, 2010 but due to the order of status-qua passed by this Court in the instant Writ Petition, the DCC could not hand over the possession to the project office despite the repeated requests by the Ministry of Local Government. In the mean time, the time for completion of the project work has lapsed and there is a possibility to withdraw the grants for the project sanctioned by the ADB. The said project is very much needed for environment, health and economic development of the DCC and also to help make progress in achieving the millennium development goals (MDG).

4. Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka (respondent No. 5) contested this Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter-alia, that as per the RS (plots corresponding to the SA and that of the CS) and the City Survey records, the ownership of the land in question was vested with the Bangladesh Government represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, the Public Works and Nagar Development Department, the Agriculture Development Board, the Water Development Board and the Zila Parisad, Dhaka after acquisition by the WDB and the Roads and Highways Department. As the ownership of the land in question was vested with the Bangladesh Government represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and the other Government bodies, the invitation of applications for allotment of the plots by the DCC for the purpose of the business of bricks, sand etc and payment of advance for such plots by the petitioners is a matter of the petitioners and that of the DCC, not of the Government or respondent No. 5 and, hence, no liability in this regard incurs upon the Government or respondent No. 5. The DCC is not the owner of the land/plots in question and, hence, the DCC has no right to give allotment of plots to any one, be it any third party or the petitioners. The Government or respondent No. 5 does not have any motive or plan, to give allotment of the land in question and Aroths to anyone.

5. Mr Qumrul Haque Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, candidly submits that the DCC, as a statutory body, is carrying out the functions on behalf of the State; and the petitioners by depositing respective Salami to the DCC pursuant to its advertisement dated 22-7-2005 have acquired legitimate right to get proper document of lease of the respective plots and Aroths from the DCC. He further submits that the DCC having taken Salami-money and other charges is bound under the law to execute proper lease deeds in favour of the petitioners, but it is not executing and registering such documents which is arbitrary and illegal and, as such, the respondents are liable to be directed to execute and register proper documents of lease in favour of the petitioners with respect to the plots allotted in their favour. He next submits that it shall be an arbitrary and illegal action by the respondents to evict the petitioners from their respective plots inasmuch as the petitioners are enjoying the plots and Aroths by running bricks, stone and sand businesses thereon since long before and if they are evicted now, the petitioners shall suffer irreparable loss and injury.

6. In support of his submissions, he relies on the Judgment of this Court passed in the Writ Petition No. 5469 of 2005 and submits that the DCC had allotted another 45 Bighas of land from CS plot Nos. 636, 640, 647, 649, 652, 663 of the same Mouza for using as Aroths of the members of ."Mirpur Bricks, Stone and Sand Business Samity" and, accordingly, the DCC had invited applications on 12-3-1986 from the sand, bricks and stone businessmen which was published in the "Dainik Novo Ovijan" and, thereafter, 140 members of that Samity filed applications for allotment in their favour paying Salami of Taka 1,00,000 (one lac) each through Pay Order and on receiving the Salami the DCC allowed only 56 members to run their businesses constructing semi-pucca Aroths under open sky and, thereafter, the members of the said Samity filed applications for allotment of their respective Aroths and. when the DCC was not executing any registered lease deed in favour of the said Samity, one Hazi Abdul Mannan alias Manu Miah as President of the Samity filed the aforesaid Writ Petition No. 5469 of 2005 before the High Court Division against the DCC and others praying for direction upon the respondents for allotment of the Aroths and, after hearing, this Court was pleased to issue a Rule Nisi upon the respondents in tandem with an order of injunction, which was made absolute by a Division Bench of this Court vide its Judgment and Order dated 10-12-2009 and, subsequently, the same was affirmed by the Appellate Division vide its Judgment and Order dated 23-10-2014. He candidly submits that the present petition is of the same nature and the petitioners being on similar footing are entitled to get the same relief.

7. By making the above submissions, the learned Advocate for the petitioners prays for making the Rule absolute.

8. Per contra, Mr Manzill Murshid, the learned Advocate for respondent No. 5, submits that it is now admitted by the DCC that they are not the owner of the property; the Government of Bangladesh is the owner of the property and the DCC was simply looking after the property. He submits that, as a routine work, on behalf of the Government, the Office of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka has taken initiatives for eviction of the illegal occupiers from the land in question. In an endeavour to substantiate his above count of submissions, he refers to the. Judgment passed in the Writ Petition No. 3503 of 2009 and submits that in the said Writ Petition, the High Court Division declared the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority (BIWTA) to be the owner of the lands in question and directed the concerned authority to survey the area of the rivers in context of CS and RS maps within 30-11-2009 and also ordered the concerned authorities to remove all the shops and other structures/buildings within two years from the Government- land starting from the embankment towards the bank of the rivers. He posits that the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka operated the drive to evict all the trespassers from the land of the river as per the order of the High Court Division passed in the aforesaid Writ Petition No. 3503 of 2009 and though some people were evicted, the petitioners could not be evicted because of injunction.

9. By referring to Rule 77(Ka) of the Acquisition Manual, 1977 (shortly, Acquisition Manual), he submits that without prior permission of the Ministry of Land, the acquired-land shall not be used for the purposes other than it was acquired for and the Acquisition Manual also envisages that the acquired-land shall not be sold, leased out or transferred in any manner without the permission of the Ministry and, therefore, the land in question cannot be given lease by the DCC in the manner the petitioners prayed for. To this end, he submits that the present Rule is liable to be discharged outright on the ground of defect of party, for the Ministry of land and BIWTA have not been made party to this petition though they are necessary party.

10. Regarding payment of Taka 1 lac to the DCC as claimed by the petitioners in their statement, Mr Murshid contends that some unscrupulous officials of the DCC floated advertisement for lease in collaboration with the petitioners in an attempt to lease out the property in an illegal way. He contends that by paying the claimed Taka 1 (one) lac, the petitioners have already used the case land to conduct their businesses for more than 7 years and, therefore, the question of suffering any financial loss in their businesses does not arise, if they are evicted from the land in question. He argues that since the proposal for leasing out the land through advertisement published by the DCC was made without approval from the competent authority, it does not have any binding effect and, further adds that, even for the sake of argument, if the proposal is taken to be a valid one, the same being monthly in nature, no right has been created by the lease of one year in favour of the petitioners and, more importantly, the relationship between the petitioners and the DCC has not even reached at a contractual stage. He strenuously argues that any lease is terminable by the proper authority and for enforcing a general commercial contract, no writ petition is maintainable. To substantiate his above arguments, he refers to the following case laws: (i) Managing Director, WASA vs All 27 BLD (AD) 298 = 59 DLR (AD) 185 and (ii) Md Nazrul Islam vs Monzurul Islam Liton 17 BLT (AD) 198.

11. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the DCC (respondent Nos. 1-4), submits that no prior approval was taken from the Government to allot the land in question. He submits that the land in question having been, at first, acquired by the WDB in LA Case No. 20/76-77 for making flood protection embankment and, then, after construction of the same, the said land having been handed over to the DCC in the year 1989, has now been selected for modern slaughter-house project by the DCC, as the Asian Development Bank (ADB) has come up in the year 2009 to support the said slaughter house project. In an endeavour to show us the vagueness of the petitioners' claim, he points out to a particular averment of this Writ Petition wherein the petitioners claim that they are enjoying possession of the Aroths since 2005 by paying Salami through Pay Order and, then, by taking us through the annexures, he submits that they could not submit any documents before this Court in corroboration of their claim. He contends that the DCC has no relationship with the so-called Samity, as the petitioners were never issued any allotment letters, nor were they handed over possession by the DCC. He then refers to the annexure F, which are the letters from the DCC to the petitioners to deposit Salami, and alleges that the same is forged and fabricated, for, the DCC has never issued any notice to, pay the balance Salami and, then, argues that as the petitioners have filed the instant writ petition with forged and fabricated documents upon suppressing the actual facts, they have come before this Court with unclean hands. He submits that the Rule is liable to be discharged solely on this ground. Lastly, he submits that since the petitioners have been illegally possessing the alleged land, the DCC has every right to evict the illegal occupiers.

12. By putting forward the above submissions, the learned Advocate, for the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka (respondent No. 5) and the learned Senior Advocate for the DCC (respondent Nos. 1-4) pray for discharging the Rule.

13. After hearing the learned Advocates for the petitioners and respondent Nos. 1-5, having perused the writ petition, the affidavits-in-opposition along with their annexures and the relevant laws and decisions placed before us, it appears that in this writ petition, the petitioners are praying for a direction from this Court upon the respondents for executing registered lease deeds allotting the commercial plots of the area mentioned in Paragraph 4 of the writ petition in favour of the petitioners.

14. Apparently, the petitioners have sought for the aforesaid direction from this Court by invoking Article 102(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution. In order to see whether the petitioner's standing and the facts of the case fit into the above provision of the Constitution, we should first look at the aforesaid Article of the Constitution, which is reproduced below:

Article 102(2) the High Court Division may, if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law—

(a) on the application of any person aggrieved, make an order—

(i) directing a person performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or 	of a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that which he is required by law to do; or

15. In constitutional parlance, the above underlined provisions of Article 102(2)(a)(i) is known as the writ of mandamus. In carrying out the examination, hereinafter of the above provision, although it may seem that we are highlighting the underlined-expressions of the Article 102(2)(a)(i), which jointly stands as follows: "the High Court Division may on the application of any person aggrieved, make an order directing a person to do that which is required by law to do" in fact, we would explore the entire provision.

<u>16. By employing the word may in  the expression "the High Court Division may" the Constitution framers made it clear that the power conferred upon the High Court Division under Article 102(2) of the Constitution is a discretionary power; meaning that when a petitioner shall be able to satisfy this Court that there is no forum for redress of the grievance of the petitioner or the forum, which is in place, is not equipped to effectively remedy the grievance of the petitioner, only then, this forum would be available for the petitioner.</u>

<u>17. Let us, now, take up the examination of the expressions "on the application of any person aggrieved". The phraseology 'on the application' suggests that an aggrieved person should place his grievance before the High Court Division in the form of an application. The term 'application', though, implies a written application, however, the High Court Division is well empowered to entertain an oral application of an aggrieved person who having appeared before this Court in person shows some document or paper from printing or electronic device. At times, this Court in appropriate cases, which are rare, when takes cognizance of an allegation/information as to violation of fundamental rights without any written application, then, it is to be understood that this Court has exercised its power under sub-Article (1) of Article 102 of the Constitution; not under sub-Article (2) of Article 102 of the Constitution. Regarding the next phraseology of the aforesaid expression "person aggrieved", our view is that in order to acquire the status of 'person aggrieved', someone at the very outset is required to show that her/his grievance is related to or arising out of her/his legal right. In others words, a person would not be recognized as 'person aggrieved' unless s/he can show to this Court that her/his legal right has been breached.Through the case of R vs Guardians of Lewisham Union [1897] 1 QB 498, the English Courts laid down a principle that for issuance of a writ of mandamus, the applicant must satisfy the Court that there is existence of her/his legal right in the matter. The Indian Courts also emphasizes on having a specific legal right of the applicant of the writ of mandamus, which is evident from the case of MS Jain vs Haryana AIR 1977 SC and in subsequent numerous cases. Although in England, the House of Lords, in the recent past, in the case of JRC vs Federation of Self-employed has discarded the Lewisham Union Principle, our Constitution being a written one where it is engraved that the applicant must be a 'person aggrieved'; meaning that a person's legal right must be infringed, there is no scope for our Court to walk in the English path. In Telekhal Progressive Fisherman vs Bangladesh, our Apex Court made it clear that 'In order to entitle a person to ask for performance of any public duty by mandamus it is necessary to show that he has a legal right for claiming such performance apart from the fact that he is interested in the performance of the duty'. Further lengthy discussion on this issue is not needed in the backdrop of availability of series of case-laws on the writ of mandamus of our jurisdiction where it has been settled that a person claiming that his legal right has been infringed due to the failure to perform legal duty by a functionary of the Republic or local authority, then, if the said person approaches this Court with an application stating therein her/his grievance, s/he is called the "person aggrieved".</u>

<u>18. Next comes the expression "to do that which he is required by law to do" A State-functionary who is duty bound to perform a function; but he is not doing it, in that event, when the petitioner successfully makes out a case that finding no other equally efficacious forum he has approached this Court, then the High Court Division may direct the concerned public servant/authority to do the needful.</u>

<u>19. In a writ of mandamus, thus, all that the petitioner is required to satisfy this Court that, firstly, he has a legal right in the matter in question, secondly, the functionary of the Republic or local authority is legally bound to do something in the said matter but due to the failure/inaction of the said State-functionary to carry out his/its legal duty the petitioner has been aggrieved, only then, by exercising the discretionary power, this Court would be in a position to pass the necessary direction upon the concerned State-functionary/local authority.</u>

20. We may now suitably embark on the examination as to whether the petitioners have any legal right in the matter. It is the petitioners claim that by paying Salami to the DCC they have entered into a contract with the DCC and, that is how, they have acquired a legal right to get the registered lease document. In rebutting the above claim, both the DCC and the Government contend that the DCC is not the owner of the case land and it does not have authority to lease out the case land to anyone. It is the clear case of the Government that the case land, after acquisition, was handed over to the DCC to look after the same and if the DCC is to lease out the case land, it was imperative for the DCC to obtain prior approval from the Government i.e. the Ministry of Land. The petitioners could not show this Court that the DCC is the owner of the case land or, at least, the DCC upon obtaining approval from the Government took the initiative to float the advertisement for lease. In fact, when the DCC was being castigated by this Court during the hearing of this Rule about their dubious role in dealing with the case land, they came up with an affidavit clearly disowning the said advertisement for lease and with a further averment that the DCC has formed an enquiry committee to investigate into the above attempt of leasing out the case land under the garb of the authority of the DCC. An impression is given before this Court by Mr Mahbubey Alam, who appears as the Senior Counsel of the DCC, that the petitioners influenced some unscrupulous officials of the DCC to take the above illegal initiatives of floating advertisements without taking approval from the competent authority and, for the said illegal activities, an enquiry committee is in place, though at a belated stage.

21. Thus, it appears from the statements of the writ petition, the affidavits-in-opposition and the oral contentions that the DCC is not the owner of the case land and it has no authority to float any advertisement for lease of the case land. For the sake of argument, if it is seen that it has been done lawfully by the DCC, however, there has not been any contract for long-term-lease between the petitioners and the DCC, for, there appears that the arrangement was attempted to be made by the crooked DCC officials to enter into a monthly tenancy contract and, the said attempted arrangement of entering into a monthly contract was also at the very initial stage, which neither does create any legal right for the petitioners, nor does create any legal obligation upon the DCC to make a lease-deed in favour of the petitioners.

22. The above discussions led us to hold that the petitioners do not have any legal right on the case land, for, firstly, the DCC is not the owner of the case land as per the admission of the DCC, secondly, the DCC, being in-charge of the management of the case, cannot take any initiative for leasing out the case land without the permission from the Government, thirdly, the petitioners could not show us any paper that they were made to believe by the DCC at the time of depositing Salami that the DCC is the owner of the case land or the DCC being the custodian of the Government property has got approval from the Government to lease out the same and, finally, there has not been any lawful long-term-lease agreement in the eye of law between the petitioners and the DCC which can be enforced by a Court of law.

23. Now, let us see whether the DCC, as a local authority, has failed to perform the functions which it is bound by law to do. From the analysis of the facts of the case made hereinbefore, it is found that no monthly or long-term legal contract for lease whatsoever has been made by the DCC with the petitioners with regard to the case land and, therefore, we find that the DCC is not legally required to register the alleged contracts towards making registered lease' documents with the petitioners.

24. It follows that this Court does not find any ground to pass any direction upon the DCC to do something which it is required by law to do and, accordingly, there is no reason for issuance of a writ of mandamus and, for the reasons stated hereinbefore, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

25. An inevitable question, at this stage, comes up as to whether the DCC or the Government/Deputy Commissioner of Dhaka is competent to evict the petitioners from the case land. The answer does not warrant any further long discussions given that the basis of possession of the case land by the petitioners has been found by this Court to be illegal and, furthermore, in Writ Petition No. 3503 of 2009, this Court has directed the concerned authorities to evict the illegal occupiers from the case land and, therefore, the petitioners and other illegal occupiers are liable to be evicted. Moreover, by paying the nominal advance of Taka one lac, the petitioners have already enjoyed the possession of the case land for nearly 10 (ten) years and, therefore, the petitioners' claim as to suffering financial loss is not sustainable and, thus, they are liable to be evicted.

26. Mr Qumrul Haque Siddique, the learned Senior Counsel, in an endeavour to get the instant Rule absolute, relied on the decision of the Appellate Division passed in the CPLA No. 759 of 2010 arising out of Writ Petition No. 5469 of 2005. We have minutely read the Judgments passed by the High Court Division and the Appellate Division and it appears to us that the DCC or the Government did not place the facts of not having the title/ownership of the DCC before any of the Courts and, consequently, none of the Courts had the occasion to examine the said facts and, therefore, the facts of the referred case being different from the facts of the present case, the decision of the same is not applicable here in this case.

27. Before parting with this Judgment, this Court feels it pertinent to note here that since the DCC has informed this Court by way of filing a sworn-in-affidavit that an enquiry committee has been formed to track down the unscrupulous officials of the DCC who had attempted to lease out the case-lands in an illegal manner, this Court expects that there shall be a thorough and fair investigation in order to dig out the illegal activities done by some corrupt officials of the DCC and, thereafter, the DCC shall take appropriate legal action against them so that the other officials of the DCC get warned and, thereby, refrain from indulging themselves in any illegal activity in future.

28. In the result, the Rule is discharged. However, there shall not any order as to costs. The order of status-quo passed by this Court earlier is hereby vacated. The Government, in particular, the Deputy Commissioner of Dhaka, shall be at liberty to evict the illegal occupiers, including the petitioners, from the case land.

The office is directed to send a copy of this order at once to the Mayor of the Dhaka North City Corporation, the Mayor of the Dhaka South City Corporation, the Secretary Ministry of LGERD, the Secretary Ministry of Land, the Secretary Ministry of Water Resources, Director General of the WAPDA, the Director of the BIWTA and the Deputy Commissioner of Dhaka for their information and necessary action following this Court's order passed in this Judgment hereinabove.

End.

full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury, J: As the facts and circumstances of both the Writ Petition Nos. 1932 of 2017 and 3636 of 2017 are intertwined, they have been heard together and this consolidated judgment disposes of them.

2. In the Writ Petition No. 1932 of 2017, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Memo No. 35.00.0000.030.07.003.15-06 dated 3-1-2017 (Annexure-'A' to the Writ Petition) issued by the respondent No. 2 cancelling the Invitation For Proposal No. 01/EOI/SE/SRC/2014-2015 dated 29-9-2015 (Armexure-'D-1' to the Writ Petition) and directing issuance of fresh requests for Expression of Interests (EOIs), publication of requests for Expression of Interests (EOIs) bearing Memo Nos. 418 and 434 both dated 24-1-2017 (Annexures-'B' & 'B-1' to the Writ Petition respectively) in "The Daily Kaler Kantho" dated 26-1-2017 inviting fresh Expression of Interests (EOIs), non-communication of the reasons for cancellation of the Invitation For Proposal No. 1/ EOI/ SE/SRC/ 2014-2015 dated 29-9-2015 pursuant to the petitioner's application dated 12-1-2017 (Annexure-'M' to the Writ Petition) and failure of the respondent No. 11 to take any action in response to the petitioner's complaint dated 26-1-2017 (Annexure-'N' to the Writ Petition) should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and why the respondents should not be directed to approve the Combined Technical and Financial Evaluation dated 18-2-2016 (Annexure-F-1 to the Writ Petition) and award the contract in favour of the petitioner for the work covered under the Invitation For Proposal dated 29-9-2015 (Annexure-'D-1') within a stipulated period and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

3. In the Writ Petition No. 3636 of 2017, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the publication of a request for Expression of Interest (EOI) bearing Memo No. 1002 dated 22-2-2017 (Annexure-'A' to the Writ Petition) in "The Daily Jugantor" dated 24-2-2017 inviting a fresh Expression of Interest (EOI) in respect of Sherpur Bridge Toll Plaza should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and why the respondents should not be directed to approve the Combined Technical and Financial Evaluation dated 18-2-2016 (Annexure-T-1' to the Writ Petition) and award the contract in favour of the petitioner for the work covered under the Invitation For Proposal dated 29-9-2015 (Annexure-'D' to the Writ Petition) and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

4. The case of the petitioner, as set out in both the Writ Petitions, in short, is as follows:

The petitioner-company is a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1994. This company is the leading supplier, installer and operator of Computerized Toll System, Truck Scale, Gate Control & Security System, Weight in Motion System, RFID Human & Vehicle Access Control System and Design, Supply and Upgradation in Bangladesh. This company is also the market leader of Electronic Toll Collection System and Operation and Maintenance (ETC) for Roads & Highways of Bangladesh. 31. The case of the petitioner mainly rests upon three propositions, namely, malafides, violation of the principle of natural justice and legitimate expectation. Now let us examine the decisions of various jurisdictions on the signification and scope of the concepts of mala fides (bad faith), principle of natural justice and legitimate expectation.

32. In the decision in the case of Bangladesh Soya-Protein Project Ltd vs Secretary, Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka reported in 22 BLD (HCD) 378, it was spelt out in paragraph 23:

"23. Now let us first consider what is meant by the word 'legitimate expectation'. This phrase was first coined by Lord Denning in the case of Schmidt. vs Secretary of State for Home Affairs (1969) 2 Ch 149. The question, in that case, was whether the Home Secretary ought to have given a hearing to the foreign alien students before their prayer for extension of stay in the United Kingdom was refused. Lord Denning MR referring to the decision of the House of Lords in Ridge vs Baldwin (1964) AC 40 held at p. 170 EF as follows:

“....... an administrative body may, in a proper case, be bound to give a person who is affected by their decision an opportunity of making representations. It all depends on whether he has some right or interest, or, I would add, some legitimate expectation, of which it would not be fair to deprive him without hearing what he has to say."

33. But this phrase 'legitimate expectation' was limited at that time, first of all, to a legal right which was contravened. The legal position prevalent at that time was explained by Lord Denning himself referring to foreign alien students in the following manner at p.171AB:

"He has no right to enter this country except by leave: and, if he is given leave to come for a limited period, he has no right to stay for a day longer than the permitted time. If his permit is revoked before the time limit expires, he ought, I think, to be given an opportunity of making representations: for he would have a legitimate expectation of being allowed to stay for the permitted time. Except in such a case, a foreign alien has no right-and, I would add, no legitimate expectation-of being allowed to stay. He can be refused without reasons given and without a hearing."

34. The 'ratio decidendi' of this case shows, as explained by Lord Denning himself, that the legitimate expectation of a person can only be enforced if he has got a legal right, but not otherwise.

35. But there was already a change in the legal outlook which would be apparent from the decision in Reg vs Criminal Injuries Compensation Board, Ex Parte Lain (1967) 2 QB 864 where expectations which, although strictly speaking, were not legally enforceable but had some reasonable basis, were treated as legitimate expectations.

36. In the case of Findlay vs Secretary of State, (1984) 3 All ER 801, Lord Scarman, explained the principle of legitimate expectation, at p. 830B-C, in the following manner:

"The doctrine of legitimate expectation has an important place in the developing law of judicial review. It is, however, not necessary to explore the doctrine in this case, it is enough merely to note that a legitimate expectation can provide a sufficient interest to enable one who cannot point to the existence of a substantive right to obtain the leave of the Court to apply for judicial review."

37. In the case of Food Corporation of India vs M/s Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries, AIR '1993 SC 1601 in denying the highest tenderer's right to have his tender accepted, the principle of legitimate expectation was also considered by the Supreme Court of India. JS Verma, J. held as follows:

"There is no unfettered decision in public law: A public authority possesses powers only to use them for public good. This imposes the duty to act fairly and to adopt a procedure which is 'fair-play in action'. Due observance of this obligation as a part of good administration raises a reasonable or legitimate expectation in every citizen to be treated fairly in his interaction with the State and its instrumentalities, with this element forming a necessary component of the decision-making process in all State actions.

To satisfy this requirement of nonarbitrariness in a State action, it is, therefore, necessary to consider and give due weight to the reasonable or legitimate expectations of the persons likely to be affected by the decision or else that unfairness in the exercise of the power may amount to an abuse or excess of power apart from affecting the bona fides of the decision in a given case. The decision so made would be exposed to challenge on the ground of arbitrariness. Rule of law does not completely eliminate discretion in the exercise of power, as it is unrealistic, but provides for control of its exercise by judicial review. (Paragraph-7).

The mere reasonable or legitimate  expectation of a citizen in such a situation, may not by itself be a distinct enforceable right, but failure to consider and give due  weight to it may render the decision  arbitrary, and this is how the requirement  of due consideration of a legitimate  expectation forms part of the principle of nonarbitrariness a necessary concomitant of the rule of law. Every legitimate  expectation is a relevant factor requiring due consideration in a fair decision-making process. Whether the expectation of the claimant is reasonable or legitimate in the context is a question of fact in each case.  Whenever the question arises, it is to be determined not according to the claimant's perception but in larger public interest wherein other more important considerations may outweigh what would  otherwise have been the legitimate  expectation of the claimant. A bona fide decision of the public authority reached in this manner would satisfy the requirement of non-arbitrariness and withstand judicial scrutiny. The doctrine of legitimate expectation gets assimilated in the rule of law and operates in our legal system in this manner and to this extent." (Paragraph-8).

38. In the case of Union of India vs Hindustan Development Corporation, AIR 1994 SC 988, in order to create a healthy competition between the big manufacturers who formed a cartel and small manufacturers, the railway authorities introduced a dual pricing policy which was challenged. The Supreme Court of India in this case considered the question of legitimate expectation in detail referring to a number of decisions of home and abroad. K. Jayachandra Reddy, J. explained the principle as follows:

........ it is generally agreed that legitimate expectation gives the applicant sufficient locus standi for judicial review and that the doctrine of legitimate expectation is to be confined mostly to right of a fair hearing before a decision which results in negativing a promise or with-drawing an undertaking is taken. The doctrine does not give scope to claim relief straightaway from the administrative authorities as no crystallized right as such is involved. The protection of such legitimate expectation does not require the fulfillment of the expectation where an overriding public interest requires otherwise.

In other words, where a person's legitimate expectation is not fulfilled by taking a particular decision, then the decision-maker should justify the denial of such expectation by showing some overriding public interest.

Therefore even if substantive protection of such expectation is contemplated, that does not grant an absolute right to a particular person. It simply ensures the circumstances in which that expectation may be denied or restricted. A case of legitimate expectation would arise when a body by representation or by past practice aroused expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfil.

The protection of legitimate expectation is limited to that extent and a judicial review can be within those limits. But as discussed above, a person who bases his claim on the doctrine of legitimate expectation, in the first instance, must satisfy that there is a foundation and thus has locus standi to make such a claim. In considering the same, several factors which give rise to such legitimate expectation must be present. The decision taken by the authority must be found to be arbitrary, unreasonable and not taken in public interest. If it is a question of policy, even by way of change of old policy, the Courts cannot interfere with a decision.

In a given case, whether there are such facts and circumstances giving rise to a legitimate expectation, it would primarily be a question of fact. If these tests are  satisfied and if the Court is satisfied that a case of legitimate expectation is made out,  then the next question would be whether failure to give an opportunity of hearing before the decision affecting such  legitimate expectation is taken, has resulted  in failure of justice and whether on that  ground the decision should be quashed. If that be so what should be that relief is again a matter which depends on several factors."  (Paragraphs- 33 and 34).

39. The learned Judge then concluded as follows:

"However, it is generally accepted and also clear that legitimate expectation being less than right operate in the field of public and not private law and that to some extent such legitimate expectation ought to be protected, though not guaranteed." (Paragraph-35).

40. The principle of legitimate expectation again came up for consideration before the Supreme Court of India in the case of Madras City Wine Merchants Association vs State of TN, (1994) 5 SCC 509. S Mohan, J. held as follows:

"...... legitimate expectation may arise—

(a)	if there is an express promise given by a public authority; or

(b)	because of the existence of a regular practice which the claimant can reasonably expect to continue;

(c)	Such an expectation must be reasonable. However, if there is a change in policy or in public interest the position is altered by a rule or legislation, no question of legitimate expectation would arise." (Paragraph-48).

41. The Supreme Court of India again considered the principle of legitimate expectation in relation to a change of policy of the Government in the case of Punjab Communications Ltd vs Union of India, AIR 1999 SC 1813. M. Jagannadha Rao, J on consideration of a large number of cases observed as follows:

............ the doctrine of legitimate expectation in the substantive sense has been accepted as part of our law and that the decision-maker can normally be compelled to give effect to his representation in regard to the expectation based on previous practice or past conduct unless some overriding public interest comes in the way." (Paragraph-37).

42. In the case of Nur Muhammad vs Moulvi Mainuddin Ahmed, 39 DLR (AD) 1, their Lordships of the Appellate Division referred to the case of Federation of Pakistan vs Saeed Ahmed, PLD 1974 151(168) wherein Hamoodur Rahman, CJ expressed himself in the following terms:

"Indeed mala fide acts stand on the same footing as acts done without jurisdiction. Similarly coram non judice also stand on the same footing because these words would literally mean that they have been done by an authority or body exercising judicial or quasi-judicial powers which was not properly constituted even under the law under which it was set up and that its decision is not a decision of a competent authority. If this be so, then such acts do not also qualify for validation and they have not been saved from scrutiny by the ouster clause, no matter how widely that ouster clause may be worded."

43. A mala fide act is, by its nature, an act without jurisdiction. No Legislature when it grants power to take action or pass an order contemplates a mala fide exercise of statute. It may be explained that a mala fide order means one which is passed not for the purpose contemplated by the enactment granting the power to pass the order, but for some other collateral or ulterior purpose.

44. In the case of Mrs Lalima Begum vs The Chairman, 1st Court of Settlement, Dhaka, 17 BLD (HCD) 270 = 49 DLR 325, it was observed in paragraph 14:

"14. The principle of fairness in Government action requires that the Government functionaries must act according to law and must perform their duties in good faith. Public accountability and acceptance demand that the Government actions must correspond to good conscience and fair play..."

45. The principle of natural justice is applied to administrative process to ensure procedural fairness and to free it from arbitrariness. Violation of this principle results in jurisdictional errors. Thus in a sense, violation of this principle constitutes procedural ultra vires. It is, however, impossible to give an exact connotation of this principle as its contents are flexible and variable depending on the circumstances of each case, i.e., the nature of the function of the public functionary, the rules under which he has to act and the subject matter he has to deal with. This principle is classified into two categories-(i) a man cannot be condemned unheard (audi alteram partem) and (ii) a man cannot be the judge in his own cause (nemo debet esse judex in propria causa). The contents of the principle vary with the varying circumstances and those cannot be petrified or fitted into rigid moulds. They are flexible and turn on the facts and circumstances of each case. In applying the principle, there is a need to balance the competing interests of administrative justice and the exigencies of efficient administration. The principle was applied originally to courts of justice and now extends to any person or body deciding issues affecting the rights or interests of individuals where a reasonable citizen would have legitimate expectation that the decision-making process would be subject to some rules of fair procedure. These rules apply, even though there may be no positive words in the statute requiring their, application.

46. Lord Atkin in R. vs Electricity Commissioners ([1924] 1 KB 171) observed that the rules of natural justice applied to 'any body of persons having legal authority to determine questions affecting the rights of subjects, and having the duty to act judicially'. The expression 'having the duty to act judicially' was used in England to limit the application of the rules to decision making bodies similar in nature to a court of law. Lord Reid, however, freed these rules from the bondage in the landmark case of Ridge vs Baldwin ([1964] AC 40). But even before this decision, the rules of natural justice were being applied in our country to administrative proceedings which might affect the person, property or other rights of the parties concerned in the dispute. In all proceedings by whomsoever held, whether judicial or administrative, the principle of natural justice has to be observed if 'the proceedings might result in consequences affecting the person or property or other right of the parties concerned.

47. In England, the application of the principle of natural justice has been expanded by introducing the concept of 'fairness'. In Re Infant H(K) ([1967] 1 All ER. 226), it was held that whether the function discharged is quasi-judicial Or administrative, the authority must act fairly. It is sometimes thought that the concepts of 'acting fairly' and 'natural justice' are different things, but this is wrong as Lord Scarman correctly observes that the Courts have extended the requirement of natural justice, namely, the duty to act fairly, so that it is required of a purely administrative act (Council of Civil Service Union vs Minister for the Civil Service [1984] 3 All ER 935). The 'acting fairly' doctrine has at least proved useful as a device for evading, some of the previous confusions. The Courts now have two strings to their bow. An administrative act may be held to be subject to the requirements of natural justice either because it affects rights or interests and therefore involves a duty to act judicially, in accordance with the classic authorities and Ridge vs Baldwin; or it may simply be held that in our modern approach, it automatically involves a duty to act fairly and in accordance with natural justice. The Indian Supreme Court has adopted this principle holding "...... this rule of fair play, must not be jettisoned save in very exceptional circumstances where compulsive necessity so demands" (Swadeshi Cotton Mills vs India, AIR 1981 818).

48. The English Courts have further expanded the horizon of natural justice by importing the concept of 'legitimate expectation' and holding that from promise or from established practice, a duty to act fairly and thus to comply with natural justice may arise. Thus the concepts of 'fairness' and 'legitimate expectation' have expanded the applicability of natural justice beyond the sphere of right. To cite a few examples, not only in the case of cancellation of licence which involves denial of a right, but also in the case of first time grant of licence and renewal of licence, the principle of natural justice is attracted in a limited way in consideration of legitimate expectation. An applicant for registration as a citizen, though devoid of any legal right, is entitled to a fair hearing and an opportunity to controvert any allegation levelled against him. An alien seeking a visa has no entitlement to one, but once he has the necessary documents, he does have the type of entitlement that should now be protected by due process, and the Government should not have the power to exclude him summarily.

49. In the case of Chingleput Bottlers vs Majestic Bottlers reported in AIR 1984 SC 1030, the Indian Supreme Court has made certain observations which create an impression that the rules of natural justice are not applicable where it is a matter of privilege and no right or legitimate expectation is involved. But the application of the rules of natural justice are no longer tied to the dichotomy of right-privilege. It has been stated in "Administrative Law" by HWR Wade, 5th edition at page-465: "For the purpose of natural justice, the question which matters is not whether the claimant has some legal right, but whether the legal power is being exercised over him to his disadvantage. It is not a matter of property or of vested interests, but simply of the exercise of Governmental power in a manner which is fair. In the American jurisdiction, the right-privilege dichotomy was used to deny due process hearing where no right was involved. But starting with Gonzalez vs Freeman (334 F. 2d 570), the Courts gradually shifted in favour of the privilege cases and in the words of Professor Schwartz, "The privilege-right dichotomy is in the process of being completely eroded" ("Administrative Law", 1976, Page 230). Article 31 of our Constitution incorporating the concept of procedural due process, the English decisions expanding the frontiers of natural justice are fully applicable in Bangladesh.

50. In English law, the rules of natural justice perform a function, within a limited field, similar to the concept of procedural due process as it exists in the American jurisdiction. Following the English decisions, the Courts of this subcontinent have held that the principle of natural justice should be deemed incorporated in every statute unless it is excluded expressly or by necessary implication by any statute.

51. The basic principle of fair procedure is that before taking any action against a man, the authority should give him notice of the case and afford him a fair opportunity to answer the case against him and to put his own case. The person sought to be affected must know the allegation and the materials to be used against him and he must be given a fair opportunity to correct or contradict them. The right to a fair hearing is now of universal application whenever a decision affecting the rights or interest of a man is made. But such a notice is not required where the action does not affect the complaining party.

52. It is often said that mala fides or bad faith vitiates everything and a mala fide act is a nullity. What is mala fides? Relying on some observations of the Indian Supreme Court in some decisions, Durgadas Basu J held, "It is commonplace to state that mala fides does not necessarily involve a malicious intention. It is enough if the aggrieved party establishes: (i) that the authority making the impugned order did not apply its mind at all to the matter in question; or (ii) that the impugned order was made for a purpose or upon a ground other than what is mentioned in the order." (Ram Chandra vs Secretary to the Government of WB, AIR 1964 Cal 265).

53. To render an action mala fide, "There must be existing definite evidence of bias and action which cannot be attributed to be otherwise bona fide; actions not otherwise bona fide, however, by themselves would not amount to be mala fide unless the same is in accompaniment with some other factors which would depict a bad motive or intent on the part of the doer of the act" (Punjab vs Khanna, AIR 2001 SC 343).

54. The principle of reasonableness is used in testing the validity of all administrative actions and an unreasonable action is taken to have never been authorized by the Legislature and is treated as ultra vires. According to Lord Greene, an action of an authority is unreasonable when it is so unreasonable that no man acting reasonably could have taken it. This has now come to be known as Wednesbury unreasonableness. (Associated Provincial Picture vs Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223).

55. In the decision in the case of Sirajul Islam (Md) vs Bangladesh reported in 60 DLR 79, it has been held that the mere reasonable or "legitimate expectation" of a citizen, in such a situation, may not by itself be a distinct enforceable right, but failure to consider and give due weight to it may render the decision arbitrary, and this is how the requirement of due consideration of "legitimate expectation" forms part of the principle of non-arbitrariness, a necessary concomitant of the rule of law. Every "legitimate expectation" is a relevant factor requiring due consideration in a fair decision-making process. Whether the expectation of the claimant is reasonable or legitimate is essentially a question of fact in each case.

56. In the decision in the case of The Chairman, Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation vs Nasir Ahmed. Chowdhury reported in 22 BLD (AD) 199 = 7 BLC (AD) 144, it has been held that an expectation could be based on an express promise or representation or by an established past action of settled conduct and the representation must be clear and unambiguous. It could be a representation to an individual or generally to a class of persons. It has been further held in that decision that every such legitimate expectation does not by itself fructify into a right and therefore it does not amount to a right in the conventional sense.

57. In the case of Dhaka City Corporation vs Firoza Begum, 65 DLR (AD) 145 relied on by Mr Md Ramzan Ali Sikder, it was observed in paragraph 24(v):

"24.(v) A person basing his claim on the doctrine of legitimate expectation has to satisfy that he relied on the representation of the authority and the denial of that expectation would work to his detriment. The Court can interfere only if the decision taken by the authority is found to be arbitrary, unreasonable or in gross abuse of power or in violation of the principle of natural justice and not taken in public interest."

58. It has further been held in the above-mentioned case (65 DLR (AD) 145) that the root of the principle of legitimate expectation is constitutional principle of rule of law which requires regularity, predictability and certainty in the Government's dealing with the public.

59. In the case of the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works vs Md Jalil, 48 DLR (AD) 10 referred to by Mr Md Ramzan Ali Sikder, it was spelt out, amongst others, in paragraph 16:

"16 ..... The High Court Division could interfere with the findings of a Tribunal of fact under its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102, only if it could be shown that the Tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence/facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it had acted mala fide or in violation of any principle of natural justice..."

60. In the case of Star Enterprises vs City and Industrial Development Corporation of Maharashtra Ltd which was decided by the Indian Supreme Court on 30-5-1990 in Civil Appeal Nos. 2076-2078 of 1990, it was held in paragraph 10:

"10. In recent times, judicial review of administrative action has become expansive and is becoming wider day by day. The traditional limitations have been vanishing and the sphere of judicial scrutiny is being expanded. State activity too is becoming fast pervasive. As the State has descended into the commercial field and giant public sector undertakings have grown up, the stake of the public exchequer is also large justifying larger social audit, judicial control and review by opening of the public gaze; these necessitate recording of reasons for executive actions including cases of rejection of the highest offers. That very often involves long stakes and availability of reasons for any action on the record assures credibility to the action; disciplines public conduct and improves the culture of accountability. Looking for reasons in support of such action provides an opportunity for an objective review in appropriate cases both by the administrative superior and by the judicial process. The submission of Mr Dwivedi, therefore, commends itself to our acceptance, namely, that when the highest offers of the type in question are rejected, reasons sufficient to indicate the stand of the appropriate authority should be made available and ordinarily the same should be communicated to the concerned parties unless there be any specific justification not to do so."

61. In the case of Ram Pravesh Singh vs State of Bihar which was decided by the Supreme Court of India on 22-9-2006 in Case No. Appeal (Civil) 4191 of 2004 adverted to by Mr Md Ramzan Ali Sikder, the Indian Supreme Court spelt out in paragraph 14:

"14. What is legitimate expectation?  Obviously, it is not a legal right. It is an expectation of a benefit, relief or remedy that may ordinarily flow from a promise or established practice. The term 'established practice' refers to a regular, consistent, predictable and, certain conduct, process or activity of the decision-making authority.  The expectation should be legitimate, that is, reasonable, logical and valid. Any expectation which is based on sporadic or casual or random acts, or which is unreasonable, illogical or invalid cannot be a legitimate expectation. Not being a right, it is not enforceable as such. It is a concept fashioned by Courts, for judicial review of administrative action. It is procedural in character based on the requirement of a higher degree of fairness in administrative action, as a consequence of the promise made, or practice established.  In short, a person can be said to have a 'legitimate expectation' of a particular treatment, if any representation or promise is made by an authority, either expressly or impliedly, or if the regular and consistent past practice of the authority gives room for such expectation in the normal course. As a ground for relief, the efficacy of the doctrine is rather weak as its slot is just above 'fairness in action' but far below 'promissory estoppel'. It may only entitle an expectant: (a)' to an opportunity to show cause before the expectation is dashed; or (b) to an explanation as to the cause for denial. In appropriate cases, Courts may grant a direction requiring the Authority to follow the promised procedure or established practice. A legitimate expectation, even when made out, does not always entitle the expectant to a relief. Public interest, change in policy, conduct of the expectant or any other valid or bonafide reason given by the decision-maker, may be sufficient to negative the 'legitimate expectation'."

62. In the case of Dipak Kumar Sarkar vs State of WB which was decided by the Calcutta High Court on 5-12-2003 relied on by both Mr Khaled Hamid Chowdhury and Mr SM Zahurul Islam, the relevant portion of paragraph 6 runs as follows:

"6 ...... According to me, unless and until a contract exists, no right can be claimed by the participants in the tender. If any right in such circumstances arises, that will be governed by the civil laws. Therefore, where is the scope of intervention of the Writ Court? The Writ Court is only concerned in respect of the legitimate expectation or, at best, in a case of promissory estoppel. This is not a case of promissory estoppel. Therefore, it is necessary to know whether any legitimate expectation arises in the circumstances to get an affirmative order finally in the writ petition or not. Admittedly, when no work order has been issued, no such right can be accrued or can be attached to any right of contractual obligation....... "

63. In the case of Concord Pragatee Consortium Limited vs Bangladesh Power Development Board which was decided by the High Court Division on 5-2-2014 in the Writ Petition No. 2782 of 2013, it was observed in paragraph 60:

"60. Our above view should not be misunderstood to be a conservative stand as we are not curtailing the power of the High Court Division nor this judgment is aimed at reduction of the number of briefs of the members of this Bar. This Court in the past has never hesitated or shall not be shaky in the future to entertain writ petitions in fit and proper cases, for example, where an action taken or order passed by the Government or any statutory body or even by any Constitutional body that is ex-facie illegal, mala fide, or the same suffers from malice-in-law or coram non judice in carrying out its functions within administrative capacity, inspite of the existence of other alternative forums."

64. Ultimately the High Court Division in the aforementioned case held that the Review Panel is an equally efficacious forum for adjudication of the grievance of the petitioner and on that count, the Rule was discharged on the ground of incompetency of the Writ Petition.

65. In the case of PTR Exports (Madras) Pvt. Ltd. vs Union of India, AIR 1996 SC 3461 relied on by both Mr Khaled Hamid Chowdhury and Mr SM Zahurul Islam, it was observed in paragraph 5:

"5. It would, therefore, be clear that grant of licence depends upon the policy prevailing as on the date of the grant of the licence. The Court, therefore, would not bind the Government with a policy which was existing on the date of application as per previous policy. A prior decision would not bind the Government for all times to come.

When the Government is satisfied that change in the policy was necessary in the public interest, it would be entitled to revise the policy and lay down new policy.

66. The principle of legitimate expectation, as we see it, is predicated upon the following:

(a) The statement or practice giving rise to the legitimate expectation must be sufficiently clear 	and unambiguous, and expressed or carried out in such a way as to show that it was intended to be binding.

(b) The statement or practice must be shown to be applicable and relevant to the case in hand.

(c) Legitimate expectation is enforced in order to achieve fairness.

(d) If the statement said to be binding was given in response to any information from the citizen, it will not be binding if that information is less than frank, and if it is not indicated that a binding statement is being sought.

(e) He who seeks to enforce must be a person to whom (or a member of the class to which) the statement was made or the practice applied.

(f) Even though a case is made out, the legitimate expectation shall not be enforced if there is overriding public interest which requires otherwise.
