full_judgment:
This Rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure,1908 at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos.1 to 6 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 3-11-2003 passed by Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Naogaon in Title Appeal No. 12 of 2000 dismissing the appeal and affirming those dated 24-1-2000 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Court No.13, Naogaon in Other Class Suit No. 92 of 1990 should not be set aside and or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Short facts necessary for disposal of the instant Rule are that the petitioner as plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 92 of 1990 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Court No. 13, Naogaon praying for a decree of declaration of title and recovery of khas possession against the principal defendants and asserted that Mohor Chan Shah, Ful Chan Shah, Ray -Chan Shah, Rup Chan Shah and Pushpa Beoa were the original CS recorded owner of CS Khatian No. 134 which is described in "Ka" schedule, and the "Ka" schedule land along with another land was sold in auction in Execution Case No. 178 of 1933 in execution of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 3277 of 1932. Naogaon Co-operative Land Mortgage Bank Ltd purchased the "Ka" schedule property in auction and the said bank by registered deed dated 9-11-1938 sold the same to one Abdul Sardar @ Abdur Rahman, who subsequently transferred 271/2 decimals of land by registered deed dated 25-2-1944 in favour of one Abdul Hye who died leaving behind his only brother Mohammad Miah. Mohammad Miah subsequently died, leaving behind his only son Abdus Sukkur who sold 271/2 decimals of land by registered deed dated 7-5-1953 in favour of one Md. Warhead Hossain, who is the father of defendant No. 7, and SA Khatian No. 136 was prepared in the name of Md. Warhead Hossain, who died leaving behind his son Abdul Mazid (defendant No. 7) and daughter Mahbuba Bibi and RS record was prepared in their name. The defendant No. 7 obtained 20 decimals of land by amicable partition and by registered deed dated 28-4-1973 he transferred 20 decimals of land in favour of the plaintiff, and after purchase, the plaintiff took over possession of his 20 decimals of land. The defendants forcefully dispossessed the plaintiff from "ga" schedule property and hence the suit.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 to 6 entered an appearance in the suit by filing written statement and asserted that Md. Wahed Miah was the original owner of 42 decimals of the land of dag Nos. 651,652,653 and 654, and the concerned authority prepared SA Khatian No 136 and 137 in his name. Md. Wahed Miah died leaving behind his son Abdul Mazid and daughter Mahbuban Bibi and RS Khatian Nos. 24 and 25 were prepared in their name. Abdul Mazid transferred 3 decimals of land by registered deed No. 9438 and 9437 dated 19-7-1986. The defendant No. 7 by registered deed Nos. 9438 and 9437 sold 8 decimals of land to defendant No. 1, and 7 decimals of land to defendant No. 6, and 1 decimal of land to defendant No. 5 by 3 registered deeds of sale, all dated 19-7-1986. Defendant No. 5 constructed political office on his .01 acres of land and 7 decimals of the land of defendant No.6. Mahbuba sold her 14 decimals of land to defendant Nos. 8 to 10. Defendant No. 8 sold 1 (one) decimal of land to defendant No. 1. Defendant No. 7 constructed two shops on his 9 decimals of land. The defendants are possessing suit land by mutating their name. Defendant No. 7 did not sell the suit land to the plaintiff and he has no possession of the suit land for which the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. During the trial of the suit both parties adduced evidence in support of their respective cases and after concluding trial of the case, the Senior Assistant Judge, Court No. 13, Naogaon by its judgment and decree dated 244-2000 dismissed the suit.

5. Being aggrieved with and dissatisfied by judgment and decree dated 24-1-2000 passed by the trial Court, the plaintiff-petitioner filed Title Appeal No. 12 of 2000 in the Court of District Judge, Naogaon which was heard and disposed of by Joint District Judge, Court No. 3, Naogaon who after hearing the parties and on perusal of the records was pleased to dismiss the appeal by its judgment and decree dated 3-11-2003 against which the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner filed the instant civil revision and obtained the Rule.

6. No one appears on behalf of either party.

7. I have perused the revisional application, judgment and decree passed by the courts below and the evidence on records.

8. The main issue involved in the instant Rule as to whether the revisional court is legally competent to interfere with the concurrent finding of facts arrived at by the Courts below considering the material evidence on record.

9. On perusal of the impugned judgment and decree of the trial court, it appears that the trial Court dismissed the suit holding that admittedly Md. Wahed Miah was the original owner of the suit land and after his death his only son Md. Abdul Mazid (defendant No. 7) and daughter Mahbuban Bibi inherited the suit land and by amicable settlement, the defendant No. 7 obtained 20 decimals of land. The plaintiff in his evidence stated different dates as regards his dispossession from the suit land. Mozibur Rahman and Akkas who were present at the time of alleged dispossession were not examined by the plaintiff and the plaintiff totally failed to prove dispossession from the suit land.

10. On scrutiny of the evidence it appears that both the courts below after proper assessment of the evidence on record found that after purchase the plaintiff did not enter into possession of the suit land and failed to prove the date of dispossession, and concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the courts below as regards possession of the plaintiff cannot be set aside by the revisional court unless the revisional court found misreading and non-reading of material evidence on records which is material for proper and effectual adjudication of the material issue of the suit and the Courts below misdirected in passing the judgment and decree.

11. On perusal of the records, it appears that on 29-9-1986 the plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 263 of 1986 in the Court of Munsif, Naogaon and subsequently the said suit was renumbered as Other Class Suit No. 92 of 1990. In the plaint, the plaintiff stated that the cause of action of the suit is 26-8-1986. During the trial of the suit, PW 1 was examined on 29-3-1998, and PW 2 and 3 were examined on 3-6-1998. PW 1 stated that বেদখলের তারিখ ২৮-৪-১৯৭৩ (পরের তারিখ খেলাল নাই) ১১ বছর আগে বেদখল করেছে and PW 2 stated that বিবাদীরা বেদখল করেছে ১০ বছর আগে ভাদ্র মাসের ৯ তারিখে। ঘর দরজা করে বেদখল করেছে and PW 3 stated that বিবাদীরা জোর করে ঘর করেছে। ৭/৮ বছর আগে ভাদ্র মাসের ৮/৯ তারিখে।

12. On perusal of the evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 it appears that they have mentioned 3 different dates as regards dispossession of the plaintiff from the suit land and contradicted each other on material point. The suit was filed for declaration of title and recovery of possession and admittedly the defendants-opposite parties are in possession of the suit land. Since the plaintiff failed to prove his possession in and dispossession from the suit land by any reliable evidence, he is not entitled to get a decree of the declaration of title and recovery of possession.

13. Jurisdiction of the High Court Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been constructed several times by the Privy Council. In the year 1884, in the case of Raja Amir Hossain Khan vs Sheo Bakshay Singh, II I.A. 237, the Privy Council examined the provision of section 622 of the former Civil Procedure Code which substantially correspondence to section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and it has been observed as follows;

"Question before the High Court Division was whether the Subordinate Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction acted illegally, or with material irregularity. If it appeared that it had jurisdiction to decided the question before it, then it could decide it rightly or wrongly, and even if the court bellow decides the question wrongly, it could not be said that it acted illegally or with material irregularity"

14. The Privy Council, subsequently in the year 1917, in the case of Balakrishna Lldayar vs Vasudeva Aiyar, 44 IA 261 = 22 CWN 50 interpreted section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and held as follows;

"It may be observed that the section applies to the jurisdiction along the irregular exercise or non-exercise of it or the illegal assumption of it. The section is not directed against the emulation of law or fact in which the question of jurisdiction is not involved."

15. In the case of Joy Chand Lal Babu vs Kamalakaha Chowdhury, reported in 1 DLR 46, the Privy Council, in interpreting section 115 of the Code held as under;

"Although error in a decision of. the Subordinate Court does not by itself involve that it had acted illegally or with material irregularity so as to justify interference in revision under sub-section (c) nevertheless, if the erroneous decision results in the subordinate Court's exercising a jurisdiction not vested in it by law or failing to exercise a jurisdiction so vested, a case for revision arises under sub-section (a) or (b), and sub-section (c), can be ignored."

16. Our Apex Court in the Case of Ramjan Khan alias Ramjan Ali Khan vs Obaidul Haq Chowdhury, reported in 28 DLR (AD) 57, judgment was delivered by Justice Kemaluddin Hossain, concurred the above view of the Privy Council and observed as follows;

"High Court exercising its revisional jurisdiction under section 115 CPC cannot interfere with the decision of the subordinate court, unless it had exercised its jurisdiction not conferred by law or has failed to exercise jurisdiction so conferred upon it, or has acted illegally in the exercise of jurisdiction which mean that it has committed a breach of some provision of law, or with material irregularity in the exercise of its jurisdiction , which mean that it has committed some error of procedure during the course of trial and this breach or error has affected its ultimate exercise of jurisdiction. Except within this narrow ambit, the High Court has no power to interfere with the conclusion of the subordinate court either on a question of law or fact, however, profoundly it may differ the subordinate court."

17. In the case of Bangladesh vs Chan Mia, reported in 44 DLR (AD) .98 our Apex Court interpreted the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that case, it was observed as follows; "It was no function of the High Court Division to sit in appeal over that finding of the lower appellate Court in the revisional jurisdiction. The High Court Division was only concerned with the question as to whether the lower Court in giving that finding committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice."

18. In the case of Habibullah vs Sher Ali Khan, reported in 57 DLR (AD) 55 our Apex Court examined the power of the revisional Court and enunciated the principle as under;

"The High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment of the Courts below when the same has been made either upon misreading or non-reading or non-consideration of the material evidence and the said non-reading and non-consideration of the evidence caused failure of justice. The High Court Division is also competent to set aside the judgment of the lower appellate court when the same has been passed on the basis of evidence which cannot be considered legal evidence and had the same been not taken into consideration the judgment would not have been one as has been made."

19. In the case of Habibur Rahman Bhuiyan (Md) vs Gulman Begum, reported in 64 DLR (AD) 133 our Appellate Division settled the jurisdiction of the revisional court and it has

been observed as follows;

"When a finding of fact is based on consideration of the materials on record, those findings are immune from interference by the revisional court, except there is a non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence on record. The High Court Division has no jurisdiction to sit on appeal over a finding of fact"

20. In the case of Srinibash Mukhopadhyaya vs Elahi Haider, reported in 10 DLR 521 the High Court Division examined the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and it has been held as follows;

"The jurisdiction under section 115, Civil Procedure, is purely discretionary and it is to be exercised upon the same general principle upon which such discretionary orders are made"

21. In the case of Abdur Rahim vs Arifur Rahman, reported in 50 DLR 166 interpreted the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and it has been observed as follows;

"The scope of section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is now well settled. Consistent pronouncement by the highest Court of the country have made it abundantly clear that a court of revision under section 115(1) can interfere with the finding of fact as the final court of fact, only in exceptional circumstances when the findings are shockingly perverse or these are vitiated by non-reading or misreading of the material evidence or misconstruction of any important documents affecting the merit of the suit".

22. In the case of Nurjahan Begum vs Nur Rahman, reported in 59 DLR 98 High Court Division considered the view expressed by our Apex Court in 36 DLR (AD) 248 and it has been held as follows;

"It is an established principle of law that the revisional Court does not interfere with the concurrent finding of fact save in exceptional circumstances. The decision of our Apex Court has set limit of the revisional power our Appellate Division in the case of Santosh Kumar Chakraborty vs MA Motaleb Hossain, reported in 36 DLR (AD) 248 held that the High Court Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure only can interfere with the concurrent finding of the Courts below where it is found glaring misconception of law and non-consideration of material evidence."

23. In the case of Wazuddin vs Serajuddin, reported in 61 DLR 788, High Court Division examined the question of maintainability of the suit filed for declaration of title and recovery of possession and it has been held as follows;

"In a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession the plaintiff must prove his cause of action, in other words, his possession in and dispossession from the suit land in order to prove that the suit is within time".

24. In the case of Bangladesh, represented by the DC, Bogra vs Sudhir Chandra Nath, reported in 64 DLR 309 High Court Division constructed the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and it has been held as under;

"The well settled law is that unless there are gross misreading and non-consideration of material evidence on record or misconstructions of any document or the finding is perverse and contrary to law or evidence resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, the concurrent finding of fact cannot be interfered with by the revisional court."

<u>25. On a reading of the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it appears that if the judgment and decree are based on misreading and non-reading of the material evidence on record and the courts below misdirected in passing the judgment and decree, the High Court Division is empowered to exercise its jurisdiction. Where the subordinate Court has exercised jurisdiction not vested in it by law or has failed to exercise jurisdiction so vested or has acted in exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity then the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be properly invoked to satisfy itself the correctness or legality or propriety of any decision of the lower appellate Court, but to satisfy itself to the legality, propriety or correctness of the decision shall not act as an appellate Court to re-assess the evidence to arrive at its own finding or decision on fact.</u>

26. In the above facts and the circumstances of the case and on perusal of the evidence on records and the judgment and decree of the courts below, I am of the view that both the Courts below on proper assessment of the evidence on record arrived at a finding that the plaintiff failed to prove his possession in and dispossession from the suit land. Since this concurrent finding of fact is based on due consideration of the material evidence on records, this Court has no jurisdiction to interfere with the above concurrent finding of fact arrived at by the Courts below.

27. In view of the above, there is no merit in the Rule and the same is required to be discharged.

28. In the result, the Rule is hereby discharged.

29. Send down the LCR at once.

However, there shall be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Sikder Mahmudur Razi with Md Amirul Haq, Advocates ------ For the Petitioners. 
Ranjan Chakravorty Advocate ----- For the Opposite-Parties Nos. 2-3.
parties:
Syed Abul Kalam and another ------ Petitioners
Vs 
Syeda Khairunnesa and others ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Md Mozibur Rahman Miah, J: At the instance of plaintiff No. 2, this rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the Judgment and decree dated 7-5-2012 passed by the learned Special District Judge, Faridpur in Title Appeal No. 64 of 2010 dismissing the appeal and affirming the Judgment and decree dated 16-3-2010 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Faridpur in Title Suit No. 264 of 2009 dismissing the suit should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The salient facts leading to issuance of the rule are:

The present-petitioner No. 1 and another as plaintiffs originally filed a suit being Title Suit No. 130 of 1989 on 26-7-1989 in the court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Faridpur for declaration to the effect that, the registered deeds dated 18-7-1989 and 20-7-1989 executed and registered by the defendant No. 1 in favour of defendants No. 2-6 so mentioned in schedule "Ka and Kha" to the plaint are illegal, void, bassles, false and the same is not binding upon them with a further prayer that, the plaintiffs are entitled to 8 an a share to the land in question by way of partition (buy back) in -the form of preliminary and final decree under section 4 of the Partition Act so had been transferred to the defendants No. 2-6 measuring an area of 12 decimals of land.

3. The case of the plaintiffs as has been described in the plaint in short is that, One Sk Shahabuddin originally belonged to 7 decimals of land out of to 32 decimals of land of SA plot No. 29 and 5 decimals of land out of 18 decimals of plot No. 30 in total 12 decimals of land and SA khatian being khatian No. 320 was correctly prepared in his name. During enjoying title and possession over the said properties, Sk Shahabuddin transferred the said 12 decimals of land in favour of Syed Kashem Ali the predecessor of the plaintiffs and defendants No. 1,7,8 by registered kabala dated 19-11-1973 and accordingly he was inducted into possession by the said vendor. After the demise of said Kashem Ali, on 22-1-1978 the plaintiffs and the defendants No. 1, 7 and 8 inherited the same but the said properties were not partitioned through metes and bounds. It has also been stated in the plaint that, before partition, Kashem Ali had been residing in Murshidabad, India and serving in the postal department and after partition he gave option to live in this country and had since been residing in Faridpur. The plaintiff and the defendant No. 8 had been in service at different places of this country before the demise of their father, Syed Kashem Ali while the defendant No 1 along with defendant No. 7 had been residing in the disputed property in Faridpur. After defendant No. 7 got married to one, Syed Nurul Azim, the nephew of Syed Kashem Ali they started living in the suit land. However, in order to maintain the suit properties so left by Syed Kashem Ali, the plaintiff and defendants No, 7 and 9 executed and registered a power of attorney in favour of their mother, the defendant No. 1 on 15-3-1978. After that, the defendant No. 7 being emboldened with the advice of her husband and father-in-law started locking in to bickering with defendant No. 8 on various issues including transfer of 15 decimals of land by the defendant No. 1 in favour of defendant No. 7 and her husband at throw way price on 22-3-1979. For the sake of protecting the paternal property, the plaintiff No. 1 then appeared before the notary public, Dhaka on 7-5-1979 and that of the plaintiff No. 2 as 3-3-1981 respectively and revoked the said power of attorney they had executed and registered on 15-3-1978 and the notice of revocation was duly been served upon the defendant No. 1 that is, the mother 'of the plaintiffs and defendant No. 7 and 9. Subsequently, the defendant No. 1 informed the plaintiffs that, she transferred the suit land to the wife of one, Rais Uddin and the defendant No. 3-6 that is, sons of Rais Uddin. Having been informed, the plaintiff No. 1 then on 23-7-1989 obtained the certified copy of the alleged deeds and came to learn that the suit properties have been transferred in favour of defendants No. 2 and 3-6 in collusion with the husband of the defendant No. 7 and her father-in-law dated 18-7-1989 as well as 20-7-1989 allegedly exerting the authority so have been given through the power of attorney. It has further been stated in the plaint that, by virtue of the alleged deeds the defendants No. 2-6 never acquired any right, title and possession over the said suit property who are mere strangers in the suit land for which the plaintiffs are entitled to get their share in the suit properties on invoking the jurisdiction of section 4 of the Partition Act so left by their father, Syed Mokshed Ali. It has further been stated in the plaint that, the plaintiff No. 2 also revoked the power of attorney on 3-3-1981 which was duly conveyed to his mother, the defendant No. 1 on 6-3-1981 and the defendants No. 2-8 were quite aware of the said revocation and on such assertion, the plaintiff finally prayed for decreeing the suit.

4. The defendants No. 1-6 in order to contest the suit though filed a joint written statement but eventually they did not contest the said suit. The present-opposite party No. 1 who was 'defendant No, 7 only contested the said suit by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that, the husband of the defendant No. 1 that is, her father and that of the plaintiffs, Syed Kashem Ali was the national of Murshidabad, India and after partition he opted for the then east Pakistan and rolled in to this country and stated stayed in Faridpur and before setting for this country, Syed Kashem Ali handed over all his property of Murshidabad in favour of his two sons the defendants No. 8 and the plaintiff No. 2 who has been enjoying the same. It has further been stated that, Syed Kashem Ali had purchased lands in different Mouzas in Faridpur out of which he transferred 14/15 acres of land to defendant No. 1 by way of registered deed and handed over the same to the recipient No. 1 in exchange for paying her dower money. After the demise of Syed Kashem Ali, his successors executed and registered a power of attorney in favour of defendant No. 1 on 15-3-1978 stipulating some terms and -conditions therein. The plaintiffs did never reside in the' suit land and the defendant No. 7 used to take care of her mother. It has further been stated therein the written statement that, earlier the plaintiff No. 1 claimed to have got the suit land from his father for his Wife vide an "Osywatnama" and prayed for probate before the then learned Subordinate Judge, Faridpur without any knowledge the of the defendants No. 1 and 7 which was ultimately dismissed though exparte. The suit properties has duly been transferred in favour of the defendants No. 2-6 by the defendant No. 1 by registered kabalas dated 18-7-89 and 20-7- 1989 within the very knowledge of the plaintiffs and defendant's and the purchasers got possession therein accordingly. The defendant No. 7 subsequently purchased 10 decimals of land out of 12 decimals of land on 6-11-1983 from the defendants No. 2-6 within the knowledge of the plaintiffs and she had also been inducted into possession of the demised property. It has further been stated that, the plaintiffs have got no title and possession over the suit land and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs.

5. In view of the said pleadings, the suit was at first heard by the learned Assistant Judge, and by Judgment and decree dated 6-3-1997 the suit was decreed against the defendant No. 7. Against the said Judgment and decree, the defendant No. 7 then preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 33 of1997 and the said appeal was on transferred heard by the learned Additional. District Judge, Faridpur who allowed the same and sent back the case on remand to the trial court by his Judgment and decree dated 12-7-1999.

6. Challenging the said Judgment and decree of the appellate court below, the plaintiffs as petitioners then filed a Civil Revision being Civil Revision No. 213 of 2000 before this court and on the heels of an amicable settlement among the parties during pendency of the rule, the plaintiffs-petitioners then filed an application before this court for discharging the rule for non-prosecution. Accordingly, this court by Judgment and order dated 8-4-2008 discharged the rule for non-prosecution finding that, the parties to the rule have settled the dispute among themselves out of the court.

7. After the said disposal of the rule by this court, dated 8-4-2008, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Faridpur Sadar, Faridpur took up the matter for hearing. From Annexure-A-2 to the revision it reveals that, several dates have been fixed for hearing on the compromise petition so filed by the contending parties but eventually the said compromise could not be materialized for which the learned Senior Assistant Judge ultimately took up the said suit for dispose of on contest.

8. The learned Senior Assistant Judge then framed as many as 5 different issues. To prove the case, the plaintiff examined 5 witnesses while the defendant No. 7 examined 4 witnesses in support of their respective cases. Apart from that the contending parties also produced several documents which were also marked as exhibits.

9. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, on conclusion of 'the trial however dismissed the suit by his Judgment and decree dated 16-3-2010.

10. Challenging the said Judgment and decree so passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, the present-petitioners as appellants then preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 64 of 2010 before the learned District Judge, Faridpur. The said appeal was on transferred heard by the learned Special District Judge, Faridpur. The learned Judge, after hearing the parties to the appeal then dismissed the appeal and thereby affirmed the Judgment and decree so passed by the trial court consequent to dismissed the suit.

11. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the concurrent Judgment and decree so passed by the learned Judges of the courts below, the plaintiffs No. 1 and 2 as petitioners then came before this court and obtained the instant rule.

12. Mr Sikder Mahmudur Razi, along with Mr Muhammad Amirul Haq, the learned counsels appearing for the petitioners upon taking me to the revisional application, in particular, the grounds couched thereof, as well as other materials and evidence on record specially the revocation of power of attorney and the evidences so have been adduced by the plaintiff's and defendant's witnesses at the very outset submits that, as per exhibit-5, exhibit-"Ka" and "Ka-2" as well as written statement so filed by the defendants Nos. 1-6 it clearly shows that, the defendant No. 1 had duly received the notice of revocation' of the power of attorney executed on 15-3-1978 so served by the plaintiff-petitioner No. 1 by putting her signature on the notice having no ambiguity over receiving of the notice by the defendant No. 1.

13. The learned counsel next submits that, since at the relevant time of registering the power of attorney dated 15-3-1978 there had been no necessity for registration for the same though it was done so in case of revocation of the said power of attorney a notarial act is sufficient having no requirement of registering any registrar deed of revocation of power of attorney since it was not mandatory one.

14. The learned counsel goes on to submit that, the very provision so have been enunciated in Registration Manual specially paragraph No. 147 under chapter. No. 6, is not applicable in revoking the power of attorney executed by the plaintiffs on 7-5-1979 as well as 3-3-1981 in as much as the power of attorney was not authenticated one for which the very deed of revocation executed by the plaintiffs Nos. 1 and 2, the provision provided in paragraph No. 147 of the manual is not applicable.

15. Quoting the provision of section 32 and section 33 of the Registration Act, the learned counsel further submits that, mere giving authority to sell the property to the attorney is not sufficient rather the attorney should be abide by the recital of the said power of attorney as no where in the 'power of attorney' the principals has ever given authority to the agent/attorney (the defendant No. 1) to present the said sale deed before any registrar or sub-registrar and since there has been no such stipulation in the power of attorney, the very sale by the defendant No. 1 in favour of the defendants Nos. 2-6 was totally invalid transfer.

16. On pointing out the affidavit so accompanied with the alleged sale deeds dated .18-7-1989 and 20-7-1989 marked as exhibit Nos. 6 and 6A it also shows that, the Defendant No.1 executed those 2 deeds in her personal capacity as she sworn-in the said affidavit by not representing the principals (plaintiffs) of the power of attorney which is also clear violation of Article-4 of President's Order No. 142 of 1792 for which the said deed has not acted upon.

17. The learned counsel further submits that, inspite of the fact that the defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 7 refrained from appearing before the court to defend their assertion made in the written statement the husband of the defendant No. 7 represented those defendants in the suit which he cannot under the provision of section 120 of Evidence Act.

18. In support of his submission, the learned counsel then also placed his reliance in the decision reported in 4 BLC 195. Insofar as it relates to the authenticity of their 'revocation of power of attorney' dated 7-5-1979 as well as 3-3-1981, the learned counsel further submits that, even if the power of attorney dated 15-3-1978 is a registered one but there has been no hard and first rule or provision to revoke the said power of attorney by any registered instruments rather a simple notice by the principal is sufficient to revoke the said power of attorney and in support of his such assertion the learned counsel has also relied upon a decision reported in AIR 2004 Madraz.

19. By quoting the evidences of plaintiff's witnesses, the learned counsel further submits that, all the witnesses apart from the plaintiff No. 1 himself are disinterested witnesses who palpably supported the case of the plaintiffs with regard to the execution of the deed of revocation as well as holding possession in the suit properties. Out of those, PW 3 an Advocate who had relation with the defendant No. 1 and her husband supported the case of the plaintiffs.

20. Moreover, PW 4, the very attesting witness of the power of attorney and PW 5 the clark of the sub-registry office proved the 'power of attorney' so executed by the plaintiff No. 2 in favour of the plaintiff No. 1 giving authority to the plaintiff No. 1 to conduct the case on his (plaintiff No. 2) behalf which was also marked as exhibit-17 and that very PW 5 by producing the volume of the record also proved the power of attorney but none of the courts below have ever considered the said vital evidences the learned counsel further added.

21. By filing a supplementary affidavit dated 13-4-2017, the learned counsel for the petitioners submits that, the impugned Judgment and decree passed by the courts below is nothing but the product of non-reading and misreading of the evidence on record as well misquotation of the provision of law and therefore, both the courts below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of Justice in not considering the case of the plaintiffs in its proper prospective.

22. It has further been contended in the supplementary affidavit that, in the power of attorney dated 15-3-1978, there embodied no terms and conditions for transfer of the properties mentioned therein the deed on presenting it before any Sub-registry Office and therefore, the impugned transfer deeds are totally illegal and by said transfer no vested right has ever accrued upon its recipients.

23. It has further been contended in the supplementary Affidavit that, the impugned deeds dated 18-7-1989 and 20-7-1989 were not executed and registered on following the mandatory provision of law but this vital aspect has not been considered by the learned Judges while dismissing the suit.

24. It has lastly been contended that, the alleged power of attorney has been revoked by the plaintiffs on observing due process of law as notice was duly served upon its attorney that is the defendant No. 1 and the said attorney had received the said notice ceasing her authority to transfer the suit land. With such submission and basing on the decisions, the learned counsel finally prays for making the rule absolute.

25. Paradoxically, Mr Ranjan Chakravorty, the learned counsel appearing for the opposite parties No. 2-3 vehemently opposes the contention so have been taken by the learned counsel for the petitioners and contends that, since the power of attorney dated 15-3-1978 which was marked as exhibit-"Kha" by the defendant was a registered one so any revocation of the same should have to be made by a registered document.

26. The learned counsel next submits that, the petitioners has given much emphasis on the authentication of the power of attorney but since the power of attorney was registered one so there has been no necessity to authenticate it again. Giving reference to filing of the money suit No. 11 of 1981 the decree of which was marked as exhibit-"Ga" filed by the defendant No. 1, the learned counsel then avers that, the said decree obtained by the defendant No. 1 clearly proves that, the alleged deed of revocation executed by the plaintiffs No. 1 and 2 has not been acted upon because the money suit was decreed in her favour on 3-9-1982 though the alleged revocation was made in the year 1979 and 1981. In that regard, the learned counsel has placed his reliance in the decision reported in 38 DLR 240.

27. Drawing my attention to paragraph No. 147 and 148 of the Registration Manual, the learned counsel further submits that, the trial court has rightly disowned exhibit-6 and 6 the deeds of revocation of power of attorney as those documents has not been executed in compliance with the said Registration Manual.

28. Mr Chakravorty, further submits that, both the courts below by discussing all the plaintiff's and the defendant's witnesses very rightly came to a finding that, the alleged revocation has not been acted upon so there is no reason to declare the deeds so executed and registered by the Defendant No. 1 as illegal and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

29. The learned counsel next submits that, since the deeds of revocation has not been proved, so the plaintiffs were required to file a separate suit declaration that power of attorney is not binding upon them else, the suit in not maintainable in its present from.

30. The learned counsel further submits that, since the plaintiffs have utterly failed to adduce the plaintiff No. 2 or any witness to prove his (plaintiff No. 2) existence in thus country and that of his alleged signature put in the revocation deed, the revocation alleged to have been executed by him cannot be sustained.

31. The learned counsel by showing the signature appears in the alleged notice revoking the power of attorney (Exhibit-5) submits that, since there is no signature alleged to have been put by the defendant No. 1 on it so it clearly proves that, the said notice was manufactured one and produced before the court in an afterthought manner. At the midst of passing of the Judgment, the learned counsel for the opposite parties produced some papers showing that the subsequent transferees from the defendant No. 1 have also mutated their respective name in the khatian and paid rent in their name.

32. In countenance of his submission, the learned counsel has also relied on some decisions reported in 5 BLT (AD) 135 = 49 DLR (AD) 96 as well as 7 BLT (AD) 7. Apart from that, the learned counsel has also placed his reliance in the decisions reported in 21 BLD (AD) 157 = 54 DLR (AD) 7, 5 KC 14 as well as 26 BLD 271.

33. I have heard the learned counsels for the contending parties, perused the revisional application in particular, the grounds taken thereof as well as the supplementary affidavit so filed by the petitioners and the evidences adduced by the parties and considered the submission so advanced at the bar. In view of the submission and counter submission of the learned counsel it appears to me that, the bone of contention among the parties revolves around the very deeds of revocation of power of attorney though with regard to the execution and registration of the power of attorney there has been no dispute among the parties. The main dispute among the parties is whether the very revocation of power of attorney so furnished by the plaintiff No. 1 dated 7-5-1979 as well as plaintiff No. 2 dated 3-3-1981 has at all been accomplished in accordance with law or not.

34. In order to arrive at a decision with regard to the effectiveness of those deeds of revocation of power of attorney I seem it proper to go through the power of attorney first in particular, the very preamble of the same recital of which runs as follows:

"Since we brothers and sister almost always remain outside from this place on our respective place of business and service and as we are unable to maintain and look after the property, make, constitute and appoint our widow mother Mst. Ashrafunnessa wife of late Syed kashem Ali of Guhelaxmipur, PO & Dist. Faridpur, our true and lawful attorney, for us, in our name and on our behalf to grant leases upon such terms and conditions and in such manner as she shall think proper in respect of the house and property, which now do or hereafter shall belong to us or wherein were or any person or persons or body or bodied politic or corporate, in trust for us, now have or has or hereafter shall or may have any title or interest whatsoever, or which we hold or shall hereafter hold in trust for any person or persons or body or bodies politic or corporate whomsoever."

35. So on going through the said of power of attorney it shows that, the principals, in other words 3 sons of defendant No. 1 since had been residing at various parts of the country so for the proper management and maintenance of the suit properties, they had given the authority to their mother to oversee the property in their absence. Incidentally, in the power of attorney there had been given an authority to transfer the property mentioned in the deed though fact remains, in that power of attorney, there has been no stipulation about revocating the power of attorney. The dispute arose for revoking the said power of attorney moment the defendant No. 1 brought her daughter the defendant No. 7 in her house and transferred some of the property in her favour (daughter) apart from the suit property. Subsequently, on exerting authority, the defendant No. 1 even transferred the suit properties in favour of the defendants Nos. 2-6 who are quite strangers to the suit property. So, it is clear that, there had been a long drawn intention of the defendant No. 1 to transfer the suit property in favour of her daughter, the defendant No. 7. And the said desire was however materialized subsequently a transferring the suit land (101/2 decimals) by those defendants Nos. 2-6 to defendant No. 7 on 7-11-1993.

36. Now the crux of the dispute among the parties revolves around the legal basis of the said revocation of the power of attorney as the opposite parties challenged the legality of the alleged revocation so made by way of a 'declaration' sworn-in before a Notary Public. As I have earlier stated that, there has been no stipulation in the power of attorney authorising the principal to revoke the power of attorney but as per the registration manual that is, in Paragraph No. 147 there has been outlined some procedure for revocation of power of attorney where there has been no mention that a power of attorney should have to be registered one. Rather, it has stipulated therein that, a power of attorney must be authenticated one. In that regard, the learned counsel for the opposite parties contends that, since the power of attorney through which the defendant No. 1 was given the authority to sell the property so by virtue of the said authority, she transferred the suit property having no illegality in it rather it was done in line with the authority outlined in the power of attorney. But on the contrary, it is the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioners that, since the power of attorney is not authenticated one either by any Magistrate or by a notary public, so there has been no necessity to register the said "deed of revocation."

37. Now, the question crops-up whether the notice of the said revocation has duly been served upon the agent that is, the defendant No. 1. It is the contention of the learned counsel for the opposite parties that, since there has been no signature of defendant No. 1 on the said notice of revocation (exhibit-5) so it clearly proves, no notice had ever been served upon the defendant No. 1 before executing and registering disputed two deeds in question. But on the other hand, the learned counsel for the petitioners submits that, in the exhibit-5 there has been a signature with date put by the defendant No. 1 on the right hand side of the said notice which was also asserted by the plaintiff no.1 while he deposed as PW 1 which was not controverted by cross examining him.

38. In order to have a clear idea about the legal necessity of registering a deed of revocation I feel it expedient to reproduce paragraph no-147 and 148 so outlined in the registration manual. In Paragraph 147 of part-VI the following procedure has been provided:

147. Revocation of powers: A principal desiring to revoke an authenticated power should, if it is available, produce it before the registering officer with an application in order to get it cancelled. The Registering officer should then enter in red ink the words "power revoked, see page of the file of revocation of powers" above the original entry in the register of power of attorney authenticated and also on the power itself, if it is presented with the application. The date and signature of the registering officer should invariably be given in such cases.

148. Procedure of receipt of application for or notice of revocation of powers— Each registering officer shall place in a file all applications for, or notices of revocation of power of attorney whether authenticated in his office or in any other office. The date of receipt and the signature of the registering officer shall be written across the notice a copy of the notice or application should be exhibited on the notice-board of the office. The registering officer may also keep a list of all revoked powers before him for ready reference, so as to make sure whether any such power of attorney has become inoperative or not.

39. As has been stated earlier that, in those two paragraphs, just procedure has been enunciated as regards to revocation of power of attorney in where I do not find, the revocation will have to be registered one though emphasis was given that, a power of attorney must be authenticated one. Since it is admitted that the power of attorney is not authenticated one, so there has been no necessity to present the said deed of revocation for registration.

40. So far as regards to giving effects of a sale deed' by the defendant No. 1 who is the agent of the principal, the procedure has also been laid down in sections 32 and 33 of the Registration Act. For the convenience of understanding, I also reproduce the said sections here which runs as under

Section: 32—

Persons to Present documents for registration—"Except in the cases mentioned in section 89, every document to be registered under this Act, whether such registration be compulsory or optional, shall be presented

(a) by some person executing or claiming under the same, or, in the case of a copy of a decree or order, claiming under the decree or order, or

(b) by the representative or assign of such person, or (c) by the agent of such person, representative or assign, duly authorized by power-of-attorney executed and authenticated in the manner hereinafter mentioned."

"Section: 33—

Power of attorney recognizable for purposes of section-32 (1) For the purposes of section 32, the following powers-of-attorney shall alone be recognized, namely:—

(a)	if the principal at the time of executing the power-of-attorney resides in any part of (Bangladesh) in which this Act is for the time being in force, a power-of-attorney executed before and authenticated by the Registered or Sub-Registrar within whose district or sub-district the principal resides;

(b)	if the principal at the time aforesaid resides in any other part of (Bangladesh) a power-of-attorney executed before and authenticated by any Magistrate;

(c) if the principal at the time aforesaid does not reside in (Bangladesh) a power-of-attorney executed before and authenticated by a Notary Public, or any Court, Judge, magistrate, (Bangladesh) Counsel or Vice-Counsel or representative of the Government."

41. In section 32 of the Registration Act, there are as many as three clauses that is clause (a), (b) and (c) out of which Clause-(c) is important here to adjudicate the instant rule. In Clause-(C) it has been stipulated that:

(c) by the agent of such person, representative or assign, duly authorized

by power-of-attorney executed and authenticated in the manner hereinafter mention.

Whereas in section 33 there has been also 3 Clauses-namely (a), (b) and (c) out of which Clause-(b) is pertinent here. In clause (b) it has been stipulated that:

(b) if the principal at the time aforesaid reside in any other part of Bangladesh, a power-of-attorney executed before and authenticated by any Magistrate.

42. So from those provision enshrined in Registration Act, as well as the Registration Manual it appear to me that, a power-of-attorney must be authenticated either by a Sub-registrar or by a Magistrate.

43. Now question remains, whether the notice of revocation by the plaintiffs Nos. 1 and 2 has at all been served upon the defendant No. 1 that is the mother of the plaintiffs Nos. 1 and 2, 7 and 8. It is true, a signature was put in the said notice by, Ashrafunnessa, the defendant No. 1 but there has been no date beneath her signature and signature was put in the right side of the notice.

44. It is the contention of the learned counsel for the opposite parties that, since the defendant No. 1 did never put any signature and that very notice has subsequently been manufactured only to file the instant suit. But it has to be seen, whether that very signature put on the notice has got any resemblance with her admitted signature put in other documents. In that posture, learned counsel for the petitioners draws my attention to other documents where the signature of the defendants No. 1 appeared. In doing so, the learned counsel placed before me exhibit-'Ka', `Ka'-1, 'Ka-2' and the written statement jointly filed by the defendants Nos. 1- 6 where the signature of the defendant No. 1 appeared. In order to verify the submission advanced by the learned counsel for the petitioners, I myself examine and compare the signature so appeared in the notice with those of the documents produced and 1 find that, all the signature put by the defendant No. 1 are of same.

45. Now question may arise, whether that very notice was served before executing and registering the disputed deeds or not. In that regard, I have also perused the deeds of revocation which were marked by the plaintiffs as of exhibits-6 and 6-A, From exhibit-6, the revocation of power-of-attorney dated 5-5-1979 I find it accompanied by a notarial certificate which proves that, the revocation deed is authenticated one.

46. Moreover, since those documents (Deed of revocation) were marked as exhibit no-6 and 6-1 without any objection on the part of the defendants when it was taken into evidence so the defendants cannot raise any question about the authenticity of those revocation deeds as well as notice of revocation so served upon the defendant No. 1.

47. So far as regards to the revocation made by Syed Abu Saleh, the plaintiff No. 2, the notice of such very revocation has not been served upon the defendant No. 1 because there has been no endorsement of the defendant No. 1 on that notice. Though the revocation deed was marked as exhibit-6A even though the very 'notice' of said revocation has not been marked as exhibit rather it was kept with the record.

48. Now let me peruse the evidence so given by the plaintiffs No. 1 as PW 1 who in his examination in chief stated as follows:

ফলে আমার মাতার বরাবরে দেওয়া power of attorney রদ রহিত করি power of attorney রদ রহিত করনের কপি আমার মাতাকে প্রদান করি আমার মাতা উহার কপি প্রাপ্ত হইয়া প্রাপ্তি স্বীকার পত্র সহ করিয়াছেন।

49. This very PW 1 has extensively been cross examined by the defendant No. 7 by putting some questions against which the said PW 1 made the following reply:

"Power of attorney বাদীর নোটিশ মার কাছে আমি নিজে নিয়ে গিয়াছি।বাতিলের সময় আমি উপস্থিত ছিলাম। আর কে কে ছিল স্মরণ নাই। দুই power of attorney বাতিলের নোটিশ ছিল এম এ. রেজা লেখা হয়েছিল ০৭.০৫.১৯৭৯ইং তারিখে (আমারটা) ২নং বাদীর বাতিল দর্শানোর লেখক ছিল এম.এ. রেজা এবং ৩-৩-১৯৮১ইং তারিখে লেখা হয়। দলিলে কে কে স্বাক্ষী বলতে পারবোনা উক্ত উভয় বাতিল দলিলের কোন স্বাক্ষীদের আমি মামলায় স্বাক্ষী মানিনী।

50. So from the above cross examination by the defendant No. 7 it has established that, the said notice was served upon the mother of the plaintiffs Nos. 1 and 2. In the plaint since the plaintiffs did not claim that the said notice had been served upon their mother in presence of some witness to prove the service of notice upon the defendant No. 1, so the question about the presence of any witnesses while the said notice was served upon the defendant No. 1 does not arise.

51. So far as regards to the holding of possession in the suit land the plaintiff No. 1 as PW-1 in his chief clearly stated that:

নালিশী বাসা বাড়ীতে আমি স্ব-পরিবারে থাকিতেছি অপর একজন ভাড়াটিয়া নালিশী বাড়ীতে আছে এবং বাদীদের অংশের আটআনা সাহাম দাবী করিতেছি।

52. That very assertion of residing in the Suit properties by the plaintiff No. 1 could not be controverted by the defendant No. 7 by cross examining the plaintiff No. 1. Even, all the 3 witnesses of the plaintiffs who are the adjacent land, owners and out of whom the pw-3 is an Advocate who are related with the family of the plaintiffs and defendant No. 1 in his respective deposition clearly mentioned that, he came to learn that the plaintiffs Nos. 1 and 2 revoked the power of attorney. In that regard, the learned counsel for the opposite parties asserts that, since they are all hearsay witness so their testimony cannot be believable. But the said assertion of the learned counsel for the opposite parties has got no substance in view of the fact that, the plaintiff did not claim that at the time of revoking the power of attorney those very PWs were present.

53. Now let me revert to the Judgment passed by the learned Judges of the courts below. While disposing of the suit, the learned Assistant Judge has taken 3 issues altogether for adjudication that is, issue Nos. 1, 4 and 5 and the learned Senior Assistant Judge, upon discussing the materials and evidence on record found all the three issues in favour of the defendant. But adjudicating all those three issues together is clearly contrary to the provision of Order XX, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Because, at one place of the Judgment, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, came to a conclusion stating that: "from the scrutinized of the deposition of PW-1 and 5 it is clear that the alleged revocation deed dated 7-5-1979 and 3-3-1981 so exhibited as 6 and 6A cannot sustain as those did not corroborate by each other."

54. As I observe above, plaintiff did not claim that any witness was present at the time of revocation of power of attorney rather what the pws stated they heard the very fact from the plaintiffs. And what they heard has just expressed in their respective deposition having no reason to disbelieve the said testimony of the plaintiff's witnesses and so, the observation of the learned trial court has got no legal substance.

55. On the other hand, the learned Special District Judge, while affirming the Judgment of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, has made some absurd observation with regard to the revocation of Power of attorney and is not going through the respective provision of Power of Attorney Act 1882. Though very erroneously found the provision of section 2(44) in it, though on going through the said Act, I do not find there has been any subsection 44 in section 2 of the said Power Attorney Act.

56. Curiously enough, both the court below in their respective Judgment left some portions blank which are evident at Page No. 90 of the trial court's Judgment as well as Page Nos. 64 and 65 of the appellate court's Judgment which is not desirable from a judicial officer. So the Judgment pronounced by the learned Judges of the courts below giving some absurd proposition in their respective Judgment simply cannot be sustained.

57. Further, It has been stated hereinabove that, initially the suit was decreed in favour of the plaintiffs-petitioners and in the appeal the suit was sent back to the trial court against which the plaintiffs filed a revision before this court. And upon an amicable arrangement, among the parties the plaintiffs-petitioners deemed it wise to pray for discharging the rule to usher an amicable settlement among the parties and in view of such understanding, the plaintiffs-petitioners then filed an application for discharging the rule for non-prosecution. And in Paragraph No. 2 of that very application they clearly stated that, the brother and sister came to an amicable settlement out of the court for which they would no longer proceed with the rule and they prayed for discharging the rule and in view of the said application (Annexure-A to this revision) this court by order dated 8-4-2008 discharged the rule for non-prosecution. Even in the body of the order this court also mentioned about the settlement among the parties .out of the court. And subsequently, from Annexure-A2 to this revision it clearly shows that, the plaintiff. petitioners had taken all out initiative to settle the dispute among the brothers and sister out of the court but eventually, that cannot be materialized due to the inaction of defendant No. 7.

58. Now, let me go through the decision so have been placed before me by the learned counsel for the petitioners. In the decision so have been reported in 1981. BLD (AD) 86 = 33 DLR (AD) 124 it has been propounded as under:

"Power of attorney-it registration contention that a power of attorney empowering a person to execute a deed of transfer of immovable property requires registration is not tenable as a power of attorney executed in terms of Registration Act or under other provisions of law which confers a valid power on the attorney to act as an agent for the principal does not require registration except that its authentication under the law is necessary.

59. So in the cited decision, it has been settled that, the power of attorney has to be authenticated one. The learned counsel has then placed his reliance in the decision reported in 4 BLC 195 whether it has been held as under:

A person not a party to the suit nor a husband nor a wife nor an attorney got no authority to give testimony in a suit supporting the case either of the plaintiff or of the defendant. The PW 1 deposed in the suit as son for the plaintiff the mother. The PW-1 was neither a party to the suit nor was an attorney on the basis of the power executed by the plaintiff in his favour to give testimony on her behalf in support of the plaint case and hence the PW1 was an incompetent person to give testimony on behalf of the plaintiff in support of the plaint case which stands disproved.

60. By citing the decision, the learned counsel for the petitioner tried to impress before this court that, since DW 1 who happens to be the husband of Defendant No. 7 was not a party to the suit and having not given any authority to act on behalf of the case of the defendant No. 7 so his very testimony in support of the defendant No. 7 cannot be taken into consideration.

61. The learned counsel next placed his reliance in a decision reported in AIR 424 Madraj where it has been held that:

"Cancellation of power of Attorney by plaintiff by a 'notice' to a agent was valid since document was not coupled with interest concurrent finding of Lower Courts that, Power of Attorney and sale deed executed in pursuance thereof was invalid-proper."

62. In that regard though the learned counsel for the opposite parties contents that, that very decision reported in AIR 2004 Madraj is not applicable, because the facts stated therein is totally different with that of the facts described in the instant case. But on going through the ratio so settled in the said decision, I find that since from Paragraph-147 there having no provision to register a "deed of revocation" so mere giving a "notice" by the principal to its attorney is suffice to cancel the power of attorney. And lastly, the learned counsel has placed his reliance in the decision reported in 50 DLR 156. In that decision, it has been settled the provision of section 4 of the Partition Act which reads as follows:

"The stranger purchaser will not acceptable in other members of the family cannot come into the undivided dwelling house and possess it forcibly and section 4 of the of the Partition Act does not permit it.

<u>63. On close examination of the said decision, I find that, since the suit properties belonged to both the plaintiffs and the defendants and the said property has subsequently been transferred to defendants Nos. 2-6 who were admittedly strangers, so for the protection of the interest of a joint family, any member can seek partition of the undivided land through buy back and that very decision is quite applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case of the plaintiffs.</u>

64. Now let me perused the decision so have been relied upon by the learned counsel for the opposite parties. The learned counsel for the opposite parties at first placed his reliance in the decision reported in 26 BLD (AD) 271 which was given on the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. I have gone through the decision and in that decision, a deed of gift was given in favour of the plaintiff by the donor and subsequently the said donor cancelled the said deed of gift. The facts so have been described in the cited decision appears to be quite distinguishable with 'the facts of the instant case because in the instant case no deed of gift among the parties has been executed rather the plaintiffs has just prayed for declaration that the deed so have been executed in favour of 2-6 is not binding upon them so, no question of giving possession is here.

65. The learned counsel for the opposite parties also placed his reliance in the decision reported in 38 DLR 240 where the provision of sections 33 and 85 of the Registration Act have been discussed where it has been propounded that, though the deeds have not been authenticated by any Notary Public but when it was duly executed and registered would be termed as valid document and acceptable in law. This very contention has not been disputed here rather the disputed question before me is whether the revocation made by the plaintiffs Nos. 1 and 2 is valid or not.

66. The point decided in the above cited decision has not been attracted with the facts and circumstances of the instant case because the question of revocation has not been discussed in the cited decision.

67. The learned counsel has also placed his reliance in a decision reported in 21 BLD (AD) 157 = 54 DLR (AD) 7. I do not find how that very decision can be applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. Because, the petitioners have just sought declaration about the propriety of two deeds which have been executed and registered by the defendant No. 1. So that very decision is not applicable in the instant case rather it totally goes favours the case of the plaintiffs because they have rightly sought declaration challenging the veracity of the said 2 deeds.

68. The learned counsel has lastly placed his reliance in the decision reported in 5 BLC 14. In the said decision it has been held as under:

"In the present case from the recital of the power of attorney it appears that the agent himself has an interest in the property and hence such agency cannot be revoked unilaterally to the prejudice of such interest.

69. Perhaps, the learned counsel could not comprehend what is the claim of the plaintiffs in the suit. In the instant suit the plaintiffs -plainly claimed title so far as to regards to their respective share in the suit properties so there has been no occasion for the plaintiffs to claim the ownership of the properties so held by the defendant No. 1 herself. That very cited decision is also contrary to the case of the defendant because the plaintiffs Nos. 1 and 2 revoked the power rested upon the Defendant No. 1 so far as regards to their interest in the suit properties concerned not other co-sharer including their sister, defendant No. 7 it held in the suit lands. So in that regard, the agent or the attorney, defendant No. 1 has got no occasion to be prejudiced in respect of her share of land.

70. As I have stated earlier that, while passing the Judgment, the learned counsel for the opposite parties has produced some documents showing that, the subsequent transferees has mutated their name in the khatian as well as are paying rent of their purchased property. Though the learned counsel did not explain as to what presented them to produce those documents during the appeal. This court simply cannot evaluate these very documents at that stage as none of those ever produced before the courts below and for that reason, I do not find any reason to accept those documents.

71. Before parting with this Judgment, I must say that, it is the defendant that is defendants Nos. 1 and 7 upon whom the onus was shifted to prove that the 'notice' which was marked as Exhibit-5 has not been served upon defendant No. 1 but they have miserably failed to discharge such onus nor the DW 1 can be authorised to represent the defendants No. 1 and 7 in the suit.

72. Moreover, it is not the case of the defendants that during the trial or during the appeal the defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 7 were not in this contrary. So it is the defendant No. 1 who is liable to disprove her signature on exhibit-5 but the defendant No. 1 has palpably failed to discharge her onus.

73. On the other hand, the defendant No. 7 during pendency of the appeal has transferred the suit property to respondents Nos. 16-17 vide registered kabala dated 22-3-2012 which clearly exemplify that, in a malafide intention the defendant Nos. 1 and 7 only in order to deprive the plaintiffs from enjoying their inherited property transferred the lands.

74. Then again, there is no explanation on the part of the defendant No. 7, the circumstances that prevented her to appear before the court and give testimony in favour of her mother as well as for herself. The manner of the defendant No. 7 and defendant 1 clearly signify that, it is no one but the husband of the defendant No. 7 who deposed as DW 1 was the root of all evils who orchestrated all the design to destroy the family bondage among the plaintiffs and the defendants Nos. 7, 8 and 9.

75. On the aforesaid discussion and observation I find that though the plaintiff No. 1 has been able to prove his case by serving the notice of revocation of the power of attorney upon the defendant No. 1 but the plaintiff No. 2 has failed to prove that the notice of his revocation has ever been served upon the defendant No. 1 although, it is the contention of the plaintiff No. 1, that vide a "power of attorney" so executed by the plaintiff No. 2 which was marked as exhibit-17 he was authorized to conduct the case on his behalf and he (plaintiff No. 2) has been residing in Kustia for his own business. But that very facts cannot be substantiated by any independent witnesses. Had it been the case, then I am of the view that, the plaintiff No. 2 failed to prove that the defendant No. 1 was aware of his revocation of power of attorney.

76. Regard being had to above the facts and circumstances, the rule so far as regards to the petitioner 1 succeeds.

77. Resultantly, the rule is made absolute-in-part.

78. The case of the plaintiff-petitioner No. 1 has been proved. Hence, the plaintiff-petitioner No. 1 is entitled to inherit the property so left by his father, Late Syed Kashem Ali and to get his due share through partition.

79. Accordingly, the deeds dated 18-7-1989 and 20-7-1989 so far as it relates to the share of the petitioner No. 1 in the said two deeds is declared illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff-petitioner No. 1.

80. The Defendants-opposite parties are thus directed to apportion due share to the petitioner No. 1 amicably within 60 days from the date of receipt of this judgment by the trial court in default the petitioner No. 1 is at liberty to get his share through process of the court.

81. The judgment and decree so passed by the courts below is set aside and the suit is decreed in part.

Let a copy of this Judgment along with lower court records be sent to the court concern at once.

End.
